The answer is simple: As long as the task is assigned to a local variable (in a live stack frame), the garbage collector sees it as reachable, and hence the object never ends up on the finalization queue. Of course, if we assign `null` to variable `t`, or quit from the method without retaining the reference to the task (either by returning, assigning it to a field, or whatnot), the task is unreachable again, and the behavior from [Figure 30.4](#part0040.html_ch30fig04) comes back.

In short, if you can handle exceptions meaningfully, never forget to put in place code that does so, either by waiting for the task or setting up a continuation.

##### The UnobservedTaskException Event

There’s another way to deal with unhandled task exceptions at a global level. The `TaskScheduler` type, which represents the default scheduler used by the TPL, exposes a static event called `UnobservedTaskException`, where you can still handle such exceptions as a last resort:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_017.html_p1529pro02)

TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException += (sender, e) => {
    e.Exception.Flatten().Handle(ex => {
        // Try to handle the exception, returning true or false.
    });

    // If we get here, we can tell the TPL not to "escalate" on the finalizer.
    e.SetObserved();
};

Personally, I believe it’s rather unlikely and superhuman if you can meaningfully recover from unhandled exceptions without knowing the bigger context of from where the error originates. If you think you can, this event might prove useful, though.

##### Unhandled Exceptions in .NET 4.5

Starting with .NET 4.5, the default behavior of the TPL has changed with regards to unhandled exceptions. This change was motivated by the new asynchronous programming features that rely on the `Task` and `Task<T>` types to represent asynchronous operations. We’ll talk much more about those features in [Chapter 31](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31), but here is a little example showing the use of `Task<T>` in this context:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_018.html_p1530pro01)

async Task<int> Return(int value, TimeSpan delay)
{
    await Task.Delay(delay);
    return value;
}

As you can see, asynchronous methods can return a `Task<T>` object. This object will ultimately hold the result of the computation, which gets set using a regular `return` statement. However, it’s also possible for an asynchronous method to return `Task` or `void`. Such methods don’t really return a result in an asynchronous manner. Nonetheless, a caller may still be interested to track the completion of the asynchronous operation. Using a `Task`-returning asynchronous method, this can be achieved. A `void`-returning asynchronous method can only be used as a fire-and-forget method (unless other progress tracking mechanisms are used):

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_019.html_p1530pro02)

async Task Throw(Exception error, TimeSpan delay)
{
    await Task.Delay(delay);
    throw error;
}

In the preceding example, an exception object is thrown after the specified delay. The exception ends up in the returned `Task` object, causing the task to go into the `Faulted` state with its `Exception` property set. A caller may await this task, or hook up a continuation, to observe the `Task`’s result. However, it’s perfectly fine to abandon the task object, as well:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_020.html_p1530pro03)

async void button_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    // 1\. Using await (see Chapter 31)
    try
    {
        await Throw(new Exception(), TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
    }
    catch (Exception ex)
    {
        // Can observe the exception here.
    }

    // 2\. Using a continuation (see next section)
    Throw(new Exception(), TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5)).ContinueWith(t =>
    {
        // Can observe the exception here.
    });

    // 3\. Forget about the Task
    Throw(new Exception(), TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
}

If the third approach is chosen in this example, no user code is holding on to the `Task` object, and no one will be observing its failure. Because this coding pattern could be quite common when using the new asynchronous programming features, a decision was made to make the unhandled exception behavior a bit softer.

Starting with .NET 4.5, the default behavior for unobserved exceptions from the TPL has changed such that the process is no longer killed. The `UnobservedTaskException` event is still raised though, allowing one to observe such exceptions. This can prove useful during development time to make sure no serious exceptions get dropped on the floor. You can also restore the original behavior by adding a flag to the app.config file for the application:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_021.html_p1531pro01)

<configuration>
    <runtime>
        <ThrowUnobservedTaskExceptions enabled="true"/>
    </runtime>
</configuration>

This change of default behavior isn’t meant to encourage developers to be sloppier about exceptions. It’s a good practice to test your libraries and components with this flag enabled. Application developers using your libraries can then rest assured that all libraries they depend on never leave exceptions unhandled or tend to swallow exceptions they can’t catch. At that point, the final call about how to treat unobserved exceptions in application code is left to the application developer.

#### Continuations

One advantage of using tasks is their better composition compared to lower-level constructs such as threads. As mentioned at the beginning of the “[Task Parallelism](#part0040.html_ch30lev1sec3)” section, earlier in this chapter, tasks can produce a result of some type. Taking some further action based on the result (which also could be an error or even a cancellation) is a common thing to do. This is where continuations come in.

##### The Basic Concept

Although they sound scary, continuations are really simple constructs. Before going into the specifics of their use in conjunction with tasks, let’s explore them from a conceptual point of view. Consider the following piece of imperative sequential synchronous code:

int c = Add(a, b);
Console.WriteLine(c);

This piece of code calls a method `Add`, which at some point returns the sum of `a` and `b`, which we receive and can use to continue to use (for example, to print it to the screen). Let’s examine a few things about this code.

First, notice how sequencing plays an important role in the code: The call to the `Console.WriteLine` method cannot take place until `Add` returns. The semicolon syntax in languages such as C# makes the sequential execution nature explicit syntactically.

Second, and related to the previous point, this code is inherently synchronous: You can’t do anything but sit and wait for `Add` to come back before other work can be done. Although this seems tied to the notion of sequencing, we can still have sequencing without being synchronous. This is where continuations come in.

In continuation passing style (CPS), the preceding code fragment is rewritten in the following style, which at first might look a little weird:

Add(a, b, c => {
    Console.WriteLine(c);
});

Now we call some method `Add`, which not only takes in its two inputs, it also accepts a callback parameter that receives the result of the computation. This is where execution *continues* after `Add`’s computation finishes (and hence the name continuation). Here’s how the `Add` method is implemented:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_022.html_p1532pro01)

static void Add(int a, int b, Action<int> continueWith)
{
    continueWith(a + b);
}

Notice we still have sequencing of operations going on: First, `a` and `b` are added together to be fed into the continuation function, which then runs after the addition takes place. Those operations are still sequential in nature. However, this is no longer the semicolon kind of sequencing we’re used to from languages such as C#. Now all the remaining code to execute after the addition sits in a lambda expression.

One essential difference that’s become visible after making this transformation is the change in `Add`’s return type. Now, the `Add` method returns `void`. It’s not that we have lost the result of the addition, though; the result will be fed into the continuation.

So far, we haven’t done anything truly different from the synchrony point of view. This code is still intrinsically synchronous: Calling `Add` computes the sum of its first two arguments, followed by a call to the continuation function. However, now we could easily introduce concurrency in the `Add` method to compute the sum of `a` and `b` without blocking the caller to `Add`. As soon as that value is available, the continuation function can be called, still on a different thread. In the world of CPS, the introduction of asynchrony becomes quite easy:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_023.html_p1533pro01)

static void Add(int a, int b, Action<int> continueWith)
{
    new Thread(() => continueWith(a + b)).Start();
}

Now the `Add` method is an asynchronous method from the caller’s point of view. At the point this method returns, work is going on in the background without blocking the caller. When the sum value is available, the continuation will be called in the *future*.

##### Hidden Continuations in the .NET Framework

Continuations have been prominent in the .NET Framework without them being called such. Probably the best example of them is the asynchronous method invocation pattern, illustrated here using `BeginInvoke` and `EndInvoke` on delegates:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_024.html_p1533pro02)

Func<int, int, int> add = (a, b) => a + b;
add.BeginInvoke(3, 4, iar => {
    int c = add.EndInvoke(iar);
    Console.WriteLine(c);
}, /* state */ null);

// The main thread can continue asynchronous while the delegate is being
// invoked. At some point the AsyncCallback continuation will be called.

This is nothing but CPS entrenched in the .NET Framework, with some noise due to the `BeginInvoke` and `EndInvoke` methods, the `IAsyncResult` dragon, the `AsyncCallback` delegate, and a largely redundant state parameter. Other than this, we’re dealing with a continuation here.

##### Continuations on Tasks

The concept of continuations is exposed on `Task` and `Task<TResult>` in the form of the `ContinueWith` method. The function passed to this method gets called when the task completes. Usually, the continuation function results in the creation of a new task that runs the continuation code. All of this allows sequencing of asynchronous operations in a one-at-a-time fashion. Here’s an example:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_025.html_p1533pro03)

Task<int> first = new Task<int>(() => {
    // Do lots of work here. For simplicity's sake, let's return 42 verbatim.
    return 42;
});

Task<string> second = first.ContinueWith(t => {
    // Compute based on the first task's result. By trivial example:
    return t.Result.ToString();
});

Console.WriteLine(second.Result);

Notice how a continuation gives rise to a new `Task` or `Task<TResult>`, where the type of the returned data can differ from the original task. In fact, `ContinueWith` is a form of function composition on steroids, in the context of asynchronous computation.

The previous code fragment is rather incomplete, though. It assumes the first task did complete successfully because it just dots into the `Result` property to do its work. To be more robust against failures, various properties on the “antecedent task” (which is the previous task that was run before the continuation is invoked) can be used to inspect the situation we’re dealing with. For example, the `IsFaulted` property will reveal there was an exception, which in turn can be retrieved from the `Exception` property.

##### Specifying Continuation Options

There are different ways to define continuations, reducing a lot of the typical clutter inside the `ContinueWith` lambda expression to deal with checking for faulted state or cancellation (explained in the section “[Cancellation of Tasks](#part0040.html_ch30lev2sec10)”). Enter `TaskContinuationOptions`.

Before we list those options, it should be mentioned that a task can have more than just a single continuation:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_026.html_p1534pro01)

var answer = Task<int>.Factory.StartNew(() => 42);
answer.ContinueWith(t => Console.WriteLine("C1 " + t.Result));
answer.ContinueWith(t => Console.WriteLine("C2 " + t.Result));
Console.ReadLine();

If there’s just a single continuation, as shown in the preceding section’s example, it’s quite common to use a fluent interface pattern of dotting sequenced continuations together as a long chain:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_027.html_p1534pro02)

Task<int>.Factory.StartNew(() => 42)
    .ContinueWith(t => t.Result / 2)
    .ContinueWith(t => t.Result.ToString())
    .ContinueWith(t => Console.WriteLine("42 / 2 = " + t.Result));

This works nicely if you put all error-handling or cancellation-handling logic inside the continuation functions. However, if you want to take distinct continuation actions for the different states a task can complete in, you must use the first style of assigning tasks to temporary variables to specify multiple continuations. [Figure 30.5](#part0040.html_ch30fig05) contrasts those two styles.

![Image](images/00761.jpeg)

FIGURE 30.5 Sequencing versus parallel continuations.

So, here are some of the continuation option flags that can be specified when creating a new continuation:

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) `NotOn*` flags prevent the continuation from running if the specified state is true for the antecedent task. Suffixes for this family of flags include `Faulted`, `Canceled`, and `RanToCompletion`.

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) `OnlyOn*` flags, for the same three states as specified in the previous bullet point, cause the continuation to be called only if the antecedent task finished in the specified state.

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) `ExecuteSynchronously` causes the continuation to run synchronously on the thread where the antecedent task completed. This option should be used only when the continuation is short running.

Other continuation options are the same as for the `TaskCreationOptions`, allowing for the specification of fairness preference, the long-running hint, or to attach the task to its parent.

An example of a task with two continuations, one for success and one for failure, is shown in the following code fragment:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_028.html_p1535pro01)

var answer = Task<int>.Factory.StartNew(() => {
    // Left to the reader: Compute a value "res"; may throw.
    return res;
});

answer.ContinueWith(t => {
    // Will only be called in success cases.
    Console.WriteLine(t.Result);
}, TaskContinuationOptions.OnlyOnRanToCompletion);

answer.ContinueWith(t => {
    // Will only be called in error cases. Handle any exception we can handle.
    t.Exception.Flatten().Handle(ex => {
       // See section "Exploring AggregateException" for more information.
       return false;
    });
}, TaskContinuationOptions.OnlyOnFaulted);

An alternative way of writing this code is to write a single continuation without specific `TaskContinuationOptions`. Instead, the task object’s `Status` property can be inspected inside the continuation delegate.

##### Using Await Expressions

If you think all of this manual plumbing with continuation delegates and flags is rather tedious, you’re absolutely right. Starting with .NET 4.5, the need to write a continuation by hand should be reduced significantly thanks to the introduction of the new asynchronous programming features. Taking the previous section’s code as an example, here’s how you could achieve a very similar effect using C# 5.0’s `await` syntax:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_029.html_p1536pro01)

try
{
    var res = await answer;
    Console.WriteLine(res);
}
catch (SomeException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine("An error occurred: " + ex.Message);
}

The use of `await` expressions hands over the tedious job of rewriting code in continuation passing style to the compiler. Through some hoops with intermediate helper types called awaiters, this code is basically turned into a `ContinueWith` method call on the `answer` task object.

We explore the use of `await` expressions in asynchronous methods in the next chapter. For now, remember the core idea of continuations as a way to process a task’s result by invocation of a delegate.

In summary, continuations are used to chain together asynchronous computations. As discussed in the next section, it’s also possible to cancel continuations. Given this option, and the ability to handle exceptions, continuations provide for sequencing points in chains of asynchronous computations.

#### Cancellation of Tasks

One thing that has been notoriously difficult in the world of asynchronous code (among other things, such as other threading and synchronization constructs) is the means to cancel an operation. Starting with .NET 4.0, cancellation has been unified in terms of two concepts: `CancellationToken` and `CancellationTokenSource`.

We don’t elaborate on the intricacies of the mechanism here but instead focus on the essentials of the feature. [Figure 30.6](#part0040.html_ch30fig06) summarizes the basic interactions with constructs for cancellation.

![Image](images/00762.jpeg)

FIGURE 30.6 Cancellation of a task.

The first key notion is that of a `CancellationTokenSource`. This class is where a request for cancellation comes in by means of a call to `Cancel`. The operation being cancelled can check for this situation through a so-called `CancellationToken` struct, which can be obtained from the token source using the `Token` get-only property. This lightweight object can be passed in a variety of places across the TPL and `System.Threading` APIs starting from .NET 4.0\. In the section “[Retrieving a Task’s Result](#part0040.html_ch30lev2sec7),” earlier in this chapter, you saw how the `Wait` method on a `Task` accepts a `CancellationToken`, allowing for cancellation of this operation.

Note that cancellation for tasks is done in a cooperative manner. In contrast to the `Thread.Abort` method, which throws an asynchronous `ThreadAbortException`, a cancellation token merely represents a flag the task should check periodically to quit the task’s code when it sees a request for cancellation. It can do so either by using the `IsCancellationRequested` property or by invoking `ThrowIfCancellationRequested`, both on the token value. The latter method throws an `OperationCanceledException` that takes down the task. Obviously, you can observe this error when waiting for the task or from within continuation functions.

When wait operations occur in a task, the same token should be passed to those such that the cancellation can also unblock such wait operations. Because of the cooperative nature of cancellation, it can take a while before a cancellation is granted. This also assumes the task’s code checks for cancellation on a regular-enough basis.

An example of cancellation support in tasks is shown here:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_030.html_p1537pro01)

var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();
var ct = cts.Token;

Task.Factory.StartNew(() =>
{
    while (true)
    {
        // Alternatively, ThrowIfCancellationRequested could be used,
        // requiring the caller to handle this case.
        if (ct.IsCancellationRequested)
            return;

        Console.WriteLine(DateTime.Now);
        Thread.Sleep(1000);
    }
}, ct);

Console.WriteLine("Press ENTER to stop the clock...");
Console.ReadLine();
cts.Cancel();

Console.WriteLine("Clock stopped");
Console.ReadLine();

In this piece of code, we use the `IsCancellationRequeste`d property to check for such a request, which we handle by stopping the task. Using this technique, the task’s status doesn’t transition into `Canceled` but ends up in `RanToCompletion` because it terminated gracefully. This often suffices. However, if it makes sense for the owner of the task or for continuations to check the canceled state, an `OperationCanceledException` is the way to go. An example of this pattern is shown here:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_031.html_p1538pro01)

if (ct.IsCancellationRequested)
{
    // Do cleanup if necessary (if none, the if-check can be omitted).
    ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();
}

#### Parallel Invocation

Invoking a single task suffices in many cases, but it often makes sense to achieve parallelism by running multiple tasks. Although you can simply create multiple tasks, some higher levels of abstraction exist in the TPL. One such abstraction is `Parallel.Invoke`, which takes an array of `Action` delegates to invoke in parallel. You can think of each such action resulting in a task being created. Only when all the tasks complete, the `Parallel.Invoke` call returns. This said, `Parallel.Invoke` makes no guarantees that the actions really run in parallel because of the way scheduling works. (The same worker might pick up all the actions, causing them to run sequentially.)

An example of `Parallel.Invoke` is shown here:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_032.html_p1538pro02)

Parallel.Invoke(
    () => Console.WriteLine("First task"),
    () => Console.WriteLine("Second task"),
    () => Console.WriteLine("Third task")
);

Another overload to the `Invoke` method takes in a first `ParallelOptions` parameter, which can be used to specify a number of flags. One is the degree of parallelism, used to limit the maximum number of parallel workers that get spawn to run the work. Yet another flag is a cancellation token, whose role should be self-explanatory.

In fact, the `Parallel` class is where task and data parallelism meet. This section covers only the `Invoke` method, which is much closer to task parallelism than it is to data parallelism. The “[Data Parallelism](#part0040.html_ch30lev1sec4)” section, later in this chapter, examines parallel loop constructs exposed as static methods on the `Parallel` class.

Concerning the case of errors occurring in one or more tasks, you can probably guess how those errors get surfaced to the caller of `Parallel.Invoke`. `AggregateException` is your best friend once more. Similarly, cancellation of parallel invocation work can result in an `OperationCanceledException` wrapped inside an `AggregateException`.

#### Waiting for Multiple Tasks

The `Parallel.Invoke` method shown in the preceding section brings us to an interesting facility in the TPL. Did you see the one single most important difference compared to regular tasks? Here it is: Although the individual pieces of work passed to `Parallel.Invoke` can run in parallel using asynchronous tasks, the sum of the parts is synchronous. That is, `Parallel.Invoke` doesn’t return until all of its actions have been executed (or some error or cancellation has occurred).

If you read [Chapter 29](#part0039.html_ch29) carefully, you might immediately think of a way to achieve this kind of synchronizing behavior across multiple parallel actions. What about using events such as `ManualResetEvent` or even the concept of a `CountDownEvent`? Although such a technique will work, it’s rather difficult to get right (in particular when errors and cancellation enter the mix). Moreover, if not done carefully, you might induce expensive context switches because of the low-level nature of some of those wait primitives layered on top of Win32 synchronization facilities.

Luckily, the TPL provides for `WaitAll` and `WaitAny` constructs that enable us to wait for the completion of many tasks (either waiting for all of them to complete or for at least one to complete). An example of a simple `Parallel.Invoke` clone is shown here:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_033.html_p1539pro01)

static void Main()
{
    var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();
    ParallelInvoke(cts.Token,
        () => Console.WriteLine("First task"),
        () => Console.WriteLine("Second task"),
        () => Console.WriteLine("Third task")
    );
}

static void ParallelInvoke(CancellationToken ct, params Action[] actions)
{
    var tasks = (from action in actions
                 select Task.Factory.StartNew(action, ct))
                .ToArray();

    Task.WaitAll(tasks, ct);
}

For fun, I’ve included a means to thread a cancellation token throughout the `WaitAll` call and all the `StartNew` calls that spawn the tasks. This shows one of the overloads of the `WaitAll` method on Task.

Other overloads of `WaitAll` allow specification of a timeout, and use of a cancellation token is optional (as usual). Errors in any of the child tasks appear collectively in an `AggregateException` thrown from the `WaitAll` call.

The `WaitAny` methods should be quite self-explanatory, as well, especially if you’ve had prior exposure to the equivalent method on `WaitHandle`. Those methods return an integer value indicating the index of the task in the array that completed. Overloads exist that accept a timeout value or a cancellation token. The presence of the cancellation tokens throughout the TPL API is one of the key differences with classic means to synchronize using `WaitHandle` objects. It was not uncommon before to see dummy events being passed to `Wait` methods to allow them to be unblocked:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_034.html_p1540pro01)

WaitHandle cancel = new ManualResetEvent(false);
// Assume other events exist

int i = WaitHandle.WaitAny(new[] { cancel, event1, event2 });
if (i == 0)
    // Indicates the cancellation event was signaled.

Although this pattern works well in practice, it adds unnecessary burden to your code. In other places where cancellation was desired (for instance, cooperatively inside a thread), yet a different mechanism was needed (for example, using a cancellation Boolean flag). In the world of TPL, all cancellation scenarios are unified using cancellation tokens.

#### How the Task Scheduler Works

A thorough discussion of scheduling is beyond the scope of this discussion, but a basic understanding of task scheduling in the TPL is good to have. For more in-depth information, refer to MSDN documentation.

First, note that scheduling in the TPL is extensible because you can create your own subtype of `TaskScheduler`. In fact, a scheduler is fairly easy to create by implementing just three methods. [Figure 30.7](#part0040.html_ch30fig07) shows the class diagram for the abstract base class used to implement schedulers. Italicized methods indicate abstract ones. The `QueueTask` method is the most essential one, allowing a new `Task` object to be scheduled for execution. TPL abstractions call into this method to spawn work.

![Image](images/00763.jpeg)

FIGURE 30.7 Custom TaskScheduler implementations can be provided.

We do not cover how to go about such a scheduler implementation, but we do continue to sketch how the default TPL scheduler does its work.

##### .NET 4 Thread Pool Essentials

The default `TaskScheduler` in the TPL gets passed to all sorts of APIs (including task creation, `Parallel` methods, among others) if no custom scheduler is specified. The way this scheduler works is by queuing work on the .NET thread pool, which we already discussed from a user’s point of view in [Chapter 29](#part0039.html_ch29).

Compared to earlier versions of .NET and the Common Language Runtime (CLR), the thread pool has been improved a lot to enable higher scalability and throughput. In particular, the thread pool’s queue of work items is now implemented using a data structure known as a `ConcurrentQueue`, also available in the `System.Collections.Concurrent` namespace. This queue uses lock-free algorithms to reduce the time needed to enqueue and dequeue work items. This benefits all users of the `ThreadPool` class, as well. So even if you don’t upgrade your code to use the TPL just yet, existing .NET code that uses the `QueueUserWorkItem` method to schedule background work automatically becomes faster when running it on the .NET 4 platform.

Thus far, we’ve referred to the thread pool as if there’s only one such pool. Nothing is further from the truth, for a couple of reasons. First, each application domain has its own thread pool for reasons of isolation: It shouldn’t be possible to leak delegates across application domains where they can do harm to other parts of the system.

Second, and more relevant to our discussion, local queues associated with each worker thread are used to run queued work items. Those queues are used to schedule child tasks created in the context of another (parent) task. By doing so, thread locality is preferred to execute those child tasks whenever possible. This tends to have positive effects all the way down to increased processor cache hits. One reason is that parent and child tasks usually manipulate the shared data structures (mutable or not). The technical argument that running related work on the same thread has this positive effect is based on the reasoning that the operating system scheduler tries to avoid migrating a thread across CPUs, thus increasing the likelihood of CPU cache hits when accessing memory.

[Figure 30.8](#part0040.html_ch30fig08) shows how top-level tasks (step 1) get queued in the global queue, while child tasks (step 3) get queued in the local queue of their parent. In step 2, a worker thread that’s currently idle is woken up to grab work from the global queue and start executing it.

![Image](images/00764.jpeg)

FIGURE 30.8 Global and local queues used to schedule and execute tasks.

If local queues of workers have work in them, but another worker is sitting idle, the scheduling infrastructure can employ work stealing. This mechanism enables an idle worker to steal work from another worker’s queue to maximize the throughput of the system (“keep your many cores busy”). Heuristics are applied to determine whether stealing work from another queue is worth it, and if so the work gets stolen from the queue in first-in, first-out (FIFO) order.

You can find more information about work stealing and more advanced concepts such as task inlining in the MSDN documentation related to TPL.

### Data Parallelism

We’re now ready to look at data parallelism. This means of achieving parallel computing exploits the capability to process large data sets by partitioning them into chunks, each of which gets processed in parallel. Such techniques have existed for a long time in database query processor engines but apply equally well in the context of a general-purpose programming language. This is where TPL’s data parallelism comes in, which can be found in the `System.Threading.Tasks.Parallel` class.

#### Parallel For Loops

One first form of data parallelism is exposed by the `Parallel.For` set of methods, which provide a parallel `for` loop. The idea of a parallel `for` loop is to run the iterations of the loop in parallel, followed by a wait operation for all the iterations to complete. This is similar to the `Parallel.Invoke` construct we looked at in the “[Parallel Invocation](#part0040.html_ch30lev2sec11)” section, earlier in this chapter.

An example of one of the simplest overloads of `Parallel.For` is shown here. Notice how similar this loop looks to a regular C# `for` loop, thanks to the concise syntax of lambda expressions:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_035.html_p1543pro01)

double[,] xs = GetMatrix(300, 400);
double[,] ys = GetMatrix(400, 500);
double[,] zs = new double[300, 500];

var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
Parallel.For(0, zs.GetLength(0), i =>
{
    for (int j = 0; j < zs.GetLength(1); j++)
    {
        zs[i, j] = 0.0;
        for (int k = 0; k < xs.GetLength(1); k++)
        {
            zs[i, j] += xs[i, k] * ys[k, j];
        }
    }
});
sw.Stop();
Console.WriteLine(sw.Elapsed);

This typical example of the parallel `for` loop is used to perform a matrix multiplication where each of the rows in the resulting matrix is computed in parallel. Although we’re dealing with a shared result array, there are no clashes in accessing it because each of the cells can be computed independently of each other. [Figure 30.9](#part0040.html_ch30fig09) shows the parallel partitioning of work in a schematic way.

![Image](images/00765.jpeg)

FIGURE 30.9 Data parallelism for matrix multiplication.

The use of the `Stopwatch` class from the `System.Diagnostics` namespace enables us to measure the time it takes to perform this operation using data parallelism. Testing the same code with a regular sequential `for` loop is equally simple:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_036.html_p1544pro01)

sw.Restart();
for (int i = 0; i < zs.GetLength(0); i++)
{
    for (int j = 0; j < zs.GetLength(1); j++)
    {
        zs[i, j] = 0.0;
        for (int k = 0; k < xs.GetLength(1); k++)
        {
            zs[i, j] += xs[i, k] * ys[k, j];
        }
    }
}
sw.Stop();
Console.WriteLine(sw.Elapsed);

On my machine, the parallel code completed in 751 milliseconds, whereas the sequential code took a stunning 2364 milliseconds, about three times slower. This run was done on an eight-core machine. Although there’s a substantial speedup going on here, don’t expect a linear scaling in terms of the number of cores available. There’s still overhead associated with spawning and scheduling work, too.

* * *

Note: What About Using Threads?

It’s a good exercise to try to parallelize the matrix multiplication using plain old threads, using one thread for each resulting row. In our example, this allocates no fewer than 300 threads. The cost of creating (in terms of CPU cycles and the memory impact due to allocations of each thread’s stack) and starting those threads and all the context switching will be nontrivial.

* * *

##### Simple Overloads

The simplest of overloads to `For` take in three parameters: an inclusive lower bound, an exclusive upper bound, and a delegate representing the loop body. Two families of `For` loop methods exist, one based on Int32 (C# int) values and another based on Int64 (C# long) values:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_037.html_p1544pro02)

static ParallelLoopResult For(int fromInclusive, int toExclusive,
                              Action<int> body);
static ParallelLoopResult For(long fromInclusive, long toExclusive,
                              Action<long> body);

The resulting `ParallelLoopResult` struct is explained in the next section. In many cases, this value is simply disregarded.

##### Using ParallelLoopState

A second group of overloads just extends the loop body delegate with an additional parameter of type `ParallelLoopState`:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_038.html_p1545pro01)

static ParallelLoopResult For(int fromInclusive, int toExclusive,
                              Action<int, ParallelLoopState> body);
static ParallelLoopResult For(long fromInclusive, long toExclusive,
                              Action<long, ParallelLoopState> body);

The use case for a `ParallelLoopState` is to break prematurely from the loop in a variety of ways. To see why this has to be done this way, consider the following regular for loop constructor first:

for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++)
{
    if (shouldStop(i))
        break;
    // Do work otherwise.
}

Here the break statement is used to quit from the loop based on some condition that can (but doesn’t have to) depend on the loop iteration variable. The way break statements work is by emitting a branch instruction to jump beyond the entire `for` loop. This kind of control flow doesn’t work in the same way inside lambda expressions, though. Although you can break outside a loop contained inside such a function, you can’t jump out of the lambda expression, which after all is nothing more than an anonymous method. We say that a *nonlocal jump* is not possible using a break statement.

To alleviate this, the `ParallelLoopState` class was introduced. It’s used to communicate from inside the loop that a stop of the loop is requested:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_039.html_p1545pro02)

Parallel.For(0, 1000, (i, state) =>
{
    if (shouldStop(i))
    {
        state.Break();
        return;
    }
    // Do work otherwise.
});

Because `Break` is called, the `Parallel.For` code ceases to spawn new tasks for the iterations beyond the current point where the break was requested. For example, if `shouldStop` evaluates true in iteration 10, the call to `Break` causes no iterations beyond the 10th to get scheduled. This said, it might be the case (due to the parallel execution nature) that iterations beyond the current iteration are already in flight. Those can’t be prevented from running anymore, so breaking is a best-effort service.

One invariant that `Break` ensures is that all the iterations before the point the `Break` call is issued will get executed. In the running example of breaking from the loop at the 10th iteration, this ensures that the iterations before the 10th are scheduled and get run. This mimics the behavior of a C# `break` statement as closely as possible: All iterations before the break call can execute, but iterations beyond the point are (to the extent possible) prevented from running.

An alternative way to stop a parallel loop is by calling `Stop` on the `ParallelLoopState` object. The sole difference compared to `Break` is that there’s no guarantee that work before the current iteration will get run. In our example, calling `Stop` during the 10th iteration provides no guarantees that the preceding 9 iterations get executed.

The `ParallelLoopState` class contains a few other instance members that occasionally come in handy. They include properties to check whether a stop is requested and which iteration this happened in. For example, `ShouldExitCurrentIteration` can be checked to return from the loop iteration code prematurely because a request to terminate the loop was issued. Similarly, the `IsStopped` property can be checked for a stop request. You can find more information on MSDN.

One final thing we should mention is the role of the return type on the `For` methods, which is `ParallelLoopResult`. This class exposes two instance properties that enable the caller to check whether the loop completed in its entirety (`IsCompleted`) and what the lowest break iteration was if the loop didn’t run to completion (`LowestBreakIteration`).

##### Use of ParallelOptions

Other overloads to `Parallel.For` take in a `ParallelOptions` object, which can configure up to three settings:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_040.html_p1546pro01)

public class ParallelOptions
{
    public CancellationToken CancellationToken { get; set; }
    public int MaxDegreeOfParallelism { get; set; }
    public TaskScheduler TaskScheduler { get; set; }
}

The first one allows the specification of a cancellation token that can be used to cancel the loop from executing further, causing an `OperationCanceledException` to be thrown from the `Parallel.For` code.

Using the `MaxDegreeOfParallelism` property, the number of parallel workers used to process the loop iterations can be limited. You should exercise caution when using this flag because you might be needlessly reducing the scalability of your application, especially if you use magic constant values here. You can use this flag when you happen to know about competing resources and want to divide parallel resources in one way or another. Usually, such calculations depend on the number of cores, which can be obtained through the `System.Environment` class.

Finally, the `TaskScheduler` property can be used to pass in your own scheduler. The MSDN documentation shows how to implement such a beast if you really have to (if the default scheduler lets you down for some reason).

##### Using Thread-Local Data

One final set of overloads provides for thread-local data that can be manipulated safely inside the loop body. (Only one thread can be accessing the data at a time.) A separate action is invoked to aggregate the thread-local states (manipulated by the workers from the loop’s iterations) into a global result. An example will make this clearer, but let’s show one of the overloads first:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_041.html_p1547pro01)

static ParallelLoopResult For<TLocal>(int fromInclusive, int toExclusive,
    Func<TLocal> localInit,
    Func<int, ParallelLoopState, TLocal, TLocal> body,
    Action<TLocal> localFinally);

The first function parameter, called `localInit`, is used to initialize thread-local state. Each body invocation receives the loop variable and the `ParallelLoopState` (explained in the preceding section) and the current thread-local value. In those overloads, the body is no longer an action but has become a function that returns the updated thread-local state because of the iteration’s execution. The final parameter is executed once for every thread-local that was initialized during the execution of the loop and is used to aggregate those results when the loop completes.

Here’s an example, also shown on MSDN:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_042.html_p1547pro02)

var xs = Enumerable.Range(0, 1000000).ToArray();
long total = 0;

Parallel.For<long>(0, xs.Length,
    () => 0,
    (j, loop, subtotal) => {
        subtotal += xs[j];
        return subtotal;
    },
    subtotal => Interlocked.Add(ref total, subtotal)
);

Console.WriteLine("The total is {0}", total);

For each unique worker thread that’s involved in executing the parallel `for` loop, the function for local state initialization (here simply returning 0) will be called. From this point on, the initialized data is stored in thread-local storage that’s fed to the loop body function every time the worker processes a new iteration. The updated subtotal is then returned from the loop body, to be stored in the worker thread’s thread-local storage again. When all the workers have completed all their work for the loop, the aggregation function is called, where we sum up (in a thread-safe manner) the subtotals into a global total.

I recommend carrying out the debugger experiment illustrated in [Figure 30.10](#part0040.html_ch30fig10). First, you’ll see a relatively small number of calls to the initialization function, more or less proportional to the number of processor cores (or the degree of parallelism if specified) available. This is due to the initialization happening only once per worker, which is nothing but a thread that gets reused across multiple work items.

![Image](images/00766.jpeg)

FIGURE 30.10 Observing function calls during a parallel loop with thread-local state.

After all the loop bodies have executed on the active workers, the subtotals that live in the workers’ thread-local state will be aggregated through the `finally` function that will get called once per worker.

Using the thread-local state option of a parallel `for` loop means that you don’t have to manage such state yourself (which can be rather error-prone otherwise). Usually, this technique is used when the resulting loop has to compute some kind of aggregation value.

##### AggregateException Strikes Again

It should be quite obvious that all the overloads of parallel loop constructs (and the `Parallel.Invoke` method discussed in the “[Parallel Invocation](#part0040.html_ch30lev2sec11)” section) can throw an `AggregateException` that collects all the exceptions that happened on the parallel tasks that got spawned by the data parallel construct.

#### Parallel ForEach Loops

Just as the `Parallel.For` method resembles a C# for loop, the `Parallel.ForEach` method is designed to mirror the C# `foreach` loop. Given an enumerable sequence, the `ForEach` method allows for the parallel execution of a loop body for each of the elements in the given sequence.

Most of the concepts discussed in our coverage of `For` carry over to the `ForEach` case, as well, including the use of `ParallelLoopOptions`, the `ParallelLoopState` with `Break` and `Stop` methods, and the `ParallelLoopResult`. Similarly, thread-local state can be associated with the workers that carry out the loop’s work.

In what follows, we focus on the additional concepts introduced for the `ForEach` loop that are unique to this kind of loop. But first, let’s consider a simple example of the use of this data parallel operation with one of the most extensive overloads:

[Click here to view code image](#part0074_split_043.html_p1549pro01)

var xs = Enumerable.Range(0, 1000000);
long total = 0;

Parallel.ForEach(xs,
    () => 0L,
    (x, loop, subtotal) => {
        subtotal += x;
        return subtotal;
    },
    subtotal => Interlocked.Add(ref total, subtotal)
);

Console.WriteLine("The total is {0}", total);

Here we’re iterating over the enumerable sequence with parallel loop body executions. Again, we’re using a long-valued thread-local state to compute subtotals of the sum of the sequence’s elements, which get aggregated into the final sum.

##### The Role of Partitioners

To run operations on the elements of a sequence in parallel, the sequence needs to be partitioned into chunks of work. This is where the concept of partitioners enters the picture. They play a crucial role in the PLINQ implementation, too (see the section “[Parallel LINQ](#part0030.html_ch20lev1sec4)” in [Chapter 20](#part0030.html_ch20)).

The idea of a partitioner is to let the workers that execute the loop body process more than just individual elements one at a time. For example, if you have 100 elements and 4 cores, it makes sense to have each core take care of the work for 25 elements. Such a common partitioning scheme is called *range partitioning*, where the input sequence size has to be known upfront to create index-based ranges for each worker. This scheme has a disadvantage, though: If one worker completes way before other workers are done with their part of the work, the idle worker cannot steal work.

Another way to partition a sequence is *chunk partitioning*, where chunks of a given size are processed by workers. This differs from range partitioning in that the split-up of the work is not statically based on the number of workers. For example, given 100 elements and a chunk size of 5, we get 20 units of work. If there are, say, four cores with a worker allocated for each core, they will on average execute five chunks each. This isn’t static allocation of chunks to workers, though; if a worker is presented with a chunk, it can process much faster than another worker can process its chunk, and it can readily move on to the next chunk. Overall, the throughput of the system is higher. *Load-balancing partitioning* is another name for the use of dynamic chunk-based partitioning.

You can create a partitioner by using the `Partitioner.Create` factory methods. A set of overloads is based on from and to bounds, combined with range sizes, creating a partitioner that employs *range partitioning*. Other overloads can take in an array or an `IList<T>` object, whose length is known immediately. Depending on a Boolean flag named `loadBalance`, the resulting partitioner uses range partitioning or *load-balancing chunk partitioning*.

For more information about the use of partitioners and the creation of custom partitioners, refer to the MSDN documentation about the subject.

### Summary

Taking advantage of multicore machines is becoming increasingly important. From a programmer’s point of view, various facilities in the `System.Threading` libraries make it easier to do so.

In this chapter, we explored the notion of task parallelism centered around the `Task` and `Task<TResult>` types. We discussed how to create tasks, await their results, work with continues, and deal with various aspects such as errors and cancellation. In summary, tasks are the new means to perform work asynchronously, whether it’s long running (where you’d have used threads before) or more ad hoc short-lived computations (using thread pools before). We also discussed how the task scheduler works, layered atop of the improved thread pool, employing techniques such as work stealing.

We finished our discussion of modern approaches to parallelism with a tour through data parallelism, exposed through the `Parallel` class’s loop methods. During our discussion, you learned about loop state, parallelization options, partitioning schemes, and more.

## Chapter 31. Asynchronous Programming

* * *

In This Chapter

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) [Why Asynchronous Programming Matters](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31lev1sec1)

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) [Old Asynchronous Programming Patterns](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31lev1sec2)

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) [Task-Based Asynchronous Pattern (TAP)](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31lev2sec7)

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) [Asynchronous Methods and `await` Expressions](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31lev1sec3)

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) [Behind the Scenes](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31lev1sec4)

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) [Advanced Topics](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31lev1sec5)

* * *

[Chapter 30](#part0040.html_ch30), “[Task Parallelism and Data Parallelism](#part0040.html_ch30),” covered the concept of tasks as an abstraction to represent the eventual completion and result of a background operation. Although that discussion focused on parallel execution using processor resources, tasks provide the essential glue for the new C# 5.0 asynchronous programming features as well.

In this chapter, we study the new asynchronous programming support added to .NET 4.5\. You learn the rationale of why those features were introduced, followed by an exploration of the prior art of asynchronous programming patterns that emerged over the years. After introducing the new task-based asynchronous pattern, we look at the language support built in to C# 5.0 to make asynchronous programming blend in naturally with existing well-known language features.

### Why Asynchronous Programming Matters

Throughout the previous chapters, you have repeatedly seen useful cases of asynchronous programming. For example, instead of blocking and waiting for a delegate invocation to complete, we can use the `Begin/End` pair of methods to avoid blocking. Similarly, when dealing with I/O operations, it’s very common to use an asynchronous approach to perform the operations to prevent blocked user interfaces.

Unfortunately, asynchronous programming has been notoriously hard due to the required usage of coding patterns that have an invasive effect on the structure of your code. Moreover, error handling, cancellation, progress tracking, resource management, and so on are very tedious and error-prone to wire up in an asynchronous context.

As the need for fluid user experiences on a wide range of devices has become incredibly important, we’re seeing a shift toward mandatory use of asynchronous techniques when carrying out (potentially) long-running operations. At the same time, asynchronous programming has seen increased widespread adoption in services and cloud computing to increase scalability.

Because of those trends, asynchronous programming was introduced as a first-class language and framework feature in .NET 4.5\. Before we dive into those new features, let’s take a closer look at the approaches used to deal with the problem of asynchrony before. To start off this exploration, we discuss the essential properties of asynchrony.

#### It’s All About Latency

One of the fundamental properties of computer programming is the wide range of speed, latency, and timing we’re dealing with. This is reflected in a variety of concepts, such as the memory hierarchy. For example, when accessing data there’s several orders of magnitude of difference in access times between processor registers, main memory, paged out memory, the disk, and remote resources.

To complicate matters even further, each of those layers in the memory hierarchy has a growing spectrum of speed differences associated with it. For example, processors have several levels of caching. On chips with many cores, there’s complexity around keeping those caches consistent, by means of communication between cores which introduces additional overhead. `Main` memory is increasingly often distributed in topologies where some memory is closer to one central process unit (CPU) than it is to another. This is known as nonuniform memory access (NUMA). We haven’t even talked about the advances in disk technology with solid-state drives (SSDs) and whatnot yet.

From this discussion, you should get the idea. When accessing data, there’s a huge range of latencies to get a response back. [Figure 31.1](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31fig01) shows the memory hierarchy with common access times at each level.

![Image](images/00767.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.1 The memory hierarchy.

Similarly, when performing compute-intensive tasks, it might take a long while before the result is available. Even though we’re not really bound by access times here, the overall perceived effect is the same: It can take a long time before the response comes back.

Waiting for any of those tasks to complete can have disastrous effects on user experiences and scalability of services. We discuss this in more detail in a moment.

#### What’s Asynchrony, Really?

How does the discussion of latency relate to the distinction between synchronous and asynchronous programming? To set the scene for our further discussion, let’s define some terminology first. What’s asynchrony really all about?

In synchronous or asynchronous operations, multiple parties are always involved. In other words, this terminology provides a qualification for a relationship between two or more parties. More specifically, the relevant property of this relationship is dealing with time. Let’s take a closer look.

The word *synchronous* has a Greek origin and consists of two parts. The *syn* prefix stands for *together*. Other uses of this prefix can be found in words like synergy. The second part of the word is *chronos*, which means *time*, as in chronometer. If two parties move together, hand in hand, through the arrow of time, they’re evolving synchronously. So, what does all of this have to do with computer programming? Who are those two parties we’ve been talking about?

Consider the processor as one party in this relationship. It has a clock that ticks, reflecting its forward progress in processing of instructions. At the software level, this piece of hardware is abstracted through the notion of threads. The role of the operating system is to multiplex multiple threads on the physical processors that are available, with scheduling quanta and whatnot. As such, each thread really has a clock associated with it. [Figure 31.2](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31fig02) illustrates the relationship between threads, processors, and clocks.

![Image](images/00768.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.2 Threads, processors, and clocks.

What about the second party in the synchronous relationship? Consider a network card used to post a request to a service and to get the response back. This piece of hardware leads a life of its own, interacting with the outside world through a network cable, and receiving commands from the processor to perform certain operations. Despite having those connections, it does have its own notion of time, basically related to its primitive operations of sending and receiving packets. [Figure 31.3](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31fig03) shows the network card and its notion of time.

![Image](images/00769.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.3 Time through the lenses of a network card.

If we bring those two parties together, we face two different clocks. Let’s take a look from the processor’s point of view. This is where we run our code, through the software abstraction of threads. Assume the execution of our code arrives at a point in time where we need to request data from the network. What can the processor do now? Clearly, it has to issue the request to the networking stack to perform the operation, ultimately arriving in the network card through the networking software stack and its drivers. They key question is what happens next. There are really two options.

One possibility is for the processor to tie its clock to the network card’s notion of time. This behavior is synchronous, meaning both parties decide to walk the arrow of time hand in hand. However, this is a disadvantageous situation for the processor because it cannot do useful work while the slow network card is performing its duties, awaiting the response packet to come back.

Another option is to decouple both parties and establish a protocol to initiate and complete the request. Just like before, the processor now issues the request to the network card. However, where things differ is how the response is retrieved. Instead of tying both clocks together and stalling processor activity while the request is being processed, the two parties agree on a protocol. The processor kindly asks the network card to raise a notification when the request is completed. At that point in time, both parties split up and lead their own lives with their own clocks, resulting in asynchronous behavior. When the response arrives, the network card tells the processor about the completion of its request, and the two can rendezvous again to exchange the result.

A real-world scenario can make this distinction even clearer. Compare this to a man walking into a bar and asking for a drink. In a synchronous world, the man would cease all activities while the bar tender fetches the drink. If you’re lucky, the bartender comes back with your drink quickly. However, all sorts of things may go wrong, contributing to the total latency. For example, maybe the bar is very busy, causing your request to end up in a queue of little papers on the bar top. Or maybe the lemon wedge to decorate your drink cannot be served from the cache behind the bar, requiring a roundtrip to the kitchen to fetch new lemon wedges. And what about the physical limitations of pouring a drink, constrained by the bottle or tap opening, the pressure, and so on? Clearly, you could have checked your messages on your phone or have engaged in a conversation with others at the bar while waiting for the drink to arrive. That’s what asynchrony is all about. [Figure 31.4](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31fig04) contrasts both approaches with an illustration.

![Image](images/00770.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.4 Synchronous versus asynchronous processing.

Luckily, at the hardware level, asynchrony is used to make the CPU interact with peripheral devices such as disks, network cards, graphics cards, and so on. At the software level, this is reflected in the operating system’s handling of interrupt requests (IRQs) that are used by peripherals to signal they’d like some attention, for example to complete a request. In fact, a lot of the processing of completion of I/O requests is also handled at the hardware level with technologies such as direct memory access (DMA) whereby the I/O hardware can write its result to main memory, merely signaling to the processor it can now pick up the result. You can compare this with the bartender putting your drink in front of you, instead of using a buzzer to notify you when you can go and fetch your drink from a counter yourself.

* * *

Note: Blocking, From an OS Perspective

While the bottommost layers of the I/O stack in the Windows operating system are inherently dealing with hardware-level asynchrony, higher levels of abstraction also expose synchronous functions. For example, Win32’s ReadFile application programming interface (API) has support for both synchronous and asynchronous operations, with the latter being supported through a mechanism called overlapped I/O. This facility can also be combined with so-called I/O completion ports, allowing efficient handling of completion on a thread pool.

What’s so bad about the synchronous operations? As stated before, while the I/O is in progress, the caller thread is blocked. At the kernel level, this causes the thread to transition into a wait state, forcing the scheduler to search for another thread that’s ready to execute. Such a transition into kernel mode followed by a thread context switch is quite expensive.

Various techniques exist to avoid those costly operations. For example, slim wait primitives in the .NET Framework stay in user mode whenever possible. In fact, it’s even possible to intercept all blocking thread operations at various levels, including Common Language Runtime (CLR) hosting APIs and with User Mode Scheduling (UMS) in Windows 7 and later. The large scalability of database systems like Microsoft’s SQL Server is often achieved by synchronization in user mode.

* * *

Even though asynchronous programming APIs are available, developers have shied away from using those quite often, in part, because of the lack of good language support. The preference for easier synchronous APIs exists at all levels of the software stack. In Win32, the complexity of overlapped I/O and I/O completion ports can be overwhelming. And even though a lot of such complexity with asynchronous I/O is taken care of by the CLR and the Base Class Library (BCL), having to write callback-style code is tedious, as explained in much depth throughout this chapter.

In fact, it’s fair to say that excessive abstraction can be harmful. When performing synchronous I/O operations, you’re really hiding the aspect of the latency spanning the lifetime of the request, ultimately sacrificing the current thread for the whole duration. This problem is very similar to transparent remoting, where the access patterns to a remote object are completely identical to those for a local object, therefore hiding all the costs that are hidden behind the abstraction.

The C# 5.0 language features for asynchronous methods and `await` expressions provide a tool to tackle this problem by letting the compiler take care of callback-based programming. At the same time, the explicit annotation of methods with an `async` modifier and the use of `await` expressions make it clear when and where operations with long latencies are carried out. The net result is a minimally invasive effect on the structure of the code, while adding more explicitness about the code’s behavior.

#### User Experience

Nobody likes nonresponsive user interfaces (UIs). [Figure 31.5](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31fig05) shows the devastating user experience that results when a program’s UI stops responding.

![Image](images/00771.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.5 A nonresponsive application.

But have you ever thought about how Windows knows that a user interface got stuck? The key concept to understanding this is the so-called message loop, where requests are posted to perform various UI operations. For example, the window manager may request the program to repaint its UI by posting a WM_PAINT message (for example, in response to the user resizing the window). Similarly, operations like click events or text input events are sent from the input manager to the control involved, through the message loop. Using the Spy++ tool that comes with Visual Studio, you can see those window messages, as shown in [Figure 31.6](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31fig06).

![Image](images/00772.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.6 Inspecting window messages using Spy++.

How do those window messages get processed? The answer to this question is hidden—to a varying degree—behind the abstractions of various UI frameworks such as Windows Forms and WPF. The basic idea is the same, regardless of the UI framework used. A single thread is dedicated to the job of getting messages of the queue and dispatching those for further handling. For example, the WPF `Dispatcher` and the new Windows Extensible Application Markup Language (XAML) `CoreDispatcher` types clearly convey their role through the type name.

To make things more concrete, what happens when a user clicks a button? From a window manager’s point of view, this corresponds to sending various messages such as button down, button up, and button click to the window that’s underneath the mouse cursor. For Graphics Device Interface (GDI)-based frameworks like Windows Forms, controls like a button correspond to individual windows, so the Windows input manager can post a message that uniquely identifies the control involved in the click, as well as the coordinates of the cursor (relative to the control’s origin coordinate) and the button of the mouse that was pressed. For other frameworks like Windows Presentation Foundation (WPF) and Windows XAML, controls are usually rendered in a different way, on a single canvas that stretches the entire top-level window of the application. In that case, Windows sees only a single window no matter what control on it gets clicked. When the message loop receives a click message, the dispatcher takes care of interpreting the data to figure out which rendered control was underneath the cursor when the user clicked. From a programmer’s point of view, handling a click message is as easy as hooking up an event handler to the control. The dispatcher takes care of finding the control object instance and raising the event to run the user’s code.

What’s key in this discussion is how user code runs in response to the receipt of a window message. The thread that reads from the message queue (often referred to as the dispatcher thread) is ultimately the thread where user code for event handlers gets to run. If this code takes a long time to complete, no other messages can be read from the queue. [Figure 31.7](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31fig07) shows the call stack for a button click event in Windows Forms. To see this result, use the project properties to enable native debugging on the Debug tab. If not all stack frames are shown, right-click in the Call Stack window to enable the Show External Code option.

![Image](images/00773.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.7 Dispatching a button click message to an event handler.

I’ve chosen to show a Windows Forms call stack here because it’s a bit simpler than the WPF or Windows XAML call stacks. However, if you repeat this experiment for those other UI frameworks, you’ll still see the same `user32` entries with `DispatchMessageW` sitting somewhere on the call stack. This is the window manager and input system of Windows that lives in user32.dll, dispatching a message that gets served by our so-called `WndProc` (for window procedure). You could think of this method as the UI framework’s event handler for the events sent by the native implementation of the window and input manager in the OS.

When the application doesn’t perform message processing (sometimes referred to as message pumping) for an extended period of time, the window manager will add the (Not Responding) text to the title bar. Or, if the application has its own window chrome, a classic window title bar will be rendered to indicate the application is hanging. [Figure 31.8](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31fig08) shows the message about a nonresponsive application in the title bar, alongside a Task Manager instance that shows the same information.

![Image](images/00774.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.8 Task Manager’s view of a non-responsive application.

In this case, Task Manager actually reveals what’s wrong. On this eight-CPU system, seeing an application use 12% of all CPU resources is indicative of a single thread that’s running 100% of the time. Combined with the nonresponsiveness message, it’s pretty clear the UI thread is stuck in an infinite loop.

This case study clearly shows how asynchrony is an essential technique to keep UI applications responsive. Assuming that some heavyweight CPU-bound task has to run in response to a UI event, we should offload this work to a different thread. When the work completes, we can post back to the UI thread to render the result. [Figure 31.9](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31fig09) shows the worker thread and the UI thread’s interactions in such a setting.

![Image](images/00775.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.9 Offloading computation through multithreading.

However, long-running CPU-bound activity is not the only source of blocking that often kills the user experience. I/O requests are another common source of trouble. For example, allowing the user to enter a URL to be processed may result in a lengthy download operation. This, too, should be carried out asynchronously to free up the UI thread while the request is being taken care of in the background. As explained earlier in this chapter, no long-running thread is involved with this type of I/O processing. When the request completes, a thread pool thread is woken up to run code that can pick up the result from memory and invoke user code to perform further processing of the result. At that point, we could post back to the UI thread and render the web page, as shown in [Figure 31.10](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31fig10).

![Image](images/00776.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.10 Asynchronous processing of an I/O operation.

This whirlwind tour through UI frameworks has revealed a common need for asynchronous programming to keep user experiences top class. In fact, this was one of the main motivations for the new WinRT APIs for Windows 8 applications to provide only asynchronous means to perform long-running operations. This has gotten increasingly important as UI input is increasingly based on touch, where various gestures are expected to result in prompt action. With no mouse cursor to wiggle, stuck touch-centric UIs leave the user in the dark: Did the application freeze, is the whole machine stuck, should I try again? As you’ll learn in this chapter, as a manager code developer with C# or Visual Basic, you’re in an ideal position to leverage asynchronous APIs—including those in Windows Runtime (WinRT)—thanks to great language support.

#### Scalability

Another area where asynchronous programming is quintessential is the construction of scalable services. When dealing with many requests, it’s common to initiate the processing for a request on the thread pool. This technique is used to reduce the thread creation and deletion churn that would occur if each request would use a dedicated thread. Because thread creation is rather expensive, it’s better to reuse threads using a pool mechanism.

When using a pool, a critical question to answer is how many threads should be allocated. The ideal number of threads is quite simply the same as the amount of CPUs available. Using fewer threads causes underutilization of the system, which may be warranted if many different services are run on the same machine, restricting each service to a subset of the available processing power. Using more threads isn’t a particularly good idea because of the additional context switching cost incurred.

Where things get tricky is when threads in the pool are blocked. If no new threads are allocated, new service requests can’t be processed and may end up in a request queue. Users of the service will experience longer wait times, and the system may come to a grinding halt. By adding new threads to inflate the thread pool, it would seem we can tackle this problem. However, when the blocked threads wake up, we can end up with more running threads than the ideal number, again causing excessive and expensive context switching. Not to mention the new problem of when to deflate the thread pool again. Also, threads are rather costly due to the memory allocation for their stacks, so adding more threads causes more memory pressure as well.

As you might have guessed by now, asynchrony can come to the rescue once more. When the processing of a request has to carry out a long-running operation—usually I/O bound (for example, to fetch data from disk or retrieve data from a database)—it shouldn’t cause the request processing thread to block. Instead, it should perform the operation in an asynchronous fashion, allowing the thread to accept other requests while the current request is awaiting the completion of its asynchronous operations. When the background operation finishes, a thread pool thread is woken up again to continue the associated request’s processing. This may involve other asynchronous operations, repeating those steps until a final response can be sent back to the client. Keep in mind that performing an I/O operation doesn’t require a thread to exist for the duration of the operation, so asynchrony prevents the thread pool inflation problem. [Figure 31.11](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31fig11) illustrates a service accepting requests, using asynchronous programming to prevent oversubscription of the thread pool.

![Image](images/00777.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.11 Asynchronous processing in a web server.

For the completion of an I/O operation to be reassociated with the original request, a little piece of information is flown with the I/O request. For web servers, this includes the HTTP connection that should be used to send the response back to the requesting client. Other information may include security credentials. When using ASP.NET, this synchronization is achieve using the `SynchronizationContext` class. As a matter of fact, this same mechanism is used in UI programming to post operations back to the UI thread. When reading about the new `await` expression language feature later in this chapter, you will learn how this important synchronization upon completion of asynchronous operations is taken care of transparently, by so-called `awaiter` types.

* * *

Note: About IIS, ASP.NET, and Node.JS

Web server software such as Internet Information Services (IIS) and web application frameworks such as ASP.NET have offered asynchronous capabilities for a long time, but those have been notoriously hard to use, in part because of the use of the classic Asynchronous Programming Model (APM), which is discussed later in this chapter.

A more recent and quite popular web server technology called node.js deeply embraces asynchrony and is based on JavaScript, where asynchronous programming has become a way of life. The structure of the code reflects receiving of requests, completion of various background and I/O operations, and so on. A trivial example is shown here:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_000.html_p1563pro01)

var http = require('http')
var port = process.env.port || 1337;
http.createServer(function(req, res) {
  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' });
  res.end('Hello World\n');
}).listen(port);

Despite the concise nature of the code, the logical flow of request processing is still encoded in a sea of (nested) callbacks, making more involved logic harder to write. You’ll see how the language features in C# and Visual Basic hide the complexity of callbacks.

* * *

We’ve focused mainly on the mechanics behind asynchronous request processing, but it’s good to take a step back and think about the logical flow, as well. From a logical point of view, processing a web request is still a sequential operation consisting of reading the request headers, carrying out various potentially long-running operations, and sending back the response. However, to build such a request pipeline in a scalable and performing manner, the sequential nature of the code has to disturbed at every point where long latencies may occur.

The next sections discuss various programming patterns that have been used throughout the years to deal with asynchrony. The common property of all those patterns is their invasive nature to the structure of the code, clearly reflecting the mechanics of the underling processing using callback procedures. The C# 5.0 and Visual Basic 11 features for asynchronous programming restore the logical sequential flow of performing work even when asynchrony is required. To appreciate the beauty of those new features, we start by looking at the traditional, complicated library approaches.

### Old Asynchronous Programming Patterns

To understand the fundamental properties of asynchronous programming, let’s start our discussion by taking a look at various library approaches to deal with the problem at hand. Over the years, different patterns were introduced in the .NET Framework to tackle the problem of asynchronous programming.

After learning about those patterns, you’ll be in a good position to appreciate how programming language abstractions can bring a lot of relief when writing asynchronous code.

#### Asynchronous Programming Model

The oldest of the asynchronous programming patterns was introduced right from the start, with .NET Framework 1.0\. We’ve already covered this pattern in passing in [Chapter 17](#part0027.html_ch17), “[Delegates](#part0027.html_ch17),” and in [Chapter 28](#part0038.html_ch28), “[Working with I/O](#part0038.html_ch28).” Nonetheless, let’s revisit this pattern briefly and identify its core characteristics.

This pattern consists of two related methods, using a `Begin` and `End` prefix convention. For example, asynchronous read operations on a `Stream` object are defined as follows:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_001.html_p1564pro01)

IAsyncResult BeginRead(byte[] buffer, int offset, int count,
                       AsyncCallback callback, object state);
int EndRead(IAsyncResult asyncResult);

The `BeginRead` method takes all the required parameters to start the asynchronous read operation. In this particular example, a buffer is specified for the output to be written to. In addition, an offset into the array, as well as the number of bytes to read, is specified.

Asynchrony prevents the method from returning the number of bytes read, as its synchronous `Read` counterpart would do. After all, this value isn’t known until the operation completes. Instead, the operation returns an `IAsyncResult` object that represents the operation that’s in flight. One way to obtain the result is to poll this object’s `IsCompleted` property on a periodic basis:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_002.html_p1565pro01)

public interface IAsyncResult
{
    object AsyncState { get; }
    WaitHandle AsyncWaitHandle { get; }
    bool CompletedSynchronously { get; }
    bool IsCompleted { get; }
}

This is clearly a suboptimal approach. Other approaches of waiting for the `AsyncWaitHandle` are even worse, causing the caller to block until the event is set. Instead, we’d rather get notified when the operation completes. This is achieved by passing in a delegate of type `AsyncCallback` to the `BeginRead` operation. For example:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_003.html_p1565pro02)

FileStream fs = File.OpenRead(fileName);
byte[] buffer = new byte[4 * 1024 * 1024]; // 4MB
fs.BeginRead(buffer, 0, buffer.Length, iar =>
{
    int count = fs.EndRead(iar);
    // Process the buffer's elements in the range [0, count – 1].
}, null);

Inside the callback—here specified using a lambda expression—the `EndRead` method is used to retrieve the result. This is required because the same `AsyncCallback` could be shared across multiple `BeginRead` invocations. The `state` parameter allows an object to be shared between the initiation of the operation and its completion. With the advent of closures in C#, this parameter has become less useful. Even in this little fragment, the `FileStream` object as well as the buffer array are going to be accessed from the callback.

Not only does the use of a callback make control flow more tedious, it also makes resource management much harder.
