For example, we shouldn’t dispose the `FileStream` object before the read operation has completed. However, what if something fails? Will the exception come out during the `BeginRead` call or during the `EndRead` call? Although the failure to obtain a result will only be communicated during the completion phase, it’s not uncommon for the `Begin` call of an APM to throw, as well, indicating the failure to start the operation. As a result, exception handling blocks and resource management (with the `using` statement) get spread out across different locations in the code.

Unfortunately, there are more complexities around the APM pattern. For example, there’s no out-of-the-box way to perform cancellation of an outstanding operation. Also, completion callbacks usually happen on the thread pool, as shown in [Figure 31.12](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31fig12).

![Image](images/00778.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.12 An AsyncCallback running on the thread pool.

When accessing shared state, you have to be extremely careful to make sure that no-one else is touching the state at the same time. Similarly, proper synchronization is required when performing UI operations in the context of the callback. This leads to more complexity:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_004.html_p1566pro01)

FileStream fs = File.OpenRead(fileName);
byte[] buffer = new byte[4 * 1024 * 1024]; // 4MB
fs.BeginRead(buffer, 0, buffer.Length, iar =>
{
    int count;
    try
    {
        count = fs.EndRead(iar);
    }
    catch (IOException ex)
    {
        // Handle the error.
        return;
    }
    finally
    {
        fs.Dispose();
    }

    // Post the operation to the UI message loop, e.g. in Windows Forms.
    this.Invoke(new Action(() =>
    {
        // Process the buffer's elements in the range [0, count – 1]
        // and render the result in the UI.
    });
}, null);

As you can see, it’s easy to drown in the manual plumbing when dealing with the APM pattern directly. We haven’t even gotten into what it would take to write your own asynchronous operation, requiring the (complex) implementation of `IAsyncResult` that often has to deal with multithreaded aspects and whatnot.

It’s useful to take a step back and look at the code transformation compared to an alternative synchronous approach:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_005.html_p1567pro01)

using (FileStream fs = File.OpenRead(fileName))
{
    byte[] buffer = new byte[4 * 1024 * 1024]; // 4MB
    int count;
    try
    {
        count = fs.Read(buffer, 0, buffer.Length);
    }
    catch (IOException ex)
    {
        // Handle the error.
        return;
    }

    // We never left the UI thread, so we can process the buffer's
    // elements in the range [0, count – 1] right here and now.
}

Although this code doesn’t have the desired effects of asynchrony—to avoid blocking of UI threads and improved scalability in services—it’s much easier on the eye, for sure. The invasive code surgery required to make the code asynchronous caused all of the logic to be split across two methods.

In fact, we’ve only shown a simple piece of code here, making a single asynchronous request. What if we were to process a whole file in batches of a few megabytes each time. For example, suppose that we’re analyzing a huge log file of several gigabytes. We can’t load the whole file into memory because it’s too big. If we read large chunks, we’re definitely going to block while the I/O is in progress, causing a bad user experience. So, we have to go down the asynchronous route and read the file in blocks. At the conceptual level, this is a simple loop. In synchronous code, we just write this:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_006.html_p1567pro02)

using (FileStream fs = File.OpenRead(fileName))
{
    byte[] buffer = new byte[4 * 1024 * 1024]; // 4MB
    int count;
    do
    {
        count = fs.Read(buffer, 0, buffer.Length);
        // Process the block and render results.
    } while (count == buffer.Length);
}

When we attempt to make this method use asynchronous I/O reads instead, we face the challenge of causing the next loop iteration to be triggered by the current read’s callback. [Figure 31.13](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31fig13) shows a diagram of the desired effect.

![Image](images/00779.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.13 Slicing a loop body for asynchronous processing.

As you attempt to do this, you quickly find yourself writing a state machine to handle the different phases of execution. Obviously, don’t forget to deal with exceptions properly, dispose resources at the right times, synchronize with the UI thread, and so on. I’ll leave this as a challenge for you. One little warning: This isn’t a job for the faint of heart!

#### Event-Based Asynchronous Pattern (EAP)

In .NET Framework 2.0, a new pattern for asynchronous programming was added, based on events to signal an operation’s completion. This approach makes dealing with asynchrony a little bit easier in the context of UI programming because you can use an event handler to handle the completion case. Controls such as the `PictureBox` in Windows Forms use this pattern to handle long-running load operations (for example, when a picture is downloaded from the Web). Because this control is added to a designer surface, hooking up a `LoadCompleted` event handler is fairly straightforward.

To understand the essentials of this pattern, we study the `WebClient` class. To perform download operations, various methods are provided. To keep things simple, we look at the `DownloadString` family of synchronous and asynchronous operations. The synchronous method is quite predictable:

public string DownloadString(Uri address);

Calling this method blocks the caller until the download operation completes, returning back the string, or throwing an exception in case of a failure. To take an asynchronous approach, we use the following two class members instead:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_007.html_p1569pro01)

public void DownloadStringAsync(Uri address, object userToken);
public event DownloadStringCompletedEventHandler DownloadStringCompleted;

The `DownloadStringAsync` method kicks off the operation. The overload shown here is the more general of the two that are available, providing a `userToken` parameter that you can use to correlate a request with a response. This is useful when the EAP-based class supports multiple simultaneous requests. In this case, you can use the token object to perform an equality check in the completed event handler, matching the completion with its original request. This is similar to the role played by the `IAsyncResult` object in the APM.

* * *

Note: Parallels Between APM and EAP

The APM and the EAP model share quite a few things. One such thing is the use of a state parameter shared across the initiation and completion of an operation.

In the case of the APM, this state parameter was usually used to exchange the object that has the `End` method defined on it. By using this pattern, the completion callback simply had to extract the `UserState` property, cast it back to the original type, and invoke the `End` method with the received `IAsyncResult`.

EAP changes the use of the state parameter (known as the user token) a little bit. Because the completion information is now provided through the completion event arguments, the user token merely provides an additional slot to exchange information between the request initiator and the completion handler.

User tokens are sometimes used for correlation purposes, for example to keep track of the `Uri` that’s being downloaded. In more advanced scenarios though, correlation can be get trickier. It’s not uncommon for developers to tag requests with `Guid` values, and perform dictionary operations to perform lookups in the completion handler. This can be extremely error-prone when multi-threading is involved.

At the end of the day, both patterns have their pros and cons, but there’s a common set of problems that all boil down to the need for excessive plumbing with callbacks.

* * *

To receive the response data, we have to use an event handler this time. Contrary to the APM, there’s no way to poll the request for completion or to block until it completes. Those are arguably nice properties. However, the fact remains that completion of the operation is signaled through a callback mechanism, this time using a .NET event which is merely a delegate in disguise. Assuming a code-only approach (that is, without a designer to hook up the event handler), we end up with a simple example like this:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_008.html_p1570pro01)

WebClient client = new WebClient();
client.DownloadStringCompleted += (o, e) =>
{
    // Assuming everything went well, here's how we get the result:
    string html = e.Result;
    ...
};
client.DownloadStringAsync(uri);

One particular odd effect this event-based approach has on the structure of the code is the inverted lexical order. First, while hooking up the event handler, we have to specify the code that will run after the completion. Next, we write the code to kick off the operation.

Although obtaining the result has gotten simpler by easy inspection of the `Result` property, some complexity still surrounds the error handling. The event arguments type for the `DownloadStringCompleted` event derives from the `AsyncCompletedEventArgs` class, providing the following set of commonly used properties:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_009.html_p1570pro02)

public class AsyncCompletedEventArgs : EventArgs
{
    ...
    public bool Cancelled { get; }
    public Exception Error { get; }
    public object UserState { get; }
}

Notice how you can use the `Error` property to detect whether the operation failed. To check for this case, we have to trade the convenience of `try...catch` handlers for checks on the `Error` object. Though we could rethrow the exception in our event handler simply to restore exception handling, this looks like a big hack:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_010.html_p1571pro01)

client.DownloadStringCompleted += (o, e) =>
{
    if (e.Error != null)
    {
        try
        {
            throw e.Error; // simply to restore structured exception handling?!
        }
        catch (WebException ex)
        {
            // Handle an error we can deal with.
        }
        return;
    }

    string html = e.Result;
    ...
};

As with the APM, this doesn’t take care of failure during the initialization phase of the asynchronous operation, so we have to guard against that in some cases as well.

The EAP brought some welcome enhancements to support cancellation using a `CancelAsync` method. Nonetheless, all of the plumbing required to handle cancellation properly can get quite complex as well. Similarly, the MSDN documentation guidance on writing EAP-compliant types explains how progress reporting can be added, but getting it right isn’t a trivial task either.

Ignoring all of those complexities for a moment, the bigger picture is very similar to the APM’s overall structure. When writing asynchronous code using this pattern, you have to split a logical control flow into several phases based on a callback mechanism. The set of issues that arises when performing such a callback-style transformation of the code are the same as for the APM. For example, writing a loop that does perform one asynchronous operation at a time is quite hard and incredibly error-prone. Once more, we’ll leave this as an exercise for the motivated reader.

#### Task-Based Asynchronous Pattern (TAP)

The introduction of the `Task` type in .NET 4.0 provides for a way to standardize on the object representation of an operation’s eventual completion. In fact, tasks are sometimes referred to as futures, clearly indicating their nature of having a result in the future.

Looking back at the APM, you might wonder whether we don’t already have such a type in the form of the `IAsyncResult` interface. Although they share some similarities, a couple of drawbacks apply to using this type when representing futures. One problem is the separation of callbacks from the object representing the operation. Another one is the absence of the operation’s result on the `IAsyncResult` object itself. In other words, this type can’t stand on its own without a `Begin`/`End` method pattern to complement it. Moreover, exposing asynchronous functionality using the APM can be quite tedious, having to provide an `IAsyncResult` implementation, which is an error-prone activity. This same remark applies to the EAP, where a separate object needs to be built with a method to kick off the operation, an event to signal completion, and optional cancellation and progress mechanisms.

With tasks, we have a great new way to make both the consumption of asynchronous operations and their implementation much nicer and easier. First of all, a task object provides direct access to its eventual result through properties like `Result` and `Exception`. Second, callbacks are specified on the task object itself through the `ContinueWith` method. And third, cancellation and progress reporting can be provided through built-in types such as `CancellationToken` and `IProgress<T>`.

By representing asynchronous operations using tasks, we can greatly simplify the consumption of their results and keep a high level of symmetry with the synchronous variants. For example, consider the synchronous `DownloadString` method on `WebClient`:

string DownloadString(Uri address);

In .NET 4.5, a `DownloadStringTaskAsync` method was added, using a task object to represent the eventual result. The signature is shown here:

Task<string> DownloadStringTaskAsync(Uri address);

Notice the one and only difference in the signature? Instead of returning a `string`, the method returns a `Task<string>`. From a naming point of view, such task-based asynchronous methods are suffixed with `Async`. Because the `WebClient` class already had a `DownloadStringAsync` based on the EAP, the word `Task` is added to the name.

This method is an example of the so-called Task-based Asynchronous Pattern, often abbreviated as TAP. Starting from .NET 4.5, this pattern is the recommended way to expose asynchronous functionality.

* * *

Note: Better, Again?

Critical readers might rightfully wonder whether there won’t be a new pattern again in future releases. After all, we’ve already seen the APM and the EAP that both used to be the recommended way to implement asynchronous operations.

What makes the TAP different is its tight integration with language features, as we shall see in the next sections. Asynchronous methods in C# and Visual Basic implement methods that conform to the TAP.

From an evolutionary point of view, once something ends up being baked into the compiler, it’s highly unlikely to see it getting replaced by a new pattern. The presence of the APM and EAP clearly shows how the problem at hand is a rather complex one. In some way, you could regard those library approaches as early experiments that ultimately led to the distillation of a pattern that lends itself nicely for language integration. This is where we’ve arrived today, with C# 5.0 and Visual Basic 11.

* * *

Let’s compare this pattern to the APM and the EAP one last time, to drive home the point about the great simplification the TAP provides. Using the APM, the `DownloadString` operation would consist of two methods, shown here:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_011.html_p1573pro01)

IAsyncResult BeginDownloadString(Uri address, AsyncCallback callback, object state);
string EndDownloadString(IAsyncResult result);

Notice how the return type has moved to a different method and how both methods should be glued together through the `IAsyncResult` (for example, through the `AsyncCallback`).

With the EAP, we again see two members. This time the result is received through a custom event arguments type:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_012.html_p1573pro02)

void DownloadStringAsync(Uri address);
event EventHandler<DownloadStringEventArgs> DownloadStringCompleted;

In both cases, consuming the methods is tedious due to the callback nature’s invasive nature of the code. Exposing asynchronous APIs is even more cumbersome, requiring the implementation of custom methods and types that work in concert. When using the TAP, no interface implementations or custom types are required.

Because a solid understanding of this new pattern is essential to understand the concept of asynchronous methods, we start with a thorough discussion of its different facets.

#### Method Naming and Overloading

Part of all the asynchronous patterns is convention. This is no different for the TAP. The first guideline is to give the method an `Async` suffix in its name. In case there’s already such a method for the EAP, the alternative `TaskAsync` suffix is picked. A good example of this is the `WebClient` class, which we explored in the previous section. For types that were based on the APM, no such conflict exists. A good example is on the `FileStream` class, which has the following members for `Read` and `Write` operations in .NET 4.5:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_013.html_p1573pro03)

// Sychronous methods
abstract int Read(byte[] buffer, int offset, int count);
abstract void Write(byte[] buffer, int offset, int count);

// APM methods
virtual IAsyncResult BeginRead(byte[] buffer, int offset, int count,
                               AsyncCallback callback, object state);
virtual IAsyncResult BeginWrite(byte[] buffer, int offset, int count,
                                AsyncCallback callback, object state);
virtual int EndRead(IAsyncResult asyncResult);
virtual void EndWrite(IAsyncResult asyncResult);

// TAP methods
Task<int> ReadAsync(byte[] buffer, int offset, int count);
virtual Task<int> ReadAsync(byte[] buffer, int offset, int count,
                            CancellationToken cancellationToken);
Task WriteAsync(byte[] buffer, int offset, int count);
virtual Task WriteAsync(byte[] buffer, int offset, int count,
                        CancellationToken cancellationToken);

The APM family of methods should look very familiar by now. One thing to point out though is the presence of the `virtual` keyword. Subtypes of the `System.IO.Stream` class can override those methods’ behavior, but what’s the default behavior then?

The answer lies in the presence of `abstract` synchronous methods, which should be implemented by the derived type. If such a method is not supported, `CanRead` and `CanWrite` properties can be implemented to return false. In case the subtype doesn’t override the virtual methods for asynchronous operations, the base class implementation simply wraps the synchronous counterparts. It’s worth nothing that this wrapping uses a task object internally, scheduling the synchronous invocation on the default `TaskScheduler`.

When looking at the TAP methods, notice how the most advanced overloads are also marked as `virtual`. The default implementation for those methods calls into the APM methods. This allows existing subtypes of the `Stream` class to support the new TAP pattern, without requiring additional work to revise their implementation.

* * *

Note: Converting APM Methods to TAP Methods

Given the recent addition of the TAP to the .NET Framework, you may encounter APIs that only have APM methods. To make those work nicely with the new asynchronous programming language features, the `TaskFactory` type provides a set of methods to build TAP wrappers around APM methods. For example:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_014.html_p1574pro01)

Task<TResult> FromAsync<TArg1, TArg2, TArg3, TResult>(
    Func<TArg1, TArg2, TArg3, AsyncCallback, object, IAsyncResult> beginMethod,
    Func<IAsyncResult, TResult> endMethod,
    TArg1 arg1, TArg2 arg2, TArg3 arg3, object state);

This signature may look frightening at first, but it’s rather easy to understand. The first two parameters are used to provide delegates to the `Begin` and `End` methods. This particular overload is used for APM methods that take three parameters. The signature of the `Func` delegates should clearly reflect the APM pattern with its `AsyncCallback` and `IAsyncResult` parameters.

Finally, three parameters and the APM’s typical state parameter are supplied, as well, used to kick off the underlying operation. A hot `Task<TResult>` is returned, representing the underlying running APM-based operation. Eventually, this task will contain the result or an exception that resulted upon completion of the operation. If an `OperationCanceledException` occurred, the task object will go into the `TaskStatus.Canceled` state.

An example of wrapping the `BeginRead`/`EndRead` set of methods on a stream object is shown here. Notice that you don’t have to do this because `System.IO.Stream` contains TAP methods in .NET 4.5\. However, because we’re already familiar with the `Read` method signature, I’ve chosen to use this method as an example:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_015.html_p1575pro01)

Task<int> bytesRead = Task.Factory.FromAsync<byte[], int, int, int>(
    fs.BeginRead, fs.EndRead, buffer, 0, buffer.Length, null);

The first two `int` type parameters map onto the offset and count parameters on `BeginRead`. The last `int` type parameter represents the result returned by `EndRead`.

* * *

The return type of a TAP method can be `Task` or `Task<T>`. Returned task objects are expected to be hot, meaning they are already started when they are returned to the caller. As we’ll see in a bit, asynchronous method support in the language also allows for fire-and-forget methods that return `void`.

#### Cancellation

TAP methods often provide an overload with a `CancellationToken` parameter that you can use to cancel the ongoing operation. Such an overload only exists if the underlying operation has a meaningful way to abort work. If present, the `CancellationToken` parameter is passed after the parameters that occur on the corresponding synchronous variant.

For example, if an operation gets asynchronous behavior because it’s processed through a work queue, cancellation can be achieved by deleting the item from the queue if it hasn’t started yet. Another typical example is when the asynchronous operation performs other asynchronous operations which are cancelable. In that case, the `CancellationToken` is passed down to the underlying operations, providing deep cancellation support. When writing asynchronous methods in C# or Visual Basic (as explained later on), it’s quite common to wire up cancellation in this way. The following code fragment shows this. Don’t worry about the `async` modifier on the method and the `await` expressions just yet. This will become clear in a bit:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_016.html_p1575pro02)

async Task<int> DeepCancellationAsync(CancellationToken token)
{
    ...
    int n = await stream.ReadAsync(buffer, 0, buffer.Length, token);
    ...
    return result;
}

In this example, the `DeepCancellationAsync` method has a TAP-compliant signature, taking in no parameters to the underlying operation except for a `CancellationToken`. This token gets passed down to the `ReadAsync` BCL method. An attempt to cancel our user operation ultimately results in a request to cancel the I/O operation in a best-effort manner.

Even if cancellation is supported, it’s recommended to provide an overload without a `CancellationToken` parameter. Such an overload can simply call the cancelable overload, supplying `CancellationToken.None`. This is what the nonvirtual `ReadAsync` and `WriteAsync` methods on the `Stream` class do. Subclasses can simply ignore the `CancellationToken` if no cancellation support can be provided.

#### Progress Reporting

An additional parameter may be provided to report progress for the in-flight operation, using the `IProgress<T>` type. Just like the optional parameter to supply a CancellationToken, this parameter should appear after the operation’s core parameters. A null reference can be supplied by callers of the method to indicate no progress reports are desired. An example of a signature with progress reporting is shown here:

Task ProcessRecordsAsync(int categoryId, IProgress<int> progress);

This method could process a set of records from some store, matching the specified category identification number. The progress parameter allows tracking of the operation based on `int` values, which could denote the completion percentage. Callers of the method could use this parameter to render a progress bar. The .NET Framework comes with a default implementation of this interface, called `Progress<T>`. By passing in an `Action<T>` delegate to the constructor, it’s straightforward to create a progress object with a custom progress handler:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_017.html_p1576pro01)

// Ignore the await keyword, which will be explained later on.
await ProcessRecordsAsync(new Progress<int>(percent =>
{
    // Report progress, e.g. on the UI
}));

The `Progress<T>` class also has a `ProgressChanged` event of type `EventHandler<T>`. You can use this event to attach additional progress handlers. Notice the generic parameter `T` is not constrained to derive from `EventArgs`. This constraint was removed from `EventHandler<T>`, enabling this simple `IProgress<T>` interface.

* * *

Note: Synchronizing with the UI

A common frustration with asynchronous programming has always been the need to manually synchronize with the original context, where the operation was started. Luckily, the `Progress<T>` type addresses this by capturing the current `SynchronizationContext` upon instantiation. When raising progress reporting events, handlers are invoked on the captured context. For example, if we were to call our `ProcessRecordsAsync` method with the custom `Progress<int>` object—as illustrated earlier—on the UI thread, the callbacks would occur there as well.

We discuss synchronization behavior of TAP methods in more detail later on. Later in this chapter, when discussing the `await` keyword, we come back to the topic of synchronization to learn how the new asynchronous programming language support hides a lot of the synchronization complexity.

* * *

#### Exception Behavior

During the discussion about the APM and the EAP, you saw how dealing with errors can be tricky. The problem with those patterns lies in their multiphased nature, where exceptions can occur at various stages. In the world of the APM, exceptions can come out during `Begin` and `End` method calls. When using the EAP, exceptions can occur during the `Async` start operation, but can be reported through the `Completed` event arguments as well.

For the TAP, things are much simpler. Other than method parameter usage exceptions (such as `ArgumentException`), no errors should be raised when invoking the TAP method. Instead, all exceptions have to be propagated through the returned task object. Users of the method can inspect the returned task to detect a `Faulted` state (for example, using the `ContinueWith` method).

During the discussion about asynchronous methods later in this chapter, you’ll see how those automatically propagate exceptions through the returned task object. That is, every exception thrown in the body of the asynchronous method comes out on the returned task:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_018.html_p1577pro01)

async Task<string> ReportErrorAsync()
{
    ...
    int x = await Bar();
    if (x < 0)
        throw new InvalidOperationException();
    ...
}

In this sample code fragment, an `InvalidOperationException` is thrown at some time during the asynchronous operation kicked off by a call to our `ReportErrorAsync` method. At that point, the returned `Task<string>` goes into the `Faulted` state. Continuation callbacks attached to this task now have a chance to observe the exception:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_019.html_p1577pro02)

ReportErrorAsync().ContinueWith(task =>
{
    if (task.Exception != null)
        // Handle exception
});

With the new `await` expression language feature—discussed later in this chapter—we can get rid of the manual `ContinueWith` callback voodoo and simply write the following instead:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_020.html_p1577pro03)

try
{
    string result = await ReportErrorAsync()
    // Process successful result
}
catch (InvalidOperationException ex)
{
    // Handle exception
}

Because asynchronous methods use the TAP method conventions and are the recommended way to implement asynchronous operations from now on, error handling has become much more streamlined. The rich capabilities of `await` expressions combined with typical control flow primitives makes handling asynchronous exceptions really easy.

#### Synchronization Behavior

Asynchrony is a traditional source of interesting synchronization behavior due to the callbacks getting invoked upon completion of the operation (for example, on the thread pool). Without any manual synchronization to the context of the original caller of the asynchronous operation, all sorts of things can go bad. The most common example is attempting to update the UI from a callback, as shown in [Figure 31.14](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31fig14).

![Image](images/00780.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.14 Cross-thread violations when updating the UI.

Just like the APM and the EAP, the TAP doesn’t require callbacks to happen in a particular context. When the task gets signaled—in ways discussed in the next section—continuations can run in the context of the signaling thread. For example, when wrapping an asynchronous I/O operation, the underlying completion happens on the thread pool, which will also be the place where callbacks are called from.

Automatic synchronization back to the context of the caller of the TAP-based asynchronous method is provided through `await` expressions. At the lower level of the task object, no such implicit synchronization takes place. The following piece of code shows the difference:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_021.html_p1578pro01)

private void downloadButton_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    webClient.DownloadStringTaskAsync(bing).ContinueWith(task =>
    {
        // Update the UI will fail here, because we're called on the thread pool
        // after the I/O operation of the WebClient completed.
        webBrowser.NavigateToString(task.Result);
    });
}

In this first example using `ContinueWith` to hook up a continuation to the download task, bad things will happen. [Figure 31.15](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31fig15) illustrates this problem.

![Image](images/00781.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.15 Callbacks don’t run on the UI thread.

However, if we leverage the new asynchronous programming features, synchronization is magically taken care of for us. The following code fragment shows this. For a detailed discussion of the `async` and `await` keywords, and how the synchronization is achieved, you have to wait a few more pages:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_022.html_p1579pro01)

private async void downloadButton_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    string html = await webClient.DownloadStringTaskAsync(bing);

    // The asynchronous method is resumed after the awaited task completes
    // and continues its execution on the original SynchronizationContext.
    // Hence, we can safely update the UI here.
    webBrowser.NavigateToString(task.Result);
}

Once more, this shows how asynchronous methods, `await` expressions, and the TAP work hand in hand to provide a great experience when writing asynchronous code.

#### Implementing a TAP Method, Take One

Even though the easiest way to implement TAP methods is by using the new `async` modifier on a method declaration, we start off by examining a few handcrafted TAP methods. This will clearly illustrate the nature of the `Task`-based approach to signal the eventual completion of the method’s operation. Later in this chapter, you will learn how to simplify this by using asynchronous methods.

The key aspect to providing a TAP-based method is to return a `Task` or `Task<T>` object as soon as possible, which prevents the caller of the method from getting stuck. At a later point in time, this task gets set to let the caller know a result is available. Therefore, there are two sides to a task object: the receiving end (consumer) and the signaling end (producer). The `Task` class doesn’t provide a signaling facility. If it would, everyone who has a reference to the task object would be able to influence its outcome. To keep the signaling of a task separate, a `TaskCompletionSource<T>` is used. An object of this type provides a `Task<T>` object that can be handed out to consumers, while producers can complete the task at a later point in time.

Let’s start by creating a simple TAP method that will return a task that gets signaled after a specified duration. The skeleton code looks like this:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_023.html_p1580pro01)

static Task<T> ReturnAfter<T>(T value, int milliseconds)
{
    var tcs = new TaskCompletionSource<T>();
    // Kick off work that will ultimately signal the task.
    return tcs.Task;
}

This method returns a task that will be completed with a specified value of type `T`, after the specified time elapses. One way to implement the signaling part is to use a `System.Threading.Timer`, as shown here:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_024.html_p1580pro02)

static Task<T> ReturnAfter<T>(T value, int milliseconds)
{
    var tcs = new TaskCompletionSource<T>();

    // This overload passes the timer as the state parameter to the callback.
    var timer = new Timer(state =>
    {
        ((Timer)state).Dispose();
        tcs.TrySetResult(value);
    });
    timer.Change(milliseconds, Timeout.Infinite /* no recurrence */);

    return tcs.Task;
}

Via this approach, a `Timer` is set up to fire after the specified duration, providing the result to the `Task` through the `TaskCompletionSource<T>` object. By the time this happens, the task object can already have been returned to the caller of our `ReturnAfter` method.

* * *

Note: Rooting Timer Objects

Dealing with `Timer` objects can prove quite tricky. If no reference to the timer instance is maintained, the timer can get finalized and garbage collected, preventing the timer from ever firing. To avoid this, timer objects often need manual rooting to keep them reachable by the garbage collector.

In our example, we got lucky by using a particular constructor overload, combined with the `Change` method. The details of why this approach works are outside the scope of this book. In typical cases where timers are used, the timer instance is stored in a field somewhere, keeping it alive, so there’s no issue at all.

Even better, in today’s .NET 4.5 era, you shouldn’t have to interact with the `Timer` class very often, thanks to the addition of the new `Task.Delay` method. In fact, our `ReturnAfter` example is very similar to this `Task.Delay`. Further on in this section, we replace `ReturnAfter`’s use of a `Timer` in favor of asynchronous composition with `Task.Delay`. The `Task.Delay` method takes care of rooting the timer it uses internally.

* * *

To provide cancellation support, we start by adding a `CancellationToken` parameter on the method. Because we can do deep cancellation by disposing the timer early, we wire up the timer’s `Dispose` method to the token, as shown in the next code fragment:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_025.html_p1581pro01)

static Task<T> ReturnAfter<T>(T value, int milliseconds, CancellationToken token)
{
    var tcs = new TaskCompletionSource<T>();

    var ctr = default(CancellationTokenRegistration);

    var timer = new Timer(state =>
    {
        ((Timer)state).Dispose();
        ctr.Dispose(); // A struct, thus safe to dispose the default value.
        tcs.TrySetResult(value);
    });

    if (token.CanBeCanceled)
    {
        ctr = token.Register(() =>
        {
            timer.Dispose();
            tcs.TrySetCanceled();
        });
    }

    timer.Change(milliseconds, Timeout.Infinite /* no recurrence */);

    return tcs.Task;
}

The key thing here is the use of the `Register` method to provide a callback to the `CancellationToken`. This callback is invoked when cancellation is requested through the token’s `CancellationTokenSource`. When this happens, we dispose the timer and try to move the returned task to the `Canceled` state by a call to `TrySetCanceled`. Notice the use of the `Try` family of methods on `TaskCompletionSource<T>`. This is done because the timer and the cancellation request may be racing to signal the task.

Another thing that catches attention is the use of `CanBeCanceled` to avoid hooking up cancellation if the supplied token will never reach a cancelled state. This is the case for `CancellationToken.None`, for example. Also, when using the `Register` method on `CancellationToken`, it’s important to dispose the `CancellationTokenRegistration` when the registration is no longer needed. In this case, when the timer fires, we can safely unregister our cancellation callback.

* * *

Note: Order Matters

Writing concurrent code is tricky. Luckily, the sample shown here is one of the more tricky cases that you shouldn’t encounter that often. As mentioned before, you can reimplement this method using `Task.Delay`, which simplifies matters a lot (see further).

One tricky aspect of this sample code fragment is the order of the operations. By using the `Timer` constructor overload that doesn’t take in the due time, we’ve created a timer instance that isn’t started yet. Before we kick off the timer by a call to `Change`, we wire up the cancellation support. If we were to do this after the call to `Change`, the timer may fire before we can register the cancellation callback. In that (rare) case, we would have a nondisposed `CancellationTokenRegistration` laying around.

One thing worth pointing out is that `CancellationTokenRegistration` is a struct. Therefore, if it’s not assigned because no cancelable token was passed in, we won’t cause a null reference exception when trying to call `Dispose` on it.

* * *

As mentioned before, this code is very similar to the `Task.Delay` method that ships as part of .NET 4.5’s Base Class Library (BCL). Instead of dealing with the `Timer` class ourselves—merely done here for illustrative purposes—we could build our `ReturnAfter` method on top of `Task.Delay`. An example is shown here:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_026.html_p1582pro01)

static Task<T> ReturnAfter<T>(T value, int milliseconds, CancellationToken token)
{
    return Task.Delay(milliseconds, token)
               .ContinueWith(t => value,
                             TaskContinuationOptions.OnlyOnRanToCompletion);
}

In this example, we simply delegate the work to the `Delay` method, also passing the cancellation token along. Using `ContinueWith`, we hook up a continuation to return the value but only if the delay operation ran to completion. If a cancellation occurred, the resulting task transitions into the `Canceled` state.

This approach uses the rich continuation model on tasks directly, without the need for a complicated interaction with a `TaskCompletionSource<T>` object in our own code. Nonetheless, the shape of the code is still largely the same: Somewhere deep inside the asynchronous method, there’s a piece of code that will run at a later point in time. In our `Timer`-based approach, the timer callback occupied a lot of space, so it stood out from the rest of the code. When using `ContinueWith`, there’s still a callback. It just doesn’t catch the eye at first glance.

Further on in this chapter, you’ll learn how the new language features for asynchronous programming leave the act of creating callbacks to the compiler. From a logical control flow point of view, our `ReturnAfter` is still a sequential operation. It just happens that a long pause occurs in there, and we don’t want to block during that time. This simple observation has far-reaching consequences to the shape of our code though. In other words, although the logical control flow is still very linear, the mechanics to achieve this in a nonblocking way require thorough restructuring of the code to use callbacks. With the new language features, we can rewrite our `ReturnAfter` method as follows:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_027.html_p1583pro01)

async static Task<T> ReturnAfter<T>(T value, int delay, CancellationToken token)
{
    await Task.Delay(delay, token)
    return value;
}

The meaning of the `async` modifier and the `await` expression will become clear to you after a few more pages.

* * *

Note: No Parallelism Needed

It can’t be emphasized enough. Asynchronous programming does not imply CPU-level parallelism. During this chapter’s introduction, we talked about how the hardware is smart about keeping the CPU idle while other devices such as disks and network cards can perform their I/O operations, delivering results to memory using techniques like DMA.

While the Task Parallel Library was originally built for parallel programming uses (what’s in a name?), the `Task<T>` construct is truly a so-called future, which is totally independent from the way its eventual result is obtained.

For computational asynchrony, the result may be delivered from computation on a different thread, potentially running in parallel on another CPU core. An example of this is `Task.Run`.

However, using the `TaskCompletionSource<T>`, it’s possible to create a `Task<T>` object that has no binding to the task pool in any shape or form. We’re merely using the task object as the carrier of the result that may be delivered through a callback from the asynchronous I/O stack. While such a callback takes place on the CLR thread pool, no (blocked) thread was allocated *for the entire duration* of the I/O operation.

In fact, you could go as far as using a `Task<string>` to represent a user’s answer to a question:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_028.html_p1583pro02)

// Created elsewhere, with answerSource.Task handed out.
TaskCompletionSource<string> answerSource = ...;

void submitAnswerButton_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    submitAnswerButton.Enabled = false;
    answerSource.SetResult(answerTextBox.Text);
}

Clearly, the act of awaiting the completion of the answer does not depend on parallel execution in the CPU. In this case, we’re awaiting the input of a human being, living outside the computer’s silicon. Yet, you can use `Task<T>` to represent this, as well.

* * *

#### Key Takeaways of the TAP

To conclude our discussion of the new Task-based Asynchronous Pattern, we’ll sum up its key properties.

Compared to the classic APM and EAP approaches, one of the strengths of the TAP is its single-method nature. All aspects of kicking off the operation, awaiting its successful or exceptional result, cancellation, and progress tracking are present on a single method signature. One of the key enablers for this is the `Task<T>` type.

While consuming a TAP method without dedicated language support is still quite involved—using the `ContinueWith` method—you will see how this is made simpler using the new C# 5.0 `await` expression. But even without this language support, things have gotten much more streamlined. For example, the TAP prescribes for exceptions to come out through the `Task<T>` object, even if they happen during the initialization phase of the underlying operation.

Building a TAP-based method is much simpler than building an APM or EAP method. The key difference is that no custom type implementations are required, unlike the APM’s `IAsyncResult` or the EAP’s custom event argument types. Also, the thread-safe signaling logic for the resulting task object is taken care of by types such as `TaskCancellationSource`. The even better news is that handcrafting a TAP method is no longer required thanks to the asynchronous method support in C# 5.0.

### Asynchronous Methods and await Expressions

As part of the .NET 4.5 release, new language features for asynchronous programming were added to both C# 5.0 and Visual Basic 11. Their main goal is to take away the burden of having to restructure asynchronous code using a callback pattern, as seen with the APM, EAP, and TAP. By doing so, developers can focus on the logical flow of control of their application, rather than having to worry about the mechanics of how the code ultimately executes.

In other words, the language allows users to express what they want, instead of having to express—in excruciating details—how things should be carried out at runtime. Compilers are incredibly good at making such transformations, as seen in many language features such as iterators, query expressions, dispatch logic for dynamically typed objects, and so on.

This new language support for asynchronous programming consists of two tightly coupled language features. One is the new `await` expression which allows awaiting the eventual completion of an asynchronous operation without blocking the containing method. The `await` expressions are allowed to occur only inside asynchronous methods, which is the second language feature. You can think of such methods—marked with an `async` modifier—as containers for an asynchronous workflow that may be paused while awaited asynchronous operations are in flight. During such suspensions, other activities can be carried out on the original thread. Upon completion of the awaited operation, the asynchronous method resumes its execution. The resulting asynchronous method is a TAP-based (or fire-and-forget) method itself.

In this section, we dive into both language features from a user’s point of view. This discussion focuses mainly on the logical flow of control and how `await` expressions blend nicely in with other language features such as control flow statements and exception handling constructs. Even though we examine the suspension and resumption model of asynchronous methods a bit, too, we defer a detailed analysis of the compiler transformations until the next section.

#### Declaring Asynchronous Methods

The declaration of an asynchronous method is easy and simply involves adding an `async` modifier. You can combine this modifier with other modifiers such as `static`, the accessibility modifiers, and so on. [Figure 31.16](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig16) shows a couple of valid asynchronous method declarations.

![Image](images/00782.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.16 Asynchronous method declarations.

Notice how an `Async` suffix is added to the methods to conform with the TAP guidelines. This is merely a convention that isn’t checked by the compiler, but can be checked by code analysis tools.

A few restrictions apply to asynchronous methods. One is the set of allowed return types, restricted to `void`, `Task`, and `Task<T>`. The use of `void` creates a fire-and-forget method, whose eventual outcome cannot be observed. This proves useful when writing asynchronous event handlers that have to conform to the signature of the event’s delegate:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_029.html_p1585pro01)

async void downloadButton_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    var wc = new WebClient();
    try
    {
        var html = await wc.DownloadStringTaskAsync(txtUri.Text);
        browser.NavigateToString(html);
    }
    catch (WebException ex)
    {
        MessageBox.Show("An error occurred: " + ex.Message);
    }
}

The caller of this method—the UI framework’s dispatcher pumping the message loop—does not expect a return value from invoked event handler methods. Instead, the eventual outcome of the download will be shown to the user in a browser control or using a message box for error messages.

Notice the use of an `await` expression inside the body of the method. We come back to this in a moment, but think of it as a point where the execution of the asynchronous method can be suspended, yielding control back to the caller to do useful work in the meantime. When the awaited operation completes, the rest of the code starts to run, on the UI thread in this case.

The two remaining possible return types are `Task` and `Task<T>`. By using those, the eventual completion of the asynchronous method can be observed by its callers. As discussed in the previous section, this conforms to the TAP pattern. One possible way to observe the outcome of the operation is to use the `ContinueWith` method with a callback. However, using the new `await` keyword, this is made much simpler. In fact, in the previous example, the `DownloadStringTaskAsync` is just another TAP method with the following signature:

public Task<string> DownloadStringTaskAsync(string address);

Notice this method isn’t declared with the `async` modifier. A TAP method can be handcrafted, as explained in the previous section, though the use of the `async` modifier can make things significantly easier. Because the asynchronous methods on `WebClient` are merely wrappers around the existing EAP pattern using a `TaskCompletionSource<T>`, the framework implementers had little reason to use the new language features here. However, as soon as you want to coordinate asynchronous activities, you’ll want to use `await` expressions, requiring the `async` modifier. This requirement is shown in [Figure 31.17](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig17).

![Image](images/00783.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.17 Await expressions require asynchronous methods.

* * *

Note: Contextual Keywords

While you can’t tell in a black-and-white book, the `await` token in [Figure 31.17](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig17) doesn’t have syntax highlighting indicating it’s a keyword. The reason is simple. Outside asynchronous methods, the `await` token is treated as an identifier rather than a keyword. This is nothing new in C# 5.0\. For example, you can use `where` as an identifier or a keyword for generic constraints and filters in query expressions, depending on the context. This allows for backward compatibility where existing code continues to compile as it did before.

* * *

Besides return type restrictions, a few more restrictions apply to asynchronous methods. One such restriction is that `out` and `ref` parameters are forbidden. This can be explained by the mechanics of the execution of asynchronous methods. When such a method hits an `await` expression, it may have to pause, which involves returning to the caller of the method. At that point in time, the stack unwinds and the references to stack-allocated variables are no longer valid for use within the body of the asynchronous method. If the method would try to access those at a later point in time (for example, after a resume operation triggered by the completion of an awaited task), it would access memory that no longer reflects the state when the asynchronous method was started. This poses a type safety and memory safety breach, as shown in [Figure 31.18](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig18).

![Image](images/00784.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.18 No ref or out modifiers allowed.

Finally, the `async` modifier may not appear on interface or abstract methods. The rationale for this limitation is that there’s no need to restrict the implementation of such methods to use the asynchronous method feature. It may be more convenient for the implementer to handcraft a TAP method using techniques described previously in this chapter.

To sum up the restrictions of asynchronous method declarations, take a look at [Figure 31.19](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig19), which shows some common compiler errors.

![Image](images/00785.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.19 Compiler errors for invalid asynchronous methods.

Now that we have a good understanding of valid declarations using the `async` modifier, we should take a look at `await` expressions.

#### A Primer to await Expressions

Asynchronous methods contain one or more `await` expressions. If no `await` expressions are present in the method, a compiler warning is generated telling the method will execute synchronously under all circumstances, questioning why the method was declared using the `async` modifier to begin with. [Figure 31.20](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig20) shows this warning.

![Image](images/00786.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.20 Asynchronous methods can complete synchronously.

`await` expressions provide points in an asynchronous method body where the method can be suspended and resumed. Upon hitting an `await` expression, the compiler-generated code first evaluates the operand, which we referred to as the awaited task. Next, a check is made to see whether the operation has already completed. This can occur because tasks are usually hot, meaning they’re already running when you obtain them. For example, when calling `DownloadStringTaskAsync` on the `WebClient` class, a `Task<string>` is returned to represent the download that’s in progress. In other words, by the time we get the `Task<string>` object, things are already happening. Awaiting this task doesn’t cause it to start. To make this clearer, take a look at the following example:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_030.html_p1588pro01)

async void downloadButton_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    WebClient wc = new WebClient();
    string html = await wc.DownloadStringTaskAsync(txtUri.Text);
    browser.NavigateToString(html);
}

The operand of the `await` expression is evaluated first, before a check for task completion takes place. So, we can rewrite the code as shown here, using an intermediate temporary variable:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_031.html_p1588pro02)

async void downloadButton_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    WebClient wc = new WebClient();
    Task<string> __t = wc.DownloadStringTaskAsync(txtUri.Text);
    string html = await __t;
    browser.NavigateToString(html);
}

Now it’s clear that by the time the `await` expression evaluates, the task object has already been retrieved from the `DownloadStringTaskAsync` call. In fact, we could write other code before performing the `await` operation, which would execute while the task is in flight:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_032.html_p1589pro01)

async void downloadButton_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    WebClient wc = new WebClient();
    Task<string> downloadTask = wc.DownloadStringTaskAsync(txtUri.Text);
    // Insert other work here.
    string html = await downloadTask;
    browser.NavigateToString(html);
}

By the time we arrive at the `await` expression, the task may already have completed. If that’s the case, the asynchronous method just keeps running as if it were a synchronous method. However, notice one oddity in the types of the different variables in the previous code fragment. The type of `downloadTask` is a `Task<string>`, meaning it represents an operation that eventually will complete with a string value (or an error, as discussed later on). The type of the `await` expression is `string`, though. In other words, the `await` expression unpacks the result from the `Task<string>` object, resulting in the `string` value with the downloaded HTML.

What happens if the awaited task isn’t completed by the time the `await` expression executes? This is the more common case, which is why the concept of asynchronous methods was introduced to begin with. It may be the case the download takes hours to complete, so we shouldn’t block the UI event handler while waiting for the result. This is where the magic happens. When the task hasn’t completed yet, the `await` expression causes the asynchronous method to suspend its logical control flow. At a later point in time, when the task completes, the method will resume where it left off. [Figure 31.21](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig21) shows this for our sample code fragment.

![Image](images/00787.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.21 Resuming an asynchronous method.

How this mechanism works will be revealed in the next section, and in much more detail later in this chapter. For now, we focus on the logical flow of control. Comparing this method to a synchronous counterpart, it becomes clear how little difference there is to the structure of the code:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_033.html_p1590pro01)

void downloadButton_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    WebClient wc = new WebClient();
    // Bad practice! This may block for a long time...
    string html = wc.DownloadString(txtUri.Text);
    browser.NavigateToString(html);
}

To make this code nonblocking and asynchronous, you only have to change two things. First, mark the method with the `async` modifier, and second, use an `await` expression with the asynchronous variant of the blocking method.

* * *

Note: Asynchronous Workflows in F#

The asynchronous methods and `await` expressions language features in C# 5.0 and Visual Basic 11 were largely inspired by the work done with asynchronous workflows in F#. This F# language feature is based on a more general purpose mechanism of computation expressions which allows sequencing operations in a code block to be intercepted and bound to a so-called builder type. On such workflow builder providers for asynchronous execution and is used as follows:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_034.html_p1590pro02)

async {
    let wc = new WebClient()
    let! html = wc.AsyncDownloadString(uri)
    // use the html value here
}

The `async` token in the code fragment is not a keyword, unlike the C# or Visual Basic approach. Instead, it’s interpreted as the name of a builder type that the compiler searches for.

Next, it rewrites the body of the computation expression—the part in between the curly braces—using method calls to the builder. The various “bang” variants of keywords, such as `let!`, are places where the builder instance is invoked to take over the execution.

For the asynchronous workflow builder, the `let!` implementation is very similar to the operation of the `await` keyword in C# and Visual Basic.

* * *

In fact, this is where we could stop our discussion of `await` expressions and asynchronous methods. You can just program asynchronously executing code by replacing blocking calls with TAP-based alternatives, using `await` expressions to retrieve the eventual result. The compiler magic for the containing asynchronous method takes care of the rest and rewrites the method such that it can be paused and resumed based on the awaited task’s lifecycle.

As a result, the logical flow of your code doesn’t have to be sacrificed by a mechanical transformation into a callback-based coding style. In fact, behind the scenes the compiler turns the logical sequencing of your code into a state machine that’s driven by the completion of the various awaited tasks in the method body. In the next section, we won’t yet go into all of the gory details of this state machine transformation, but instead we examine the execution model at a higher level. Later in this chapter, all the details of asynchronous method execution are revealed.

#### How Asynchronous Methods Execute

Because `await` expressions are just expressions, you can use them in (almost) all places where you can use expressions. For example, it’s perfectly fine to write the following:

string res = await Bar(await Foo() + await Qux(), 42 * await Baz());

This code evaluates as if you had written the following:

var __t1 = Foo();
var __t2 = await __t1;
var __t3 = Qux();
var __t4 = await __t3;
var __t5 = __t2 + __t4;
var __t6 = Baz();
var __t7 = await __t5;
var __t8 = 42 * __t7;
var __t9 = Bar(__t5, __t8);
string res = await __t9;

In this example, the containing asynchronous method can be suspended on no less than four occasions, corresponding to each of the `await` expressions. However, the code still executes sequentially with a top-to-bottom and left-to-right evaluation of statements and expressions. For example, the tasks returned by `Foo` and `Qux` don’t run simultaneously, which is clear from the code expansion using temporary variables. To obtain the value of the `res` variable, the method may suspend and resume four times, or less due to the short-circuiting in case an awaited task has already completed.

But what happens upon suspension of an asynchronous method? How does it manage to unblock its caller, allowing it to do more useful work while the awaited task is in flight? And how does it manage to resume at the point it left off? Those questions require us to draw a crisp line between the logical control flow and the physical control flow.

From a logical point of view, all there is to know about asynchronous methods is that `await` expressions provide points where other work can be interleaved until the awaited task completes, allowing the method to continue execution. The keyword in the preceding sentence is *interleaving*, depicted in [Figure 31.22](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig22).

![Image](images/00788.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.22 Interleaved execution due to asynchrony.

Other than those points for interleaving, the method executes as before, making its way through the logical set of sequences required to carry out a task. The fact some operations may take seconds, minutes, hours, or longer to complete doesn’t disturb the logical control flow.

At some point in time, the asynchronous method reaches a `return` statement or leaves the method in a different manner (for example, by throwing an exception). When this happens, the `Task` or `Task<T>` returned by the asynchronous method gets signaled. This allows a caller that’s awaiting the method’s completion to continue running. For example, we may refactor our running sample code of a web download as follows:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_035.html_p1592pro01)

async void downloadButton_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    try
    {
        var html = await DownloadAsync(txtUri.Text, 30000);
        browser.NavigateToString(html);
    }
    catch (WebException ex)
    {
        MessageBox.Show("An error occurred: " + ex.Message);
    }
    catch (TimeoutException)
    {
        browser.NavigateToString(TIMEOUT_PAGE);
    }
}

static async Task<string> DownloadAsync(string uri, int timeout)
{
    var wc = new WebClient();

    var downloadTask = wc.DownloadStringTaskAsync(uri);
    if (await Task.WhenAny(downloadTask, Task.Delay(timeout)) != downloadTask)
        throw new TimeoutException();

    return downloadTask.Result;
}

Ignore the details of the `DownloadAsync` helper method with timeout support for a moment. What matters more is how the click event handler for the button now awaits the outcome of this download operation. When either the underlying download completes or a timeout results, the event handler method will be resumed, fetching the result of the download into the `html` variable. If an exception occurred, it will come out at this point, transferring control to any of the `catch` blocks in the method.

Two things are of interest here. First, notice how you can use good old exception-handling mechanisms seamlessly with the new `await` expressions. Even though we’re awaiting an operation in the middle of a `try` block, the containing asynchronous method can simply pause and resume in the middle of it. How this works is explained later in this chapter. For now, all that matters is that it simply works. The second important observation about this code is how resuming the event handler method can be triggered by a resume operation in the `DownloadAsync` method that was called. The completion of the underlying download on `WebClient` can have a cascading effect of waking up the `DownloadAsync` method, causing it to complete, resulting in the awakening of its caller, `downloadButton_Click`. [Figure 31.23](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig23) shows this cascading effect.

![Image](images/00789.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.23 Cascading completion of await expressions.

This cascading effect clearly shows how both the `await` expressions and the asynchronous method features are tightly coupled and work hand in hand to deliver a great developer experience. The key ingredient to this is the rich composition enabled by the ability to await the result of an asynchronous method. This also allows for rich refactoring support, as shown in [Figure 31.24](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig24).

![Image](images/00790.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.24 Visual Studio can refactor asynchronous methods.

We discuss the mechanics behind the pause and resume mechanism of asynchronous method in much more detail later, but the basic idea is rather simple. When encountering an `await` expression, the compiler transforms the rest of the execution of the method into a callback that gets registered with the awaited task. For a `Task` or `Task<T>` object, the callback registration happens with the well-known `ContinueWith` method, through an indirection with a so-called `awaiter` type. Upon completion of the task, this callback is triggered, causing the method to resume where it left off. Because an `await` expression may occur in the middle of iterative control flow structures, the callback isn’t as easy as splitting the method into two halves for each `await` expression. Instead, a state machine gets generated, keeping track of which `await` expression caused suspension. When resuming the method, a jump is made to the code that handles the completion of the awaited task to fetch the result and continue execution.

Ultimately, the asynchronous method will encounter a `return` statement or drop out from the bottom of its definition. At that point in time, an asynchronous method returning `Task` or `Task<T>` transitions the returned task into the completed state, using the operand object (if any) that was passed to the `return` statement. Alternatively, an exception may be thrown from the body of the asynchronous method, causing the returned task object to transition to a faulted state using the exception that was thrown.

* * *

Note: Comparison to Iterators

Iterators use a similar technique of building a state machine for each phase of the enumerator. Instead of using `await` expressions, `yield` statements are used to provide points where the iterator method can be suspended and resumed. In the world of iterators, the resume operation is triggered by a `MoveNext` call, for example driven by a `foreach` loop. For asynchronous methods, the awaited task is what triggers the resume at a later point in time.

In fact, the work required to add asynchronous methods to Visual Basic 11 enabled the addition of iterators in the same release. For C#, large portions of the code for iterators could be reused to build the asynchronous method feature because the analysis and rewrite of the code is so similar to iterators.

* * *

#### Control Flow in Asynchronous Methods

The beauty of `await` expressions is they’re like any other expression, hence they can appear almost everywhere in the body of asynchronous methods. Only a few places are not allowed to contain `await` expressions, including a `lock` statement, inside a `finally` block, and in an `unsafe` code context. Other than that, possibilities are almost endless.

In particular, the use of `await` expressions deep inside control flow logic is what makes the asynchronous programming features really powerful. For example, it’s possible to write an ordinary loop construct, with an `await` expression occurring in the middle of an iteration:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_036.html_p1595pro01)

async Task<List<string>> DownloadSitesAsync(params string[] uris)
{
    var result = new List<string>();

    var wc = new WebClient();
    foreach (var uri in uris)
        result.Add(await wc.DownloadStringTaskAsync(uri));

    return result;
}

This code is still sequential. Only one site will be downloaded at a time, without any parallel download operations in flight. Using constructs like `Task.WhenAll` and `Task.WhenAny` it’s possible to kick off multiple operations and await the outcome of all of them, or wake up whenever any of the tasks has completed. You can use this to devise a batching scheme for downloading, or simply to download all sites in parallel, as shown in the next fragment:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_037.html_p1595pro02)

async Task<List<string>> DownloadSitesAsync(params string[] uris)
{
    Task<string>[] sites = (from uri in uris
                            let wc = new WebClient()
                            select wc.DownloadStringTaskAsync(uri))
                           .ToArray();
    string[] htmls = await Task.WhenAll(sites);
    return htmls.ToList();
}

In this sample implementation, we use a simple query expression to kick off a download operation for each website, producing an array of tasks that represent the in-flight downloads. Next, we await the completion of all those tasks by using `Task.WhenAll`, which returns a `Task<string[]>` that will get signaled when all the specified tasks have completed one way or another. At that point, the asynchronous method is woken up again, continuing its execution constructing a `List<string>` from all the results.

If an exception occurs during the execution of any of the download operations, it is propagated by the `Task<string[]>` object returned from the `WhenAll` call. This task collects all the exceptions that occurred in an `AggregateException`. However, the use of an `await` expression unpacks the inner exceptions and throws the first exception, which makes catching an exception more natural and similar to the synchronous code equivalent. If the only type of exception that could be thrown by awaiting a task would be `AggregateException`, the only meaningful `catch` block would be one that filters for this type of exception (or its base class, `System.Exception`). [Figure 31.25](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig25) shows the result of awaiting a faulted task, with first-chance exceptions enabled in the debugger.

![Image](images/00791.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.25 An await operation causing exception propagation.

A caller awaiting the result of `DownloadSitesAsync` can catch this exception using regular exception handling constructs, as shown here. Asynchronous methods take care of propagating exceptions that occur during the lifetime of their execution, by transitioning the returned task object into the faulted state with the exception at hand. Pretend for a moment you’re porting some existing synchronous code to provide an asynchronous alternative (or, better yet, to eliminate the synchronous code going forward). All you had to change at the call site is the name of the method, the use of an `await` expression, and putting the `async` modifier on the method. Exception handling logic is unchanged:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_038.html_p1596pro01)

async Task SampleAsync()
{
    try
    {
        var htmls = await DownloadSitesAsync("http://bing.com", "http://gnib.moc");
        // Process the sites
    }
    catch (WebException ex)
    {
        // Handle the exception
    }
}

While we’re discussing exception handling in asynchronous methods, this seems like an appropriate time to talk about resource maintenance as well. Whether you’re writing synchronous or asynchronous code, you shouldn’t forget to dispose resources when you’re done using them. This has been notoriously hard when using the APM or EAP coding styles because the disposal logic often had to be replicated in many places where things could go wrong. With asynchronous methods, you can simply think about the logical flow of control, even though it may be paused for long durations during its execution. So, if you need to access a resource for the duration of an asynchronous method, you can simply use a `using` statement. Suspension operations caused by `await` expressions can simply happen inside the block. When the block is quit eventually—gracefully or exceptionally—the resource is disposed. In other words, the guarantees of proper resource cleanup are unchanged, and you didn’t have to change your coding style:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_039.html_p1597pro01)

async Task<List<string>> DownloadSitesAsync(params string[] uris)
{
    var result = new List<string>();

    using (var wc = new WebClient())
    {
        foreach (var uri in uris)
            result.Add(await wc.DownloadStringTaskAsync(uri));
    } // May take a long time before we get here, but that's fine!

    return result;
}

In summary, asynchronous methods all retain the logical control flow, despite their potentially long-running nature, with suspend and resume cycles happening all over the place using `await` expressions. After all, why should timing and latency aspects of code execution require us to restructure our code in a fundamental way, by doing a mechanical transformation? Compilers are really good at doing such transformations, and asynchronous methods fully exploit this property. Thanks to this, you no longer have to worry about callbacks, exception propagation, resource management, and so on.

#### Intermezzo: Manual Callback Plumbing

It’s quite instructive to think about how the same asynchronous behavior could be achieved without leveraging the new asynchronous method and `await` expression language features. In this section, we rewrite the last example using manual callback style programming to show how hard it is to map logical control flow on physical, callback-driven execution.

Keep in mind, though, that this kind of manual plumbing is no longer needed thanks to new language features. However, by going through this exercise, it becomes clear how developers were led down the synchronous path before, simply because getting the asynchronous alternative right was deemed too hard and error prone.

The first thing to build a TAP-based method by hand is to create a new instance of a `TaskCompletionSource<T>`, as discussed previously in this chapter. Obviously, we will no longer use the `async` modifier on the method. Recall from the previous sections how the `return` statement in an asynchronous method really corresponds to signaling the returned task object. Returning the task object itself is taken care of by the compiler-generated code for the asynchronous method, as you will learn in the “[Behind the Scenes](#part0014.html_ch04lev3sec12)” section later in this chapter. Instead, we handle this logic ourselves, as shown here:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_040.html_p1598pro01)

Task<List<string>> DownloadSitesAsync(params string[] uris)
{
    var tcs = new TaskCompletionSource<List<string>>();
    // Kick off the asynchronous work.
    return tcs.Task;
}

Next, we need to rewrite the logical control flow in a callback based style. This is where things get really tough. In our running example, we have an `await` expression sitting right in the middle of a `using` statement and a `foreach` loop. Somehow, we need to lift all of the code that has to run after the awaited download operation completes into a continuation callback. It’s clear we’ll have to use `ContinueWith` on the task returned from the `DownloadStringTaskAsync` call somehow. But how do we make the continuation trigger another iteration through the loop and cause the disposal of the `WebClient` when dropping out of the loop? The next code fragment illustrates the troubles we encounter trying to wire up this suspend/resume logic through the use of `ContinueWith`:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_041.html_p1598pro02)

static Task<List<string>> DownloadSitesAsync(params string[] uris)
{
    var tcs = new TaskCompletionSource<List<string>>();

    var result = new List<string>();

    using (var wc = new WebClient())
    {
        foreach (var uri in uris)
        {
            var downloadTask = wc.DownloadStringTaskAsync(uri);
            downloadTask.ContinueWith(t =>
            {
                result.Add(t.Result);
                // How we can resume the loop here?
            });

            // How can we suspend here?
        }
    }

    // How to return the result to the caller?

    return tcs.Task;
}

When we need to suspend, awaiting the result of the current download, we should unblock our caller and bail out as soon as possible. For the first iteration, this should return the `TaskCompletionSource<T>`’s `Task`, allowing our caller to await our eventual completion of all the downloads. While it seems we could simply use a `break` statement to bail out from the loop, things get really tricky to get back into the loop when the in-flight download operation completes. After all, the callback that got passed to the `ContinueWith` method is an anonymous method, and we can’t really jump from one method to another.

The answer to this puzzle lies in building a little state machine that will keep track of where a suspension happened, for the continuation to jump back to that point to continue execution. Unfortunately, this results in a total overhaul of the code structure. The first step is to desugar—as in removing syntactic sugar—the control flow statements into more primitive building blocks. For example, a `foreach` loop is really a `while` loop in disguise, and a `using` statement is built based on a `try...finally` statement. At the same time, we’ll move all of the method body’s work into an anonymous method that will get called every time an awaited operation completes. The new skeleton of the code looks like this:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_042.html_p1599pro01)

Task<List<string>> DownloadSitesAsync(params string[] uris)
{
    var tcs = new TaskCompletionSource<List<string>>();

    Action moveNext = null;
    moveNext = () =>
    {
        var result = new List<string>();

        var wc = new WebClient();
        try
        {
            var e = uris.GetEnumerator();
            while (e.MoveNext())
            {
                var uri = (string)e.Current;
                var downloadTask = wc.DownloadStringTaskAsync(uri);
                // How to pause here and make the continuation resume?
            }
        }
        finally
        {
            wc.Dispose(); // Omitting null check for brevity
        }
    };
    moveNext();

    return tcs.Task;
}

Notice how the initial call to the `DownloadSitesAsync` method cooks up this anonymous method called `moveNext`, only to kick it off right before returning `tcs.Task` to the caller. During this first iteration, we make our way to the loop, obtaining the download task for the first website. At this point, we can’t block for the task to complete. Instead, we should bail out from the `moveNext` invocation, therefore unblocking our caller. However, somehow we need to make sure that the task’s eventual completion causes `moveNext` to run again, this time not starting from the beginning but picking up where we left off.

To do so, we need to maintain all of our state across invocations of the `moveNext` delegate. In particular, we should reuse the enumerator for the array, rather than obtaining a new one. Similarly, the result list and the `WebClient` instance should be reused. After all, we’re going to dispose the single instance of the `WebClient` at a later point in time. To allow for this reuse, we have to lift all of our local variables outside the `moveNext` delegate. This creates a heap-allocated closure that will outlive the `DownloadSitesAsync` initial invocation’s stack frame. The result of this refactoring is shown here:
