[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_043.html_p1601pro01)

Task<List<string>> DownloadSitesAsync(params string[] uris)
{
    var tcs = new TaskCompletionSource<List<string>>();

    List<string> result = null;
    WebClient wc = null;
    IEnumerator e = null;

    Action moveNext = null;
    moveNext = () =>
    {
        result = new List<string>();
        wc = new WebClient();
        try
        {
            e = uris.GetEnumerator();
            while (e.MoveNext())
            {
                var uri = (string)e.Current;
                var downloadTask = wc.DownloadStringTaskAsync(uri);
                // How to pause here and make the continuation resume?
            }
        }
        finally
        {
            wc.Dispose();
        }
    };
    moveNext();

    return tcs.Task;
}

This still doesn’t answer how we’ll pause and resume the `moveNext` invocation based on a `ContinueWith` call on the `downloadTask` obtained in the loop. The key insight to understanding how to do this is the observation that `moveNext`’s invocation can be caused by two different states. One state is the initial one, where the `DownloadSitesAsync` method kicks off the operation, running to the first suspension point caused by an in-flight download. Subsequently, the `moveNext` method should get called whenever a download completes, causing another iteration through the loop. We’ll encode those two different reasons for `moveNext` invocations as a state value. Upon entering the `moveNext` method, we check the case we’re in and jump to the appropriate place in the code. The final result is shown in the next code fragment:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_044.html_p1601pro02)

Task<List<string>> DownloadSitesAsync(params string[] uris)
{
    var tcs = new TaskCompletionSource<List<string>>();

    List<string> result = null;
    WebClient wc = null;
    IEnumerator e = null;

    int state = 0;
    Action moveNext = null;
    Task<string> downloadTask = null;
    moveNext = () =>
    {
        switch (state)
        {
            case 0:
                result = new List<string>();
                wc = new WebClient();
                goto case 2;
            case 2:
                bool shouldDispose = true;
                try
                {
                    switch (state)
                    {
                        case 0:
                            e = uris.GetEnumerator();
                            goto case 1;
                        case 1:
                            if (e.MoveNext())
                            {
                                var uri = (string)e.Current;
                                downloadTask = wc.DownloadStringTaskAsync(uri);
                                state = 2;
                                shouldDispose = false;
                                downloadTask.ContinueWith(_ => moveNext());
                            }
                            else
                                tcs.TrySetResult(result);
                            break;
                        case 2:
                            if (downloadTask.IsFaulted)
                            {
                                tcs.TrySetException(downloadTask.Exception);
                                return;
                            }
                            else
                            {
                                result.Add(downloadTask.Result);
                                goto case 1;
                            }
                    }
                }
                finally
                {
                    if (shouldDispose)
                        wc.Dispose();
                }
                break;
        }
    };
    moveNext();

    return tcs.Task;
}

To properly jump back into the loop, additional states are required. In fact, the loop’s structure didn’t survive at all, degenerating into a repeated `if` statement to check for loop termination instead. Notice how the `state` value is set to 2 before calling `ContinueWith`. This ensures that resuming the method through the callback of the task causes us to jump to another `case` label, where we analyze the task’s outcome. If everything went well, we add the result to the `results` list and jump back to case 1, where the loop condition is checked again. Ultimately, the loop will terminate and the `results` object is stuffed into the TAP method’s returned `Task<List<string>>` object through the completion source object. Also observe how the `using` block turned into a `try...finally` statement with an additional `shouldDispose` flag. This ensures that the `WebClient` isn’t disposed prematurely.

From this discussion, it should be clear that manual plumbing to make code behave asynchronously isn’t for the faint of heart. All of this logic is extremely hard to get right. Even worse, the code doesn’t reflect the original intent using a logical control flow anymore, making it very hard to make any changes. With asynchronous methods, all of this plumbing is left to the compiler, as you will see later.

#### Synchronization Behavior of await Expressions

Asynchronous operations usually complete on a different thread than the one making the initial request to perform the operation. You’ve seen this repeatedly when studying the APM, EAP, and TAP patterns earlier in this chapter. This is a direct artifact from the way asynchronous completion of I/O operations is carried out on the thread pool. When dealing with compute bound asynchrony, the background thread that performed the computation will likely also be the one signaling the operation’s completion.

This decoupling from the requestor’s original context has traditionally posed an additional inconvenience, requiring manual synchronization for example to update the UI with the operation’s result. A good example of this is shown below, using the `WebClient`’s EAP:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_045.html_p1603pro01)

void downloadButton_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    var wc = new WebClient();
    wc.DownloadStringCompleted += (o, args) =>
    {
        txtHtml.Text = args.Result;
    };
    wc.DownloadStringAsync(txtUri.Text);
}

Updating the UI from the `DownloadStringCompleted` event handler won’t work because it’s invalid to update the UI from a thread other than the UI thread. This is the case for all of today’s UI frameworks that are used with C#, including Windows Forms, Windows Presentation Foundation (WPF), and Windows Extensible Application Markup Language (XAML). To solve this issue, one usually resorts to techniques specific to the UI framework used. For Windows Forms, you can use the `Invoke` method on `Control` to run a piece of code on the UI loop. For WPF, Silverlight, and Windows XAML, one usually uses a similar method on the dispatcher instance. In this code example, let’s assume that we’re using Windows Forms and fix the code as follows:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_046.html_p1604pro01)

void downloadButton_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    var wc = new WebClient();
    wc.DownloadStringCompleted += (o, args) =>
    {
        txtHtml.Invoke(new Action(() =>
        {
            txtHtml.Text = args.Result;
        }));
    };
    wc.DownloadStringAsync(txtUri.Text);
}

Notice how yet another (nested) callback is needed to deal with proper synchronization with the UI thread. This leads to excessive indentation of the code, and complicates matters further when trying to write a logical control flow with asynchrony involved.

Because `await` expressions can intercept the code path for completion of asynchronous operations—to resume the asynchronous method they’re contained in—automatic synchronization can be provided as well. Consider the following alternative implementation of our download logic, this time using an asynchronous method.

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_047.html_p1604pro02)

async void downloadButton_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    var wc = new WebClient();
    txtHtml.Text = await wc.DownloadStringTaskAsync(txtUri.Text);
}

First of all, the method is now declared with the `async` modifier, allowing the use of `await` expressions inside it. Even though we already know this, it’s good to point out how the async modifier doesn’t clash with event handler methods that should conform to the event delegate’s signature. This method is simply a fire-and-forget asynchronous method that will be kicked off when the button is clicked.

* * *

Note: Guarding Against Reentrant Calls

Event handlers like the one shown earlier can obviously be called multiple times. With synchronous methods, this usually doesn’t cause surprises because the method has to run all the way to its completion before it can be invoked again. Although some exceptions apply to this rule, it’s often a safe assumption to make, especially in single-threaded UI frameworks.

However, with asynchrony involved, the first run of the click handler may still be in flight while another one is started. At that point, two download operations are ongoing, both of which will cause a UI update down the road. The outcome is not predictable because both requests can complete in any order.

To protect against this, a common pattern is to disable the button upon entering the click event handler. Using a `try...finally` statement, the button can be reenabled after the operation completes. This way, the user is prevented from starting two or more simultaneous requests.

* * *

What’s truly hidden behind the scenes here is how the `await` operation for the task causes automatic synchronization back to the UI thread when the operation completes. [Figure 31.26](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig26) shows how the assignment to the `Text` property is indeed running on the UI thread.

![Image](images/00792.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.26 Asynchronous methods resume on the original thread.

If this looks like magic to you, don’t worry. The way this works is quite easy to explain. Obviously, it wouldn’t make sense for a general-purpose language feature to be tied to any specific UI framework. In fact, when completing an asynchronous operation during the lifecycle of a web request in ASP.NET, similar requirements hold. When the operation completes, we better know the original request’s context to send the data back to the right client. If this weren’t the case, information could leak to the wrong client.

Luckily, the .NET Framework provides for an abstraction over the concept of where code runs: the `SynchronizationContext` class. UI frameworks, ASP.NET, Workflow Foundation, and other custom libraries can implement a subclass of this type to allow operations to be posted to the appropriate threads. In the case of UI frameworks, the `Post` method simply queues up the given delegate instance for execution on the UI loop.

Before returning from an asynchronous method’s internal state machine, `await` expressions capture the `SynchronizationContext.Current` object. At the moment the operation completes, the asynchronous method resumes execution on the original context by invoking its state machine through the `Post` method. A conceptually equivalent technique based on the EAP is shown here:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_048.html_p1605pro01)

void downloadButton_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    var wc = new WebClient();
    var ctx = SynchronizationContext.Current;
    wc.DownloadStringCompleted += (o, args) =>
    {
        ctx.Post(_ =>
        {
            txtHtml.Text = args.Result;
        }, null);
    };
    wc.DownloadStringAsync(txtUri.Text);
}

When running in the context of a UI framework, this causes a post back to the message loop. In another context, such as ASP.NET, this causes restoration of the context associated with the request that initiated the asynchronous operation.

The use of the `await` expression on `Task` or `Task<T>` objects (and WinRT’s `IAsyncInfo` types) causes automatic capturing of the current `SynchronizationContext` and restoration when the asynchronous method resumes. In cases where this isn’t required, this additional step can be avoided by using the `ConfigureAwait` method for `Task`-based types. The signature of this method looks like this:

public ConfiguredTaskAwaitable ConfigureAwait(bool continueOnCapturedContext)

When applying this method to a task object before awaiting it, the automatic synchronization behavior can be suppressed by passing `false`, as shown here:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_049.html_p1606pro01)

async void downloadButton_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    var wc = new WebClient();
    var html = await wc.DownloadStringTaskAsync(txtUri.Text).ConfigureAwait(false);
    // This code won't run on the UI thread, so the following is invalid now:
    txtHtml.Text = html;
}

You can use this technique as a performance optimization in cases where the context doesn’t have to be restored. The extra hop through a `Post` method on a `SynchronizationContext` can be costly in some cases, so having a way to suppress this can prove useful. Nonetheless, keep in mind that the additional cost is often negligible compared to the overall cost of the asynchronous completion, which often involves long-latency operations.

* * *

Note: ExecutionContext, Awaiter Types, and await Expressions

In reality, more information besides the `SynchronizationContext` is flown across asynchronous points. One such piece of information is the `ExecutionContext`, which stores security-related data as well as user locale and other information. Collectively, this contains all information about a logical thread of information. Whenever an asynchronous point can jump to another physical thread, this information is flown. Examples include thread pool operations, thread creation code, and so on.

While flowing the `SynchronizationContext` can be suppressed by user code, the `ExecutionContext` has to be flown to prevent security breaches and whatnot. Therefore, flowing of the `ExecutionContext` is taken care of by the so-called asynchronous method builders, discussed in the next section. The mechanism to flow the `SynchronizationContext` is provided through the await pattern implementation for `Task` and `Task<T>`, in what’s known as an awaiter type. This can be observed from the `ConfigureAwait` method return type, which is a `ConfiguredTaskAwaitable`. This struct exposes a set of methods that the `await` keyword can bind to. Behind the scenes, it uses the Boolean flag to decide whether the `SynchronizationContext` should be captured and restored across the `await` operations applied to the object.

* * *

[Figure 31.27](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig27) shows the result of running the code with `ConfigureAwait` applied to suppress flowing the `SynchronizationContext`.

![Image](images/00793.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.27 Suppressing automatic synchronization.

#### No Asynchronous Main Method?

One key property of asynchronous methods is their early return while work is carried out. The returned `Task` or `Task<T>` object is used to track the completion of the operation, which is usually done using an `await` expression. To use an `await` expression, the containing method has to be declared as asynchronous as well. You may wonder what happens if asynchrony continues to spread up the invocation chain, all the way to the `Main` method. [Figure 31.28](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig28) shows the error message that results when trying to mark the `Main` method as asynchronous.

![Image](images/00794.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.28 Compiler error when marking Main as async.

When you think about it, this error makes sense. If the `Main` method could be marked as asynchronous, who’d be there to await its eventual outcome? Would the task notion have to be carried threaded through the Common Language Runtime (CLR), all the way to the startup code of the process, ultimately providing the operating system a way to await the result?

In fact, the CLR nor the operating system know anything about asynchronous methods; they’re purely a managed code illusion built on top of managed types such as `Task` and `Task<T>`. If the CLR were to allow for asynchronous `Main` methods, it’d have to learn about those types. Instead, things are kept quite simple, and asynchronous methods are a language/library feature and nothing more. When the `Main` method quits and no other foreground threads are running, the process quits. Asynchronous operations often don’t have any thread associated, and their completion usually runs from the thread pool. Clearly, nothing would keep the process alive merely by the presence of some asynchronous work pending completion.

Luckily, you’ll rarely ever have to worry about asynchrony spreading all the way up to the `Main` entrypoint method of your application. When dealing with UI frameworks, for instance, the main thread is occupied by the message loop, which exposed a purely event-centric programming model to the user code. As you’ve seen before, event handler methods are being invoked by the UI message loop dispatcher and can be marked as `async` even though they are `void` returning. In this case, the asynchrony doesn’t leak to the `Main` method. When the UI is quit—for example, by closing the main window—control is returned to the `Main` method, causing the process to quit as well. For web applications, the structure is similar, but this time with a web server request dispatching thread that triggers user code to run. Once more, the `Main` method is not exposed to the programming model.

If you want to play around with asynchronous programming from a console application, asynchrony can often spread up to the `Main` method. If that’s the case, a common way to prevent the program from exiting prematurely is to insert a `Console.ReadLine` call. Alternatively, when a `Task` or `Task<T>` object is returned from invoked asynchronous methods, you could block waiting for completion using `Wait`. To see concurrent execution of multiple asynchronous methods, you can use methods like `Task.WaitAll`, as well:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_050.html_p1608pro01)

static void Main()
{
    var t2 = Demo(2000, "Second");
    var t1 = Demo(1000, "First");
    var t3 = Demo(3000, "Third");
    Task.WaitAll(t1, t2);
    Console.WriteLine("1 and 2 done");
    var t4 = Demo(2000, "Fourth");
    t3.Wait();
    Console.WriteLine("3 done");
    Console.ReadLine(); // t4 will complete if the user doesn't quit early
}

static async Task Demo(int delay, string message)
{
    await Task.Delay(delay);
    Console.WriteLine("{0} - {1}", DateTime.Now, message);
}

#### Asynchronous Anonymous Functions

Anonymous methods using the `delegate` keyword or using lambda expression notification can also be marked with the `async` modifier. A good example of the use of this is when calling `Task.Run`, to start work on the task pool. A couple of overloads of this method are shown here:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_051.html_p1609pro01)

public static Task Run(Action action);
public static Task<TResult> Run<TResult>(Func<Task<TResult>> function);
public static Task Run(Func<Task> function);
public static Task<TResult> Run<TResult>(Func<TResult> function);

Additional overloads provide a `CancellationToken` parameter. Notice how the function and action parameter delegate types all conform to valid asynchronous method signatures. In particular, the `Action` delegate can represent a fire-and-forget `void`-returning asynchronous method, and the `Func<Task>` and `Func<Task<TResult>>` delegates can return a result.

You can use the returned `Task` and `Task<TResult>` objects to track the completion of the functions passed to the last three overloads. Nothing prevents you from using asynchronous anonymous functions to specify those delegates. An example is shown here:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_052.html_p1609pro02)

var answerMe = Task.Run(async delegate
{
    var minimumWait = Task.Delay(1000);
    var answer = LongRunningComputation();
    await minimumWait;
    return answer;
});

This example use of `Task.Run` is a bit contrived. Most likely we wouldn’t need to mark the delegate as asynchronous to do some long-running computation on the task pool. However, if performing this work involves awaiting asynchronous operations, it’s quite handy to put some `await` expressions right inside the anonymous function passed to `Run`. In this case, the `LongRunningComputation` will be run on the task pool in parallel with the asynchronous `Delay` operation. Ultimately, when the computation finishes, we await the completion of the delay. In a more realistic scenario, this may involve awaiting another piece of data that’s needed for the next phase of the computation.

Alternatively, we can write the asynchronous function using the fat arrow lambda expression syntax, as shown here:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_053.html_p1610pro01)

var answerMe = Task.Run(async () =>
{
    var minimumWait = Task.Delay(1000);
    var answer = LongRunningComputation();
    await minimumWait;
    return answer;
});

If the delegate type specified input parameters, a parameter list can be specified on the anonymous function. The syntax for this is exactly the same as for ordinary anonymous functions, just adding the `async` keyword in front of the parameter list.

### Behind the Scenes

The act of suspending and resuming an asynchronous method upon evaluation of an `await` expression is quite tricky. In this section, we take a look behind the scenes of asynchronous methods and `await` expressions to learn how the compiler deals with resuming methods at the right point, saving state, exception handling blocks, and more.

#### The State Machine Fueling Asynchronous Methods

When an asynchronous method executes, it may come across one or more `await` expressions. At that point in time, a dialogue is started with the object being awaited. This object is commonly referred to as the task, even though it doesn’t necessarily have to be a `Task` or `Task<T>` instance. We discuss the await pattern later on, also explaining how other types can be made awaitable.

What happens upon encountering a task being awaited depends on the current state of the task. Maybe the operation it represents has already been completed, allowing us to continue to execute the current method. However, most likely we’ll be unlucky and truly need to await the operation’s outcome before we can continue execution of the current method. At this point, the asynchronous method needs to be suspended. [Figure 31.29](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig29) shows both cases.

![Image](images/00795.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.29 Suspend and resume operations.

What [Figure 31.29](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig29) doesn’t reveal is how the containing asynchronous method can be suspended and resumed. What does it even mean to suspend a method during its invocation? As discussed before, the value of asynchronous methods is in their property of providing relief to the current thread, allowing it to perform useful work while an asynchronous operation is in flight. For example, if the asynchronous method is called from a UI thread that’s pumping the UI message loop, the act of awaiting an operation should allow the thread to continue its UI processing work. To do so, the asynchronous method cannot continue to monopolize the thread, and therefore it has to return to its caller.

In the previous sections, you learned how the return type of an asynchronous method allows for tracking the method’s eventual completion by using `Task` or `Task<T>`. This object can be returned before the asynchronous method completes its work to obtain the final result. In fact, that’s the whole point of using a task to represent an operation that’s in flight and will have a result, eventually.

Because we can return from an asynchronous method prematurely, it seems we’ve found a way to suspend the method’s execution without losing a handle to its future result. However, we haven’t answered how the method can resume its execution upon the completion of the task that caused its suspension. How do we get back to the right spot in the method?

This is where the compiler magic for asynchronous methods comes in. Behind the scenes, the compiler takes the body of the method and cuts it up into pieces, each of which ends with an `await` expression. In other words, scissors are used to split the method in every spot where it might need to suspend because a task hasn’t completed yet. [Figure 31.30](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig30) illustrates this for a simple piece of sequential code.

![Image](images/00796.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.30 Cutting an asynchronous method into pieces.

In fact, this methodology of cutting a method into pieces is very similar to the way iterators are implemented. Iterators are also methods that have suspend/resume capabilities, but powered by `MoveNext` calls instead. Each `yield` statement results in a split of the method into separate phases. Each time a `MoveNext` call is made, the method moves on to the next phase by inspecting its current state. As we’ll see in just a moment, asynchronous methods use a `MoveNext` method (but not the one on the `IEnumerator` interface) inside as well.

At the point of a suspension, the method has to bail out to allow its caller to continue doing useful work. However, before it can do so, it needs to remember where it was along the method’s execution path. This is done by keeping track of a state parameter. Upon resuming the method, triggered by the completion of the awaited task, this state is inspected to jump to the right spot in the method where the task’s result will be fetched and execution will proceed beyond the `await` expression. [Figure 31.31](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig31) reveals the use of a state field in ILSpy.

![Image](images/00797.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.31 ILSpy showing state used to resume the method.

As you can see from [Figure 31.31](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig31), the asynchronous method’s compilation resulted in the creation of a compiler-generated type. Notice the implementation of an interface called `IAsyncStateMachine`. This interface is defined in the Base Class Library (BCL) and looks like this:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_054.html_p1612pro01)

namespace System.Runtime.CompilerServices
{
    public interface IAsyncStateMachine
    {
        void MoveNext();
        void SetStateMachine(IAsyncStateMachine stateMachine);
    }
}

The most interesting member on this type is the `MoveNext` method. Each time the asynchronous method is put in the running state, this method gets called. This occurs upon the initial invocation of the method to kick off its operation, as well as for each subsequent resume operation that takes place when an awaited task completes. Let’s take a look inside this method, shown in [Figure 31.32](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig32).

![Image](images/00798.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.32 ILSpy showing the MoveNext state machine method.

Quite a few things are going on inside this method. At the very start of the method, a `switch` statement is used to branch to the right location in the method based on the current state. As the asynchronous method reaches an `await` expression, it tweaks the state field to remember where it left off. The next time the method is entered because of the `await` expression task completion, it jumps to the place where the completion of the `await` expression is handled.

Notice the use of the `IsCompleted` property on the so-called `awaiter` objects. This allows for the asynchronous method to short-circuit the evaluation without going through the whole state machine carrousel in case the awaited task has already completed. The translation of an `await task` expression roughly looks like this:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_055.html_p1614pro01)

void MoveNext()
{
    switch (__state)
    {
        ...
        case 41:  goto IL_41;
        case 42:  goto IL_42;
        ...
    }
    ...
IL_41:
    ...
    var awaiter = task.GetAwaiter();
    if (!awaiter.IsCompleted)
    {
        __state = 42; // remember where to jump to after task completion
        __awaiter_17 = awaiter; // keep track of awaiter object to retrieve result
        __awaiter.OnCompleted(this.MoveNext); // (really using a method builder)
        return; // suspension completed, return to caller
    }
IL_42:
    var res = __awaiter_17.GetResult();
    ...
}

In the sample code shown here, the `await` expression ends a code block that started at `IL_41`. After obtaining the `awaiter` from the task, the method checks whether the operation completed already. In that case, execution simply falls through to the next block, `IL_42`. Alternatively, the method has to be resumed to run `IL_42` at a later point in time when the task completes. This code path puts us on a trajectory to an early return from `MoveNext`. Before this happens, the method records where it has to go next, and asks the `awaiter` to call us back when the operation completes. When that happens eventually, the `switch` statement at the start of the `MoveNext` method makes the jump to `IL_42`.

#### Returning from an Asynchronous Method

As you’ve seen during our exploration of the asynchronous method feature, the `return` keyword is used to complete the returned task. Just this once, we’ll ignore the compiler warning when writing an asynchronous method that doesn’t have any `await` expressions inside it, to show how a simple asynchronous method is implemented under the hood.

static async Task<int> Demo()
{
    return 42;
}

The reason the compiler complains, as shown in [Figure 31.33](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig33), is that the method will complete synchronously under all circumstances. In fact, the warning suggests to introduce parallelism by using `Task.Run` if the method performs compute-intensive work.

![Image](images/00799.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.33 Compiler warning when nothing is awaited.

For our purposes of understanding how the `return` statement behaves in the context of an asynchronous method, we can safely ignore this warning. We’ll make the sample more realistic in a moment by adding `await` expressions. All that matters for the time being is the fact we’re using a `return` statement to complete the asynchronous method at some point in time during its execution.

The big question is how the object passed to `return` is fed into the `Task<int>` that’s returned from the asynchronous method upon its invocation. In [Chapter 30](#part0040.html_ch30), you learned about the existence of a `TaskCompletionSource<T>` class that acts as a factory for `Task<T>` objects. Using this facility, you could rewrite the sample code as a regular method that looks like this:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_056.html_p1615pro01)

static Task<int> Demo()
{
    var __tcs = new TaskCompletionSource<int>();
    __tcs.TrySetResult(42);
    return __tcs.Task;
}

Conceptually, this is close to what’s really happing in the code generated for the asynchronous method. To be able to return to the caller with a task object before the asynchronous method completes, a task object is constructed through a `TaskCompletionSource<T>`. At each point where the asynchronous method is completed by a call to `return` (or by throwing an exception, as discussed in the next section), that same completion source object is used to transition the task object to the completed state with the given value.

Obviously, the completion of the task using `TrySetResult` usually doesn’t happen right away during the invocation of the asynchronous method. Here is a more realistic example:

static async Task<int> Demo()
{
    await Task.Delay(1000);
    return 42;
}

In this fragment, we’re awaiting a delay operation of 1 second. In other words, the `return` statement will be executed only after the delay elapses. `Task.Delay` returns a task that will complete only after the specified duration, using a `Timer` internally. In this case, the generated code looks more like this:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_057.html_p1616pro01)

static Task<int> Demo()
{
    var __tcs = new TaskCompletionSource<int>();
    var __awaiter = default(TaskAwaiter);
    var __moveNext = default(Action);
    var __state = 0;
    __moveNext = () =>
    {
        switch (__state)
        {
            case 0:
                __awaiter = Task.Delay(1000).GetAwaiter();
               if (!__awaiter.IsCompleted)
               {
                   __state = 1;
                   __awaiter.OnCompleted(__moveNext);
                   return;
               }
               else
               {
                   __state = 1;
                   goto case 1;
               }
           case 1:
              __awaiter.GetResult();
              __tcs.TrySetResult(42);
              break;
        }
    };
    __moveNext();
    return __tcs.Task;
}

In this, we recognize the state machine introduced in the previous section. To keep the discussion more concise, I’ve omitted the use of `IAsyncStateMachine` for the time being. Because this example contains just a single `await` expression, the method is cut into two phases: the part that reaches this `await` expression, and the part that runs upon the awaited task’s completion.

The first state, indicated by `__state` set to 0, evaluates the `Task.Delay(1000)` expression to obtain the task being awaited. Based on the `awaiter` pattern, the next step is to obtain an `awaiter` object and interrogate its completion state, allowing for a potential short-circuit execution. For a 1-second delay, it’s highly unlikely we’ll ever hit this path, so let’s assume `IsCompleted` returns false. In that case, the state machine changes the `__state` to 1, and registers the `__moveNext` delegate with the `awaiter`. This basically asks the `awaiter` for the delay task to call us back when the delay completes.

Eventually, the delay completes and our `__moveNext` delegate is invoked again, this time with a `__state` flag set to 1\. In this case, the `awaiter`’s result is obtained using `GetResult`. Notice this call is still present for `awaiter`s on `Task`, even though no value is returned. This is done to allow exceptions to propagate, as discussed in the next section. For brevity’s sake, I’ve excluded exception propagation code in this example. What’s more important here is the use of `TrySetResult` at the point where the `return` statement occurred in the original C# code.

Notice how the call to `TrySetResult` happened in the context of the callback from the delay operation, long after the asynchronous method returned its `Task<int>` object to its caller. This is achieved by returning `__tcs.Task` immediately after kicking off the state machine by invoking the `__moveNext` delegate.

* * *

Note: Closures! Why Not?

You might wonder how the second pass through the state machine delegate, upon the delay’s completion, will observe the state set to 1. In reality, this is taken care of by keeping the state field in the compiler-generated state machine object, which gets stored on the heap whenever the asynchronous method is paused.

In the simplified code shown earlier, I make handy use of closures. Recall from our discussion of anonymous methods and delegates how captured variables from the outer scope are hoisted onto the heap in a so-called display class. This is exactly what’s going on here. The generated code for the `__moveNext` delegate consists of a class with fields for all of the captured variables, including the `__state` flag and the `__awaiter` object.

While the asynchronous methods language feature could have been written in terms of closures to maintain state across pause and resume operations, this wasn’t done for a variety of reasons. First, if the method can complete synchronously, the use of a closure for all the variables would incur an unnecessary heap allocation. Second, because additional complexity exists around synchronization, it made more sense to use a so-called builder pattern. For example, instead of directly accessing the `TaskCompletionSource<T>`, an intermediate `AsyncTaskMethodBuilder<T>` is used. This type acts as the proxy for setting the asynchronous method’s result but also plays a role in hooking up the state machine to the awaiters.

* * *

[Figure 31.34](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig34) shows the generated state machine method for this simple example. Instead of using a `switch` statement, a regular `if` statement is used because of the small number of states. Ignoring the additional `try...catch` block (explained in the next section), you can clearly see how the state machine ultimately invokes a `SetResult` method on a builder object. This corresponds to our `TrySetResult` call in the simplified version.

![Image](images/00800.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.34 State machine for a simple asynchronous method.

Also notice how the configuration of the `awaiter` is delegated to the builder object by means of a call to `AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted`. Internally, this method hooks up the state machine’s `MoveNext` method as a callback to the `awaiter`. It does a few more things, too, such as copying the state machine object (a stack-allocated struct value) to the heap for it to survive the asynchronous method’s suspension.

So, where’s the code that returns the task to the caller of the asynchronous method? Obviously, this code can’t live in the state machine’s `MoveNext` method simply because this state machine can be invoked many times during the lifecycle of the asynchronous method. To achieve asynchrony, the task object representing the eventual outcome of the operation has to be returned before the state machine reaches its final state. [Figure 31.35](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig35) shows what the asynchronous method entrypoint looks like.

![Image](images/00801.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.35 Setting up the state machine to kick off the method.

First, this method creates a method builder object that will help to manage the asynchronous method’s lifecycle by interacting with `awaiter`s, holding on to the state machine across suspension points, signaling completion states, and so on. After calling a `Start` method on the builder, which amounts to a `MoveNext` call to the state machine and some extra bookkeeping work, the builder’s `Task` property is obtained and returned to the caller.

As we’ve explained before, this task object is used by the caller of the asynchronous method to track its status or its completion, possibly by using an `await` expression of its own. Ultimately, upon hitting a `return` statement in the original code, the state machine uses a `SetResult` call to set the task’s result.

#### Exception Propagation

The previous section discussed how successful completion of an asynchronous method is handled based on a translation of `return` statements into method calls that cause the returned task’s `Result` to get set. Under the hood, this is fueled by a builder object that acts as a proxy to a `TaskCompletionSource<T>` object, which on its own turns proxies into the returned task object.

However, a method can return to its caller in another way, too, namely when an exception occurs. In regular methods, this is achieved by unwinding the call stack and using techniques like structured exception handling (SEH) that are built in to the operating system and the runtime. When dealing with asynchronous methods, though, there’s no such thing as a call stack that can get us back to our caller.

As explained in the previous section, the key ingredient to enable asynchrony is to return a task object before the method’s eventual completion. The word *return* in the previous sentence is absolutely important because it reveals the original call stack that led to the invocation of the asynchronous method has evaporated. So, how can an exception be propagated from an asynchronous method at a later point in time?

Once more, let’s start by shrinking down our analysis to the bare-minimum code that illustrates what’s going on. Later on, we extend the example to a more realistic scenario again. Consider the following code, ignoring the compiler warning about the lack of `await` expressions in the asynchronous method:

static async Task<int> Oops()
{
    throw new Exception("Oops");
}

In this degenerate case, the exception could come out of the asynchronous method in two ways. Because the asynchronous method never suspends because of the lack of `await` expressions, the exception occurs during the initial invocation of the asynchronous method (the first phase of the state machine, if you will). At that point, it could still be thrown synchronously, allowing the caller to catch it as follows:

static void Demo()
{
    try
    {
        Oops();
    }
    catch (Exception ex)
    {
        // Will we ever get here?
    }
}

This is not how things work, though. The completion of the asynchronous method, successful or otherwise, is always communicated through the returned task object. Notice the `Demo` method above didn’t await the task returned from `Oops`. In this case, the exception goes unnoticed and doesn’t even take down the application.

* * *

Note: Unobserved Exceptions

Starting from .NET 4.5 and motivated by the introduction of asynchronous methods, unobserved exceptions on tasks do not take down the application as a whole. [Chapter 30](#part0040.html_ch30) discussed the unobserved exception escalation behavior of the Task Parallel Library (TPL) as it existed in .NET 4.0, causing the exception to be rethrown on the finalizer thread. Although you can still restore this behavior by means of a configuration flag, it’s disabled by default. For more information, see [Chapter 30](#part0040.html_ch30).

* * *

One way to observe the exception would be to use `ContinueWith` on the `Task<int>` returned from the method:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_058.html_p1620pro01)

static void Demo()
{
    Oops().ContinueWith(res =>
    {
        if (res.Exception != null)
        {
            // We'll end up here!
        }
        else
        {
            // We won't get here, due to the exceptional completion.
        }
    });
}

Obviously, the cleaner and more modern way of receiving the result of an asynchronous operation is to use the `await` keyword:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_059.html_p1620pro02)

static async void Demo()
{
    int res;
    try
    {
        res = await Oops();
    }
    catch (Exception ex)
    {
        // We'll end up here!
        return;
    }

    // We won't get here, due to the exceptional completion.
}

Whether the exception should be caught at the point of awaiting the task is a different question. As discussed in [Chapter 8](#part0018.html_ch08), “[Basics of Exceptions and Resource Management](#part0018.html_ch08),” various design principles influence proper exception handling. For example, performing a catch-all operation isn’t always desirable (to say the least), and sometimes it’s better to let the exception bubble up to our caller if we can’t handle it in a meaningful way ourselves.

If we were to omit the `catch` block in the `Demo` method shown here, the exception can propagate to the method’s caller. However, because the asynchronous method is void-returning, there’s no direct way for the caller of `Demo` to observe the exception. To allow the exception to be observed, we can change the return type of the `Demo` method to `Task`:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_060.html_p1621pro01)

static async Task Demo()
{
    int res = await Oops();
    // We won't get here, due to the exceptional completion.
    Console.WriteLine(res);
}

Now, `Demo`’s caller can await the outcome of its invocation of `Demo`, possibly catching the exception, or simply letting it propagate to its own caller.

So, how does this exception flow really work? We’ve already established that exceptions are propagated through the returned task objects on asynchronous methods. But how? Just like successful `return` statements were turned into a `SetResult` call on the method builder object, exceptions are set on the builder using a `SetException` call. As you have seen before, the method builder is really a proxy to an underlying `TaskCompletionSource<T>` object, so we can give a rough approximation of the compilation of `Oops` here:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_061.html_p1621pro02)

static Task<int> Oops()
{
    var __tcs = new TaskCompletionSource<int>();
    __tcs.TrySetException(new Exception("Oops"));
    return __tcs.Task;
}

It’s a bit more complex than this though. Whereas `return` statements are the only ways for a successful result to be returned from a method, exceptions can leak out in many ways. One is to raise an exception by using a `throw` statement. However, every piece of code running in the asynchronous method could throw an exception of its own. As a result, setting the exception on the builder cannot be done simply by rewriting all `throw` statements into `SetException` calls.

To propagate all exceptions through the returned task object, the entire body of the generated state machine is surrounded by a `try...catch` block that catches all exceptions. To illustrate this, let’s make the example a bit more realistic once more:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_062.html_p1622pro01)

static async Task<int> DivideBy(int d)
{
    if (d < 0)
        throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException("d");

    var n = await Return.Demo(); // the a delayed 42 from the previous section
    return n / d;
}

This code is intentionally flawed to have two opportunities to throw an exception. In the argument check, a `throw` statement is used to raise an error if the divisor is strictly negative. Assume the method is meant to be used to slice a cake, where a negative number of persons wanting cake is rather impossible. However, it’s totally possible for zero persons to crave cake, and the argument checking didn’t account for this case. As a result, the `Return.Demo` operation is invoked to return a cake with a surface of 42, after 1 second of baking time. At that point, our `DivideBy` method resumes by trying to slice the cake among our zero guests, causing a `DivideByZeroException` to occur.

[Figure 31.36](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig36) shows the `DivideBy` method’s generated state machine `MoveNext` method. Observe how all the user code that appeared in the original C# code is surrounded by a giant `try...catch` statement. Whenever an exception occurs, it gets set on the resulting task by using the builder’s `SetException` method.

![Image](images/00802.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.36 Catching all exceptions for proper error propagation.

On the asynchronous method caller’s end, awaiting a task object that enters a faulted state ultimately leads to a call of the `awaiter`’s `GetResult` method:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_063.html_p1622pro02)

static async Task ThrowParty(int numberOfPartyAnimals)
{
    var size = await DivideBy(numberOfPartyAnimals);
    Console.WriteLine("Everyone gets {0} amount of cake", size);
}

If, for mysterious reasons, there’s a negative number of people at the party, an `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` will be present on the task immediately after returning from `DivideBy`. This is because the code up to the first `await` expression runs synchronously upon the asynchronous method’s invocation. In this case, the generated code in `ThrowParty` will notice a positive `IsCompleted` flag on the `awaiter`, causing immediate evaluation of `GetResult`, which will propagate the original exception. Someone higher up the chain, awaiting `ThrowParty`, will now have a chance to observe this exception.

If there are zero people attending the party, the flow is quite different. Instead of synchronous exceptional completion, it takes 1 second before the cake gets sliced in `DivideBy`, causing the exception to occur at a later point in time. Through the same mechanics of successful completion, this leads to the completion of the returned task, this time in a `Faulted` state. This kicks the `ThrowParty` state machine in the back, causing it to interrogate the `DivideBy awaiter` object for its outcome by means of a call to `GetResult`. Once more, this propagates the received exception, which is a `DivideByZeroException` this time around.

[Figure 31.37](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig37) shows the propagation of a division-by-zero exception when running this sample under the debugger (with first-chance exceptions enabled through the Debug, Exceptions menu) for a party with zero attendees.

![Image](images/00803.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.37 Exception propagation for await expressions in action.

Notice how the call stack reveals information about all the await points where the exception was caught and propagated to the containing asynchronous method’s task result. If we were to scan this call stack all the way to the bottom, we’d find out the error originated from the `DivideBy` call.

* * *

Note: ExceptionDispatchInfo

To retain the invaluable information about the origin of exceptions occurring during the execution of an asynchronous method, a new helper type called `ExceptionDispatchInfo` was introduced in .NET 4.5.

In earlier versions of the .NET Framework and the CLR, the act of rethrowing a stored exception object caused the stack trace information in the exception object to get replaced by the stack trace for the place of the throw operation. This poses an issue for awaiter types that need to propagate an exception out of their `GetResult` method (for example, by grabbing the exception object stored in a faulted task object).

Deep inside the `TaskAwaiter` type, a `ThrowForNonSuccess` method is invoked upon obtaining the result of the task through the `GetResult` method. If that task is in a faulted state, an `ExceptionDispatchInfo` object is retrieved for the exception that caused the failure. Upon calling this object’s `Throw` method, the captured exception is rethrown, while ensuring that the original call stack is preserved (among other things such as so-called Watson buckets, a piece of information used for Windows error reporting).

* * *

#### Unwrapping AggregateExceptions

What about tasks that have multiple exceptions? As you might recall from [Chapter 30](#part0040.html_ch30), you can use `Task` objects for parallel computing where multiple units of work can fail. A good example of this behavior is the use of the `Parallel` class to run multiple loop iterations in parallel. To capture all possible exception states, the `AggregateException` type was introduced in .NET 4.0\. Handling such an exception can be quite tedious, though, because regular `catch` blocks cannot be used to inspect any of the object’s inner exceptions. Instead, a `Handle` method has to be called, specifying a handler method through a delegate.

Nowadays, tasks are increasingly commonly used as futures that represent the eventual completion of an asynchronous operation, thanks to the introduction of the Task Asynchronous Pattern in .NET 4.5\. In such scenarios, tasks usually hold a single exception object (for example, to denote the failure of an I/O operation). From your knowledge of asynchronous methods, it’s easy to understand that those can only set a single exception object. No parallelism is introduced by the machinery behind the asynchronous method implementation. An exception can occur in user code or when an `await` expression completes and propagates its exception upon resumption of the asynchronous method.

As discussed in the previous section, asynchronous methods simply use the builder’s `SetException` method to set an exception on the method’s result task. At the end of the caller awaiting the outcome of the operation, it’s reasonable to expect the same exception to pop out when the method resumes from the `await` expression. For example, consider the following `Throw` method with a `delay` effect:

async Task Throw(Exception ex, int delay)
{
    await Task.Delay(delay);
    throw ex;
}

Even though `Task` objects hold their exceptions through an `AggregateException` container (as you can see from the Task’s `Exception` property type), it’d be quite tedious if we had to inspect this wrapper for each and every await operation:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_064.html_p1625pro01)

async Task Sample()
{
    var error = new InvalidOperationException();
    try
    {
        await Throw(error, 1000);
    }
    catch (AggregateException ex) // This would be very tedious!
    {
        ex.Handle(inner =>
        {
           var ioe = inner as InvalidOperationException;
           if (ioe != null)
           {
               // Inspect the exception; return true if we were able to handle it.
           }
           return false;
        });
    }
}

If the `await` expression were to propagate a task’s `Exception` property as is, the only meaningful error handling would be to catch based on the `AggregateException`. Clearly, this is undesirable. For example, who would expect an asynchronous web download to throw a `WebException` wrapped inside an `AggregateException`? This would defeat part of the goal of making asynchronous methods look and feel like their synchronous counterparts. Hence, we’d like to write code like this:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_065.html_p1625pro02)

try
{
    html = await webClient.DownloadStringTaskAsync(uri);
}
catch (WebException ex) // No AggregateException business here!
{
    // Handle the exception or rethrow if we can't handle the situation properly.
}

To make the code that handles exceptional outcomes for an `await` expression as natural as possible, it was chosen for the `TaskAwaiter` types to propagate only the first (and usually the only) exception of the stored `AggregateException`.

However, when observing a `Task`’s erroneous state through its `Exception` property, or when using synchronous blocking wait operations such as the `Wait` method or the `Result` property, the original .NET 4.0 behavior is retained. Because of this, it’s still possible to get to all of the exceptions in the (rare) cases where there are indeed multiple exceptions possible:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_066.html_p1626pro01)

Task fst = Throw(new Exception("First error"),  1000);
Task snd = Throw(new Exception("Second error"), 1000);
Task doBoth = Task.WhenAll(fst, snd);
try
{
    await doBoth;
}
catch
{
    // Inspect doBoth.Exception.
}

In this example, I’m using the new .NET 4.5 capability to await multiple tasks using the `WhenAll` method. The overload used here is shown here:

public static Task WhenAll(params Task[] tasks)

When awaiting the result of the `WhenAll` call, we’re really awaiting all the specified tasks to complete. Only then will the asynchronous method that’s awaiting the `WhenAll` task be allowed to resume. However, it’s clearly possible for any of the specified tasks to complete erroneously. In this case, all the observed exceptions are collected in an `AggregateException` accessible through the resulting tasks’ `Exceptions` property.

Looking back at the example, notice how we restructured the code ever so slightly to keep the task object returned from `Task.WhenAll` in the `doBoth` variable. If we were to await the result of `WhenAll` immediately, we wouldn’t have a variable through which we can access the task’s detailed exception information at a later point in time. When awaiting `doBoth`, only one of the two delayed exceptions will be propagated using typical control flow. We can’t reliably know which one, and most likely we want to inspect all exceptions if we know parallel execution was involved anyway. To do so, we catch all exceptions but go on to inspect all the inner exceptions by accessing `doBoth.Exception` in the `catch` block. For example, we could write the following:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_067.html_p1626pro02)

try
{
    await doBoth;
}
catch
{
    doBoth.Exception.Handle(ex =>
    {
        // Inspect exception and return true if handled.
    });
}

If any of the inner exception remains unhandled (indicated by the `Handle` lambda expression returning false), a new `AggregateException` will be thrown from the `Handle` method, containing the remainder unhandled exceptions.

A long story short, the `await` expression and asynchronous method language features were designed to make the typical case of handling a single failure really easy. In cases where multiple exceptions are a possibility, you can still keep a reference to the task object around and inspect its `Exceptions` property after the completion of the `await` expression.

* * *

Note: Beware of Blocking!

Never access a `Task`’s `Result` or `Exception` property before you know for sure the task has completed. When called earlier, accessing those properties causes blocking until the task reaches a completion state. This is clearly undesirable when writing asynchronous code. In the example shown in this section, we’re accessing the `Exception` property only after evaluating the `await` expression for the task object. At that point during the execution of the asynchronous method, we have the guarantee that the `doBoth` task has run to completion. If this were not the case, we would not have gotten past the point of awaiting the task to begin with.

* * *

#### Supporting Arbitrary Control Flow

Because you can use `await` expressions in (mostly) every expression context, their containing asynchronous methods can be paused in the middle of complex control flow constructs, as well. For example, an `await` expression may occur in the middle of a loop, requiring the method to be paused and resumed at that very point, without causing additional iterations and whatnot.

Although this seems a complex undertaking, it’s not much more complicated than the simple example with linear statement sequencing shown in the previous section. The reason is rather straightforward. At the end of the day, complex control flow structures like conditional statements, loops, and so on are nothing but branch instructions in disguise. The only thing added by asynchronous methods is an additional jump table at the entry of the method and some state maintenance code. For example, consider this piece of code:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_068.html_p1627pro01)

async Task<int> CountTotalDistinctWords(IEnumerable<Uri> sites)
{
    var webClient = new WebClient();
    var words = new HashSet<string>();

    foreach (var url in sites)
    {
        var html = await webClient.DownloadStringTaskAsync(url);
        words.UnionWith(html.Split());
    }

    return words.Count;
}

This downloads a sequence of sites, one at a time in an asynchronous manner, which avoids long blocking of the caller. In fact, the whole operation may take hours to complete. Notice we could use the `Parallel.ForEach` construct, as well, but that’s a whole different topic of discussion, requiring proper synchronization and whatnot.

Recall how a `foreach` loop is really a `using` block and a `while` loop in disguise, using a pattern of methods to obtain an enumerator object and to interact with it. At the same time, a `using` statement is a fancy way of writing a `try...finally` block. The following code fragment shows the code expansion for `foreach`:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_069.html_p1628pro01)

async Task<int> CountTotalDistinctWords(IEnumerable<Uri> sites)
{
    var webClient = new WebClient();
    var words = new HashSet<string>();

    var __e = sites.GetEnumerator();
    try
    {
        while (__e.MoveNext())
        {
            var url = __e.Current;
            var html = await webClient.DownloadStringTaskAsync(url);
            words.UnionWith(html.Split());
        }
    }
    finally
    {
        __e.Dispose();
    }

    return words.Count;
}

When a download operation requires the asynchronous method to be paused because it didn’t complete synchronously, state needs to be captured to allow for a subsequent resume operation. This includes keeping all the seemingly stack-allocated variables alive, which is achieved by hoisting those onto the state machine object. Even though the `IAsyncStateMachine` implementation is a struct, it’s managed through the asynchronous method builder object, which gets hoisted to the heap upon suspending the method. [Figure 31.38](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig38) shows the fields that reveal all the variables in the code shown earlier.

![Image](images/00804.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.38 Variables kept as fields in the state machine value.

Looking at the original code, we can already expect the suspension to happen right in the middle of the `foreach` loop body. However, if we look at the deciphered code with the `try...finally` block and the `while` loop, it’s clear the place where the method gets cut into pieces is buried deeply in control flow mechanisms. Let’s take a look at how all of this is achieved. [Figure 31.39](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig39) illustrates the heart of the `MoveNext` method, ignoring the outer exception-handling mechanisms discussed in the previous sections.

![Image](images/00805.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.39 Control flow encoded in a state machine.

First of all, notice how the state-based switch logic used to resume the method has gotten a bit more complex. The reason the `num` state flag is checked both outside and inside the `try` block is because of restrictions to branching in intermediate language (IL) code. When the method needs to be resumed in the middle of the `while` loop, we also have to reenter the protected block delineated by the `try` block. It’s illegal to jump to code inside such a block at the runtime level, hence the double-checking.

Looking inside the `try` block, the `while` loop has been restructured significantly. It should be no surprise that the loop has been rewritten as an `if` statement and a `goto` statement. In the code shown in [Figure 31.39](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig39), the `IL_10A` label is where the loop condition is evaluated, causing the awaiting of a web request. When the request completes eventually, we’ll reenter the `try` block and fall through to `IL_D3` to obtain the result and store it in the `HashSet<string>` collection. Finally, the next iteration of the loop is evaluated, and the whole process starts again. If we’re lucky and the web request completes synchronously, a jump to `IL_D3` bypasses the suspend/resume cycle of the method.

There’s one more subtle thing about this code, though. Notice the use of the `flag` variable? When pausing the method upon awaiting a web request, the `MoveNext` method’s job is to bail out, freeing the calling thread to allow it to do more useful work. Unfortunately, as we return from the method, the `finally` block would get triggered, causing premature disposal of the enumerator object. Upon resuming the method, this would result in the inability to run another iteration of the loop. To prevent early execution of `finally` blocks, a Boolean flag is maintained. When the method is (re)entered, this flag is set to `true`. However, when the method is paused inside the `try` block associated with the `finally` block, the flag is set to `false` to suppress execution of the `finally` block. In this particular example, this prevents the disposal of the enumerator that’s part of the `foreach` compilation.

#### Saving Evaluation State with Stack Spilling

Because the new `await` keyword is used in an expression context, some complexity applies to maintaining the evaluation stack across the initiation of the asynchronous operation and its completion. The technique used to make this work is called stack spilling.

To understand this complexity and how to deal with it, consider the following example of an asynchronous method:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_070.html_p1630pro01)

async Task<int> Demo()
{
    return Bar() + (Foo() + (Qux() + await Baz()));
}

In this piece of code, we call four methods as part of one big expression. Of those four methods, the first three simply return an `int`. The `Baz` method, however, returns a `Task<int>` that will be awaited.

Notice the use of parentheses to prevent the left associative property of addition from evaluating the partial sums in a left-to-right order. This illustrates the growing evaluation stack, as you will see later. [Figure 31.40](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig40) shows the expression tree of this sum.

![Image](images/00806.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.40 Deep expression tree of a right-associative sum.

So, what’s going on here? Recall that C# evaluates subexpressions in a left-to-right order. Therefore, when evaluating this expression, a call is made to the `Bar` method first. Its result gets pushed onto the evaluation stack. Next, the `Foo` method is called, also pushing its result onto the stack. Because of the use of parentheses, the partial sum of those two values cannot be computed yet. So, we have to continue by evaluating the next subexpression, the method call to `Qux`. At this point, we already have three `int` values on the evaluation stack.

Now things start to get interesting. We’ve reached the unary `await` expression, whose operand is a call to `Baz`. After evaluating this method call and obtaining the `awaiter` object (as explained in the previous section), we might have to suspend execution of the `Demo` method. This happens when the `awaiter`’s `IsCompleted` property evaluates to `false`, putting us on the slow path. Recall from the previous sections how the suspension of an asynchronous method results in a premature exit, to allow our caller to do useful work while we’re awaiting the result.

We’ve already seen how the `awaiter` object is moved to a field of the state machine object, for it to be inspected upon the resumption of the method. However, in this example, there’s much more on the evaluation stack besides the `awaiter` object. What about the results of evaluating `Bar`, `Foo`, and `Qux`? Clearly, we can’t reevaluate those upon resuming the method. If we were to do so, we could end up duplicating side-effects, not to mention we’re doing twice the work. In fact, `Baz` may have been dependent on the side-effects of evaluating any of those methods. Not only should we avoid duplicate evaluation of those methods but we also shouldn’t reorder their evaluation. For example, evaluating the `await` expression first, before computing the three method calls preceding it, is inconsistent with the C# rule of left-to-right evaluation.

This is where stack spilling enters the picture. At the point of suspending a method, the contents of the evaluation stack have to be spilled into a heap-allocated object for those to survive across the suspend-resume cycle. In fact, this is similar to closures in delegates where captured variables have to be hoisted onto the heap.

In the case of asynchronous methods, the heap-allocated object that comes to the rescue is the method builder instance that stores the `IAsyncStateMachine` object to maintain the state transitions of the running asynchronous method invocation. The compiler simply introduces a `<>t__stack` field on the generated state machine class implementation. When the asynchronous method is suspended because an `awaiter` indicates its operation hasn’t completed synchronously, the contents of the evaluation stack are spilled into this field. For our running example, this amounts to three `int` values for the preceding `Bar`, `Foo`, and `Qux` evaluations. To store those, a `Tuple<int, int, int>` is created to hold the three values. Upon resuming the method, the tuple is read from the field and decomposed to push the three values back onto the evaluation stack, as shown in [Figure 31.41](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig41).

![Image](images/00807.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.41 Generated code for stack spilling.

At this point, the result of the await operation can be retrieved, as well, and the evaluation of the additions can proceed. [Figure 31.42](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig42) shows the entire lifecycle of the asynchronous method across its suspension and resumption.

![Image](images/00808.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.42 The lifecycle of an asynchronous method and its stack.

Notice how the spilling operation is bypassed in its entirety if the `awaiter` signals synchronous completion through its `IsCompleted` property. In other words, if we’re lucky and all await operations in an asynchronous method complete synchronously, the execution behavior is close to that of a synchronous method. No intermediate heap allocations are needed in such a case. In fact, even the `TaskAwaiter<T>` type is implemented as a struct to avoid heap allocations when not needed.

* * *

Note: Why the Use of Tuples?

You might wonder why a tuple is used to spill the contents of the evaluation stack into fields on the heap-allocated object. Couldn’t each evaluation stack slot be spilled into a separate field? For example, in the demo code there could be three fields for the evaluations of `Bar`, `Foo`, and `Qux`.

Although this would work just fine, it can be extremely wasteful. Because the asynchronous method can contain many `await` expressions, each of those would need its own set of fields to spill the stack at the point of the `await` expression’s slow path execution. Because stack slots are strongly typed, chances are slim existing fields from other await sites can be reused. Also, during the execution of an asynchronous method only a few await sites may be hit (because of conditional statements and whatnot). As a result, the union of all the fields for all the `await` expressions could be very large, while only few may be used for each invocation of the asynchronous method.

By using a single field in the asynchronous state machine class, the overhead for stack spilling is constant, namely one pointer-sized field. Because only one `await` expression can be in progress at any given point in time for the method’s execution, the state machine’s current state uniquely identifies what will be in this field when the method resumes. The generated code uses this property to perform a cast operation to the tuple type representing the evaluation stack state to be restored.

Notice that tuples aren’t always used. If there’s only one object on the evaluation stack at the point of an asynchronous method’s suspension, that single object is stored in the field. This eliminates the need for an intermediate tuple allocation. If there are more than 16 objects on the stack, nested tuples are generated.

* * *

### Advanced Topics

#### Building Awaitable Types

Starting from C# 3.0, new language features have not required any change to the underlying CLR infrastructure. This is no different for the asynchronous programming features introduced in C# 5.0\. As discussed in depth in the previous section, asynchronous methods use a crafty compile-time rewrite technique to produce a regular method from the runtime’s point of view. Control flow constructs are rewritten in terms of interactions with a method builder object provided in the BCL for .NET Framework 4.5.

Although you could totally imagine a runtime extension to make methods pausable—effectively hoisting the stack frame onto the heap, or using a different technique altogether—there’s no need to make such big changes to the CLR. Compile-time transformations do the trick equally well and can open up for some great flexibility, as you will see in a bit.

Looking back at language features introduced throughout the years of C# evolution, a common theme has emerged. An increasing number of those features are based on syntactic sugar that turns into method patterns. For example, the `foreach` keyword uses an enumerator pattern and isn’t tied to the `IEnumerable` or `IEnumerable<T>` interface. Dynamic dispatch logic using C# 4.0’s `dynamic` can be intercepted by the use of so-called dynamic meta objects, again decoupling the feature from specific behaviors such as .NET Reflection. Maybe the biggest of all pattern-based language features is LINQ, whose query expression syntax turns into a chain of method calls conform the query pattern.

For C# 5.0’s `await` expressions, a similar method-based translation is used. In other words, to make a type awaitable, it suffices to implement some `awaiter` pattern, one way or another. For the `Task` and `Task<T>` types, this pattern is exposed on those classes directly. However, for other types, you can use an extension method to enable `await` expressions for instances of the type. In fact, `await` support for the `IAsyncInfo` family of WinRT interfaces is enabled through an extension method defined on the `WindowsRuntimeSystemExtensions` in the `System` namespace:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_071.html_p1635pro01)

namespace System
{
    public static class WindowsRuntimeSystemExtensions
    {
        public static TaskAwaiter<T> GetAwaiter<T>(this IAsyncOperation<T> source)
        { ... }
        ...
    }
}

Simply by providing this extension method, C# and Visual Basic users can leverage the power of asynchronous methods and `await` expressions against WinRT APIs, where `IAsyncOperation<T>` is the type that plays a similar role as `Task<T>` in the .NET Framework.

In this particular case, the `awaiter` method pattern is enabled by a single `GetAwaiter` extension method, returning a `TaskAwaiter<T>` value. The compiler then resolves the next set of members in the pattern against this type. We’ve already met the `TaskAwaiter<T>` type before, because it’s used by the await support on the `Task<T>` type:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_072.html_p1635pro02)

namespace System.Threading.Tasks
{
    public class Task<T> : Task
    {
        public TaskAwaiter<T> GetAwaiter() { ... }
        ...
    }
}

In fact, all the `GetAwaiter<T>` method for `IAsyncOperation<T>` does is convert the object to a `Task<T>` using another extension method called `AsTask` and call `GetAwaiter` on it. However, the language has no ties to the `TaskAwaiter<T>` type either. All that matters is that the type exposes the right members. What are those?

First, there should be a `GetResult` method that returns the result of the asynchronous operation after it has completed. The return type of this method is what becomes the type of the `await` expression. For example, consider the following types:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_073.html_p1635pro03)

class Bar
{
    public Foo GetAwaiter() { ... }
}

class Foo
{
    public Qux GetResult() { ... }
    ...
}

After we complete the `awaiter` pattern on `Bar` and `Foo` with some other required members, we can write the following piece of code:

var res = await new Bar();

The type of `res` will be `Qux`, to conform the return type of our `GetResult` method. What else do we need to enable `await` support? As discussed earlier, one of the great things about the asynchronous programming features in C# and Visual Basic is their “pay-for-play” effect. When an asynchronous operation has already completed upon evaluating the `await` expression, the method doesn’t need to be suspended and resumed. This is a valuable optimization because an asynchronous method’s suspension requires moving objects to the heap, potentially including stack spilling operations and whatnot. For the generated code to interrogate the awaitable object for its status, an `IsCompleted` Boolean property has to be provided.

Finally, we need to deal with the case where the asynchronous operation hasn’t completed yet upon awaiting it, as signaled by the `IsCompleted` property returning `false`. In that case, the compiler-generated code will move all the required state to the heap and hand over a delegate that will trigger the resumption of the method to the `awaiter` object. When called in the future, this triggers the asynchronous method’s state machine to move forward. To receive this delegate, another `OnCompleted` method has to be provided, taking in an `Action`. Rather than simply providing a method with the right name and signature, the `awaiter` type needs to implement the `INotifyCompletion` interface, which is defined in the `System.Runtime.CompilerServices` namespace. An example of our completed `await` pattern on `Bar` and `Foo` is shown here:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_074.html_p1636pro01)

class Bar
{
    public Foo GetAwaiter() { ... }
}

class Foo : INotifyCompletion
{
    public bool IsCompleted { get { ... } }
    public void OnCompleted(Action action) { ... }
    public Qux GetResult() { ... }
}

To see the effects of awaiting a `Bar` instance, let’s start with a trivial implementation where `IsCompleted` always returns true. To see what goes on in this case, we add some `printf` debugging output to the triad of members on `Foo`. [Figure 31.43](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig43) shows which methods got called upon awaiting a `Bar` object.

![Image](images/00809.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.43 Synchronous completion of an awaitable task.

As expected, the `OnCompleted` method never got called. In fact, if we truly want to benefit from the compiler optimizations for the case of synchronous completion, we should turn our `Foo` implementation into a struct, avoiding its heap allocation altogether. Notice `TaskAwaiter<T>` does exactly this.

To investigate the case of pending asynchronous completion, change the `IsCompleted` property to return false. This time, the `OnCompleted` method gets called to hand over the asynchronous method’s continuation for us to call when the underlying awaited operation completes. Let’s complete the operation trivially by using a timer to invoke the delegate after a few seconds, as shown here:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_075.html_p1637pro01)

class Foo : INotifyCompletion
{
    public bool IsCompleted
    {
        get { return false; }
    }

    public void OnCompleted(Action action)
    {
       Task.Delay(1000).ContinueWith(_ => action());
    }

    public Qux GetResult()
    {
        return new Qux();
    }
}

After adding some `printf` logging again, we can run the code to see the effect, as shown in [Figure 31.44](#part0041_split_001.html_ch31fig44).

![Image](images/00810.jpeg)

FIGURE 31.44 Asynchronous completion of a custom awaiter.

This shows the essentials of providing an awaitable type. However, we’ve omitted quite a few things we should also address. One such thing is properly posting back to the original `SynchronizationContext`. This isn’t taken care of by the asynchronous method builder, to allow for custom `awaiter` types that want to bypass this. Even though scenarios with UI frameworks require this type of synchronization, it might be overkill in others. In fact, the `ConfigureAwait` method on `Task<T>` also provides a way to bypass this synchronization mechanism.

* * *

Note: ICriticalNotifyCompletion and ExecutionContext

In fact, asynchronous methods do flow the `ExecutionContext` on the awaiter’s behalf. This is important for security and proper restoration of other contextual information across asynchronous invocation points.

However, in some cases this context object can be captured and restored multiple times, once by the code in the asynchronous method builder and once by the underlying awaitable object (for example. when interacting with other APIs for asynchrony in the .NET Framework).
