To reduce this cost, you can implement an `ICriticalNotifyCompletion` interface in addition to `INotifyCompletion`. When this interface is implemented on an awaiter, the compiler targets its `UnsafeOnCompleted` method (declared as `SecurityCritical`) instead. You can find more information about this on MSDN.

* * *

To finish our discussion of awaitable types, let’s build a slightly more useful `awaiter` for button controls in WPF. To write a logical flow of control spanning a series of UI interactions, wouldn’t it be nice to await the user clicking a button, triggering the next step in a logical workflow?

By declaring a `GetAwaiter` extension method for the `Button` class, we can write and compile the code. In this, we use a fire-and-forget asynchronous method called from the window’s constructor:

public MainWindow()
{
    InitializeComponent();
    Workflow();
}

private async void Workflow()
{
    var i = 0;
    while (true)
    {
        Title = "Counter = " + i++;
        startButton.IsEnabled = true;

        await startButton;

        startButton.IsEnabled = false;
        await Task.Delay(1000);
    }
}

The `Workflow` method is asynchronous, nonblocking, and repeatedly awaits the user to click a button to update a counter. Upon a button click, it gets disabled for 1 second, mimicking a long-running operation to obtain the next value of the counter. Obviously, more intricate workflows could be written (for example, awaiting a user click to initiate a download, whose result determines the next UI elements to show, possibly awaiting the next user action). The high-latency resource we’re awaiting here is the human being sitting in front of the computer.

Implementing this `awaiter` is fairly straightforward. Because we always have to wait for the user’s input, the `IsCompleted` property simply returns false. In the `OnCompleted` call, we hook up an event handler (used to trigger the continuation afterward) to the button:

[Click here to view code image](#part0075_split_076.html_p1639pro01)

static class ButtonExtensions
{
    public static ButtonAwaiter GetAwaiter(this Button button)
    {
        return new ButtonAwaiter(button);
    }

    public sealed class ButtonAwaiter : INotifyCompletion
    {
        private readonly Button _button;

        public ButtonAwaiter(Button button)
        {
            _button = button;
        }

        public bool IsCompleted
        {
            get { return false; }
        }

        public void OnCompleted(Action continuation)
        {
            RoutedEventHandler onClick = null;

            onClick = new RoutedEventHandler((o, e) =>
            {
                _button.Click -= onClick;
                continuation();
            });

            _button.Click += onClick;
        }

        public void GetResult()
        {
        }
    }
}

Notice that we do not have to capture and restore the `SynchronizationContext` for our simple `awaiter`. After all, the button’s `Click` event handler will be invoked on the UI thread already, causing us to run the continuation right there, as well.

In this section, you’ve learned the basics about implementing custom awaitable types and `awaiter`s. Keep in mind that this is an advanced scenario. Quite often you can piggyback on await support for `Task` and `Task<T>` and provide a conversion method for your object to any of those types. If the need for a customer `awaiter` type still arises, consider using the built-in `TaskAwaiter<T>` type to simplify the implementation of the await pattern.

#### Yielding Control

Now that you know how custom `awaiter`s work, and how they interact with the compiler-generated code, let’s take a look at one more atypical `awaiter` that ships with the .NET Framework itself. On the `Task` class, you can find a static method called `Yield`, defined as follows:

public static YieldAwaitable Yield();

As the name of the return type implies, the result of calling `Yield` can be awaited. The effect of doing this is pausing the current asynchronous method, effectively yielding control and allowing for other work to be run before continuing the current method’s execution. Internally, this is simply accomplished by a custom `awaiter` whose `IsCompleted` property always returns false. Upon the rendezvous of the compiler-generated code with the `awaiter` object through `OnCompleted`, the continuation delegate is posted to the current `SynchronizationContext` to run at a later point in time. If no context is found, the continuation of the method is run from the task pool or thread pool.

If you use this method, the asynchronous completion of a method can be guaranteed by simply awaiting a `YieldAwaitable`. For more information about this method and its use, refer to MSDN documentation.

### Summary

This chapter showed you how the C# 5.0 asynchronous methods and `await` expression language features simplify the building of responsive and scalable applications. Asynchrony is key to avoid blocking of threads, which has been very hard to get right in the past because of the invasive code restructuring required to work with the APM and EAP patterns.

Built on top of the Task-based Asynchronous Pattern (TAP), the language features for asynchronous programming provide an easier way to build asynchronous methods. Instead of having to reshuffle a logical flow of control into a bunch of continuations, `await` expressions leave this complex task to the compiler. As a result, you can focus on the job at hand, rather than on the plumbing required. Moreover, subtle things such as proper synchronization with UI threads are handled on your behalf.

## Chapter 32. Introduction to Windows Runtime

* * *

In This Chapter

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) [What Is Windows Runtime?](#part0042.html_ch32lev1sec1)

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) [Creating a Windows Runtime Component](#part0042.html_ch32lev1sec2)

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) [Overview of the Windows Runtime APIs](#part0042.html_ch32lev1sec3)

* * *

Throughout this book, we focused almost exclusively on the use of C# to write applications powered by the Common Language Runtime (CLR) and managed code. However, starting with Windows 8, a new application platform has emerged, built to power modern style applications that are touch friendly and enable new experiences. The underlying technology of this platform is called the Windows Runtime (WinRT) and can be leveraged from managed code languages like C# and Visual Basic.

This chapter briefly introduces WinRT, focusing on its interactions with the CLR and how to build WinRT components that you can use from a wide variety of languages, including JavaScript. You also learn some helper types in the Base Class Library (BCL) that help to bridge between .NET concepts and WinRT concepts in a few rare cases.

### What Is Windows Runtime?

The ongoing evolution of the Windows operating system has traditionally posed some challenges to provide a programming model that can be leveraged from many languages and technologies. Although users of C and C++ can usually use a new Windows version’s extended application programming interfaces (APIs) straight away, developers using managed code languages have often been left out in the cold. Instead, one had to resort to interop plumbing using things such as P/Invoke and COM interop, which isn’t the most pleasant development experience.

At the same time, the desire to build rich Windows applications using different technologies also grew. In particular, developers with a web programming background haven’t been able to leverage the Windows platform directly through the HTML Document Object Model (DOM) and the JavaScript programming language. Wouldn’t it be great for this developer audience to be able to access the Windows APIs directly, and pair those APIs with HTML5 as a user interface (UI) technology?

Finally, many of the Windows APIs haven’t been particularly easy to consume because of their C-style exposure based on functions or because of their limited use of object-oriented programming styles. Therefore, even seasoned native code developers didn’t always have the nicest experience to build great applications for Windows.

Starting with Windows 8, a new application architecture has been added to the operating system to address those issues. The WinRT provides access to various APIs of the operating system for so-called WinRT applications that are deployed through the new Windows Store. Such applications are sandboxed and can be written in C#, Visual Basic, JavaScript, and C++/CX. The rich set of APIs provides access to file dialogs, UI controls, webcam dialogs, data exchange between applications, networking stacks, and much more.

* * *

Note: What’s in a Name? Metro, Windows RT, and WinRT

Applications for the Windows Store that ships with Windows 8 and beyond are built using the WinRT. During the preview phase of Windows 8, such applications were sometimes referred to as Metro-style applications, referring to the UI style based on tiles and clear typography that was pioneered in Zune and later Windows Phone 7.

In fact, the story goes this UI paradigm was inspired by the style of bus stop signs and time tables of the Metro Transit System in the Seattle area, hence its name. Due to possible trademark issues, this name was phased out in favor of Windows Store apps and New Windows 8 UI style.

The RT acronym is also used for a specific version of Windows 8, running on devices powered by an ARM processor. Originally called WOA for Windows on ARM, this version of Windows is now referred to as Windows RT. This version of the operating system doesn’t run traditional x86 or x64 desktop software. Instead, apps written for this platform are based on WinRT and deployed through the Windows Store. For example, the Surface RT is one device that’s powered by an ARM processor and runs Windows Store applications.

* * *

#### Hello World for Windows Store

To explore the WinRT APIs, we’ll use Visual Studio 2012 to create a new Windows Store application project. [Figure 32.1](#part0042.html_ch32fig01) shows the New Project dialog’s entries for this type of application.

![Image](images/00811.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.1 Windows Store app projects.

Because Windows Store apps are UI-centric, we have to choose one of the Extensible Application Markup Language (XAML)-based templates. To keep things simple, we’ll use the Blank App template. Feel free to experiment with other templates, though a discussion of the rich UI capabilities of the Windows XAML platform is beyond the scope of this book.

You should feel very comfortable if you’ve already built Windows Presentation Foundation (WPF), Silverlight, or Windows Phone applications before. To keep things simple, here we just create a UI consisting of a single button control, as shown in [Figure 32.2](#part0042.html_ch32fig02).

![Image](images/00812.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.2 Our UI experiment.

At this point, you can double-click the button control and see an event handler appear in the code behind. No surprises here:

[Click here to view code image](#part0076_split_000.html_p1646pro01)

private void Button_Click_1(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
{
}

In the next few sections, we write a bit of code for our simple UI application as a way to explore the WinRT infrastructure powering this new type of application.

#### Object-Oriented and Modern COM

At its heart, the WinRT provides an object-oriented API to access a wide range of operating system capabilities, aimed at building modern applications. For example, using the webcam from a Windows Store app built in C# looks like this:

[Click here to view code image](#part0076_split_001.html_p1646pro02)

using Windows.Foundation;
using Windows.Media.Capture;
using Windows.Storage;
using Windows.Storage.Streams;
using Windows.UI.Xaml.Media.Imaging;
...
public async Task<BitmapImage> TakePictureAsync()
{
    CameraCaptureUI cameraUI = new CameraCaptureUI();
    cameraUI.PhotoSettings.AllowCropping = true;
    cameraUI.PhotoSettings.CroppedAspectRatio = new Size(4, 3);
    cameraUI.PhotoSettings.Format = CameraCaptureUIPhotoFormat.Png;

    StorageFile file = await cameraUI.CaptureFileAsync(CameraCaptureUIMode.Photo);
    BitmapImage image = new BitmapImage();
    if (file != null)
    {
        IRandomAccessStream stream = await file.OpenAsync(FileAccessMode.Read);
        await image.SetSourceAsync(stream);
    }

    return image;
}

Notice how an instance of the `CameraCaptureUI` class is made in an object-oriented manner by invoking a constructor. Configuring the newly created object is done using various properties. Ultimately, we can call the `CaptureFileAsync` method to kick off the operation that will show the UI, enabling the user to capture a picture. Upon completion of this asynchronous operation, a `StorageFile` object is returned.

Besides the concepts of classes, properties, and methods, we’re also seeing enum values, interfaces, and namespaces in this small sample. In fact, the WinRT is built on an evolution of COM where the concept of interfaces plays a central role. Even the `CameraCaptureUI` class is backed by an interface, as you will see in a bit.

As an exercise, wire up the `TakePictureAsync` method to the button click handler, using the asynchronous programming features of C# to await the eventual result of the operation. Feel free to add an image control to the UI to display the `BitmapImage` of the capturing operation. Once everything is wired up, you can run the application by pressing F5 or by selecting the target execution environment, as shown in [Figure 32.3](#part0042.html_ch32fig03).

![Image](images/00813.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.3 Debugging the application.

The simulator mimics a tablet device that allows for different kinds of interaction, such as rotation, pinch and zoom gestures, various touch operations, etc. [Figure 32.4](#part0042.html_ch32fig04) shows the result of clicking the button to trigger the camera interaction. As you can see, an error is displayed because the application doesn’t have permissions to interact with the camera.

![Image](images/00814.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.4 The simulator using the camera.

A detailed discussion of the application model and the permissions model is beyond the scope of this book. The basic idea is that applications should declare the system capabilities they want to use in a so-called application manifest. This is shown in [Figure 32.5](#part0042.html_ch32fig05).

![Image](images/00815.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.5 Declaration of application capabilities.

If you try to rerun the application, a user prompt appears asking whether the application should be allowed access to the camera. This way users do not end up with unpleasant surprises when an application tries to access the camera at an awkward moment. Similarly, the use of other capabilities requires user consent.

* * *

Note: Application Containers

WinRT-based applications run in so-called application containers. The role of those containers is to provide a sandbox for the application to run in, restricting access to the underlying system. Access to system functionality such as webcams, the file system, and so on is provided through runtime brokers that play the role of mediators asking for user consent.

In fact, the concept of application containers is entrenched quite deeply in the Windows 8 operating system. To see this with your own eyes, try launching the executable of our simple application (under the bin\Debug folder, as usual) from a command prompt. You’ll see the following error:

The system cannot execute the specified program.

From a Developer Command Prompt, you can also run the following command to show the executable file’s headers:

dumpbin /headers App1.exe

In the list of headers, you should find an entry called optional header values containing a section called DLL characteristics. In there, you should find an entry called App Container. This shows how the C# compiler added a flag to the output executable file to let the operating system know that the executable has to run in an application container. The executable file loader in the operating system will not allow you to run this application outside a container. For the curious readers, the csc.exe command-line flag used when building a Windows Store app is `/target:appcontainerexe`.

Finally, using tools like Process Explorer from Sysinternals, you can also inspect the parent process for Windows Store apps. This will reveal a svchost.exe process that’s acting as the application container.

* * *

What’s of more interest to us is to see how the underlying WinRT works. To start our exploration, select the `CameraCaptureUI` class name in the code and press F12 to navigate to its definition. This brings up the definition of the class in a C# code format, as shown in [Figure 32.6](#part0042.html_ch32fig06).

![Image](images/00816.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.6 The CameraCaptureUI definition.

A few things are worth pointing out. First of all, notice the assembly location shown at the top of the file reveals that the class is defined in a file called Windows.winmd. We take a closer look at this file (with an unexpected extension for an assembly) in the next section. Next, notice how the class has various attributes applied to it. A thorough explanation of all of those attributes is beyond the scope of this discussion, but we do consider two important ones.

The `version` attribute allows for evolution of the type in future releases of the Windows operating system. Versioning was built in to the WinRT from day one to future-proof the platform. Next, the `threading` attribute reveals the roots of the WinRT in COM, from where the concept of single threaded apartments (STAs) originates.

While the definition view of `CameraCaptureUI` in Visual Studio reveals a few interesting things, much more is going on under the covers. To see this, we have to look at the Windows Metadata format.

#### The Windows Metadata Format

The Windows.winmd file in [Figure 32.6](#part0042.html_ch32fig06) should feel a bit strange to managed code developers. Why doesn’t this assembly have a .dll extension? The answer may be quite surprising: This is not an assembly as we’re used to in the world of managed code and the CLR. Instead, it’s a so-called Windows Metadata file, hence the .winmd extension.

What’s the difference between an assembly and a Windows Metadata file? One difference is in the runtime that’s using the files. While the CLR is in charge of reading and executing assemblies, Windows Metdata files are used by the WinRT and various tools. Another difference is that the primary goal of Windows Metadata files is to describe the structure of an API in terms of classes, interfaces, properties, and so on, but it doesn’t necessarily contain the code that implements the API. With .NET assemblies, the intermediate language (IL) code lives inside the same file.

You might wonder how Visual Studio was able to show the contents of the Windows.winmd file, given that it is not an assembly. The reason this works is because the Windows Metadata file format is based on the same metadata format as .NET assemblies. Because of this, all existing tooling simply continues to work: IntelliSense, Go to Definition, Object Browser, and so much more. In fact, we can even open the file in ILDASM, as shown in [Figure 32.7](#part0042.html_ch32fig07).

![Image](images/00817.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.7 Reading Windows.winmd in ILDASM.

As you can see, the namespaces, types, and members simply show up in the ILDASM view of the file. Notice though how a few things differ from classic .NET assemblies. In the bottom pane, you can see the declaration of the file, which reads as follows:

.assembly windowsruntime Windows
{
  .ver 255:255:255:255
}

The fact the metadata entry shows up as a `.assembly` is simply because the metadata format defines such a concept in its specification. However, to distinguish between a CLR assembly and a Windows Metadata file reusing the same metadata specification, a new `windowsruntime` attribute was added. Also notice how the `.ver` looks really strange. This number isn’t really used in WinRT, in favor of more granular versioning at the type level. We’ve seen this before when looking at the attributes on the `CameraCaptureUI` type in the previous section.

Looking back at [Figure 32.7](#part0042.html_ch32fig07), the `CameraCaptureUI` class’s metadata is shown as well. Notice how the `windowsruntime` metadata attribute also appears on the class declaration. One other thing that should catch your attention is the presence of an interface implementation directive:

implements Windows.Media.Capture.ICameraCaptureUI

Visual Studio chose not to display this interface in its rendering of the definition of a WinRT type, but ILDASM doesn’t hide any details. Because of its roots in the interface-driven world of COM, each of the WinRT classes implements an interface. We take a look at how this interface is used at runtime in just a moment.

Finally, take a look at the `CaptureFileAsync` method, shown in [Figure 32.8](#part0042.html_ch32fig08). If we were looking at a classic .NET assembly, we would see IL code here. However, the method looks just empty.

![Image](images/00818.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.8 No IL code in the Windows Metadata file.

Where does the component’s implementation live? We answer this shortly. What’s really going on here is that the Windows Metadata file describes only the structure of the API and doesn’t directly contain its implementation.

In fact, the implementation of the WinRT APIs is done in native C++ code rather than managed code. However, thanks to the use of the metadata format, it’s really easy to consume this API from various languages, including C# and Visual Basic. This is very similar to using COM interop in .NET code. Even though the implemenation of the COM component is usually not done using managed code, accessing the API feels quite natural.

The Windows Metadata file we’ve been looking at thus far is not really the .winmd file used at runtime. Notice how the file was loaded from a location with a directory called Windows Kits. This is a location where the Windows software development kit (SDK) installed a reference metadata file to, for use by tools like Visual Studio, compilers, and so on. At runtime, the metadata files are loaded from the WinMetadata folder under C:\Windows\System32\. This is shown in [Figure 32.9](#part0042.html_ch32fig09).

![Image](images/00819.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.9 WinMetadata folder on a Windows 8 machine.

The Windows.winmd file in the Windows Kits folder really plays the role of a reference assembly that contains all the WinRT APIs in a single file for use by tools. The runtime representation of those APIs is factored a bit more into separate smaller files. Nonetheless, when you open those files using ILDASM, you still won’t find any implementation code. In the next section, we discuss how the runtime locates and loads the component providing the implementation of the APIs.

In [Figure 32.10](#part0042.html_ch32fig10), you can see how Visual Studio shows this single metadata reference file in Solution Explorer. You can interpret this entry in the Solution Explorer as a reference to all the Windows Runtime APIs that are available for you as an application developer. Notice how all of .NET’s APIs for Windows Store apps are also hidden behind a single entry in Solution Explorer.

![Image](images/00820.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.10 The Windows Runtime APIs behind a single reference.

#### Activation and IInspectable

At runtime, where does the code that powers the `CameraCaptureUI` class come from? You have already seen how the Windows Metadata file doesn’t contain code. Because of WinRT’s roots in COM, you should not be surprised that WinRT components are registered in the Registry, providing a way for the runtime to look up the implementation for a given class. [Figure 32.11](#part0042.html_ch32fig11) shows the registration of the `CameraCaptureUI` class in the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE registry hive.

![Image](images/00821.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.11 The registration of the CameraCaptureUI class.

In here, the `DllPath` value refers to the .dll file on disk, containing the implementation of the given class. If you were to inspect this file using tools like dumpbin, you would notice this is, in fact, a native library rather than a managed code assembly.

The role of the .winmd file is to describe the structure of the types and members defined in this library. At runtime, this library gets loaded and the class inside of it gets activated through a so-called activation factory. Evidence of this is shown in [Figure 32.12](#part0042.html_ch32fig12), where the WebcamUI.dll file is analyzed for exported functions.

![Image](images/00822.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.12 Activation of WinRT components through a factory.

An activation factory is an object that implements an `IActivationFactory` interface, as follows:

[Click here to view code image](#part0076_split_002.html_p1654pro01)

IActivationFactory : public IInspectable
{
public:
    virtual HRESULT STDMETHODCALLTYPE ActivateInstance(
        /* [out] */ __RPC__deref_out_opt IInspectable **instance) = 0;
};

The details of the interface aren’t all that important for managed code developers. However, looking at this interface, you can learn a few things about the way the WinRT works. To create a new instance of the class, the `ActivateInstance` function is called. This function returns a new `IInspectable` object through an output parameter.

Readers familiar with COM know the `IUnknown` interface which acts as the base interface for all COM objects. In the WinRT, the `IInspectable` interface plays the same role as the root of the type hierarchy, somewhat similar to the `System.Object` base class in the CLR. This interface is shown here for completeness:

[Click here to view code image](#part0076_split_003.html_p1654pro02)

IInspectable : public IUnknown
{
public:
    virtual HRESULT STDMETHODCALLTYPE GetIids(
        /* [out] */ __RPC__out ULONG *iidCount,
        /* [out] */ __RPC__deref_out_ecount_full_opt(*iidCount) IID **iids) = 0;

    virtual HRESULT STDMETHODCALLTYPE GetRuntimeClassName(
        /* [out] */ __RPC__deref_out_opt HSTRING *className) = 0;

    virtual HRESULT STDMETHODCALLTYPE GetTrustLevel(
        /* [out] */ __RPC__out TrustLevel *trustLevel) = 0;
};

Notice how this new interface is based on the `IUnknown` interface, which shows that the WinRT is indeed a logical evolution of COM. As such, memory management is carried out through reference counting with the (inherited) `AddRef` and `Release` functions. Luckily, all this is taken care of for managed code developers by the CLR when it obtains a WinRT object instance. On top of the `IUnknown` functions, the `IInspectable` interface also adds a `GetRuntimeClassName` function to obtain the class name for the object, providing inspection capabilities. You can compare this a bit to the `GetType` method on `System.Object` in managed code. The other two members of `IInspectable` are beyond the scope of this book.

When you are using a WinRT object from managed code languages like C# and Visual Basic, they look like regular objects. Under the hood, the CLR takes care of providing the necessary wrappers around those objects, exposing them in a natural way. This is the role of language projections, which are central to the developer experience for users of the WinRT, no matter what programming language they’re using. For example, you can assign the `CameraUI` object to a `System.Object` typed variable even though the object isn’t implemented in managed code. This is just one of the illusions created by the CLR’s language projection, making the WinRT and CLR type systems line up in a natural manner. We look at more language projection features in the next section.

#### Language Projections

One reason why the WinRT was invented was to enable development of Windows Store applications from many different popular languages, including C# and Visual Basic, but also JavaScript and C++. To make this possible, a key design goal was to make the Windows APIs look and feel familiar to each developer audience. This is where the language projections fit in.

Traditionally, using Windows APIs has been vastly different for the various runtimes and languages used to build applications. For C and C++ developers, it was usually a matter of including header files with function definitions and COM interfaces. Managed code developers either had to wait for wrappers to those native APIs or had to craft such error-prone interop layers themselves using P/Invoke and COM interop. Finally, JavaScript developers never really had access to rich capabilities offered by the operating system, so they really couldn’t apply their development skills to writing great Windows applications.

To demonstrate the role of projections, the following code shows how to access the webcam from JavaScript:

[Click here to view code image](#part0076_split_004.html_p1655pro01)

function takePictureAsync()
{
    var cameraUI = new Windows.Media.Capture.CameraCaptureUI();
    cameraUI.photoSettings.allowCropping = true;
    cameraUI.photoSettings.croppedAspectRatio = { width: 4, height: 3 };
    cameraUI.photoSettings.format = Windows.Media.Capture
                                           .CameraCaptureUIPhotoFormat.png;

    cameraUI.captureFileAsync(Windows.Media.Capture.CameraCaptureUIMode.photo)
            .then(function (file) {
                // Process the file here
            });
}

[Figure 32.13](#part0042.html_ch32fig13) shows the developer experience when writing this code in a JavaScript-based Windows Store application project, illustrating browsing the WinRT APIs through IntelliSense.

![Image](images/00823.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.13 Leveraging the WinRT in JavaScript.

Notice a difference with the C# code, though. First of all, names of members on objects start with a lowercase letter, such as `captureFileAsync` rather than `CaptureFileAsync`. This is just one of the many things the language projection for JavaScript does: It makes the WinRT members’ look and feel conform to typical naming patterns in that language. Another difference that shows here is the way asynchronous operations are exposed to JavaScript developers. Even though the `CaptureFileAsync` method returns an `IAsyncOperation<StorageFile>` object, the JavaScript project turns it into a promise object. To process the result of the asynchronous operation through a promise, the `then` function is used, as shown in the sample.

* * *

Note: Asynchronous Programming

The design of the WinRT focused a lot on making sure that developers of Windows Store applications follow the path of success, making fast and fluid applications that provide great user experiences. One technique used to achieve this goal is the big bet on asynchronous programming all around the WinRT APIs. Any operation that can take longer than a few tens of milliseconds has to be carried out asynchronously. Because there’s no synchronous variant of the API available, developers are gently guided in the right direction of building responsive applications.

As managed code developers using C# or Visual Basic, we’re in the comfort seat of dealing with asynchronous programming thanks to the `await` expressions introduced as part of .NET 4.5\. As you have seen before, those work perfectly fine against the WinRT APIs. In the world of C++ and JavaScript, we still need manual callback plumbing to deal with asynchronous APIs, as shown in the JavaScript example using the `then` function. I wouldn’t be surprised if those languages eventually get better ways to write asynchronous code.

* * *

Besides naming patterns and exposure of asynchronous programming patterns, the projections take care of quite a few other mappings between the underlying WinRT APIs and the languages used on top.

In the case of managed code, the CLR provides projections for commonly used types. The CLR’s projections are built on top of the infrastructure for COM interop that has existed for ages but has been extended to support quite a few specific WinRT types. For example, a WinRT string (`HSTRING`) is mapped onto a `System.String`. Similarly, a `Windows.Foundation.Uri` looks like a `System.Uri` to managed code users. More complex types are mapped seamlessly, as well, in particular collection types and interfaces like `IEnumerable<T>`, which corresponds to `IIterable<T>` in WinRT. As a user of the platform, you usually do not have to know anything about those mappings taking place. Things just work!

You might be tempted to think asynchronous operations are also subject to a projection-based mapping. As shown in the webcam example, you can await a WinRT asynchronous method’s outcome, just as you can do with a `Task<T>` returning method in managed code. WinRT uses an `IAsyncOperation<T>` interface to represent a future result. This is a case where the CLR doesn’t provide a mapping, but helper libraries are added to the BCL to make the interop friction free. In particular, awaiting an `IAsyncInfo`-based operation is supported through the mere presence of a `GetAwaiter<T>` extension method in the `System` namespace:

[Click here to view code image](#part0076_split_005.html_p1657pro01)

// Defined in System.Runtime.WindowsRuntime.dll, which is included by default for
// Windows Store application projects.
namespace System
{
    public static class WindowsRuntimeSystemExtensions
    {
        public static TaskAwaiter<T> GetAwaiter<T>(this IAsyncOperation<T> source);
        ...
    }
}

You learned in [Chapter 31](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31), “[Asynchronous Programming](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31),” how the `await` expression compiles into a method-based pattern, so it should be clear that the `GetAwaiter<T>` extension method enables `await` support. Similar extension methods are provided by the BCL for other awaitable types from WinRT (all of which derive from `IAsyncInfo`), including `IAsyncAction`, `IAsyncOperationWithProgress<T>`, and `IAsyncActionWithProgress`. To support cancellation and progress reporting, overloads exist that take in `CancellationToken` objects and `IProgress<T>` objects.

Asynchronous programming is just one place where helper types are provided to make the interop between WinRT and managed code smoother. Another prominent place with such helper types is the I/O space. To map WinRT streams onto `System.IO.Stream` objects, a `WindowsRuntimeStreamExtensions` class with extension methods exists in the `System.IO` namespace. For a thorough explanation of all the mapping types and methods, refer to MSDN.

Besides the handful of manual mappings through easy-to-use extension methods and helper methods, interoperating with WinRT APIs is largely transparent thanks to the projections in the CLR.

### Creating a Windows Runtime Component

Besides consuming the WinRT APIs from managed code, we can also write our own components that can be used from all supported WinRT languages. For example, using C# or Visual Basic, we could write a WinRT component that’s based on managed code and that can get used to build Windows Store applications no matter what language those are written in.

The idea of providing a component-based model to share assets across different applications isn’t anything new. Both classic COM and the CLR have offered this type of componentization. The use of WinRT components is exclusive to Windows Store application projects, though, and benefits from the interop capabilities using language projections and whatnot. For example, you can build a WinRT component in C# and use it from JavaScript, where the component will look and feel familiar.

#### Writing Windows Runtime Components

Writing a WinRT component is quite straightforward, starting from built-in project templates in Visual Studio. [Figure 32.14](#part0042.html_ch32fig14) shows the project template under the Windows Store section in the New Project dialog.

![Image](images/00824.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.14 Creating a Windows Runtime Component project.

Both the WinRT component and Class Library projects produce a library that you can reuse. The difference between both project types is the reach of the resulting library. In particular, a regular class library can be used within a managed code Windows Store application, while a component allows for usage from other WinRT languages such as JavaScript.

Once the project is created, references to the WinRT APIs and the .NET Framework subset for Windows Store applications are included automatically, as shown in [Figure 32.15](#part0042.html_ch32fig15).

![Image](images/00825.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.15 References to Windows and .NET in our component.

In this example, I’ve added the component to an existing Windows Store application project called App7 that’s written using JavaScript. You learn about the cross-language usage of our component in “[Using Windows Runtime Components](#part0042.html_ch32lev2sec8)” section, later in this chapter.

A number of restrictions are put on the public types that are exposed from a Windows Runtime component library. This can be compared to the Common Language Specification (CLS) rules that you have to obey to make a managed code library usable from other managed code languages. However, the Windows Runtime rules are more stringent, and compile-time checking is carried out to detect violations. For example, public classes exposed by the component have to be declared as `sealed`. The `Class1` definition that comes with the component shows this clearly; see [Figure 32.16](#part0042.html_ch32fig16).

![Image](images/00826.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.16 A public sealed class in a WinRT component.

For private types, no such restrictions apply. After all, the goal of a WinRT component is to allow for cross-language utilization (for example, from a JavaScript-based Windows Store application project). As for the `sealed` class restriction, the WinRT doesn’t allow for general-purpose inheritance of classes across different components, hence this restriction.

The public API restrictions of WinRT components are well documented on MSDN. To set the scene, the most important restrictions follow:

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) Parameters, return types, and so on must be WinRT types or be supported through projection mappings. For example, using a primitive type (like `Int32`), a string, or a Uri is fine because the CLR maps those onto WinRT equivalents. However, exposing a `System.Random` object isn’t allowed.

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) Exposed structs can only have public fields with no other members and are meant to be used as simple wrappers for various values that are bundled together in a convenience type.

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) Public classes have to be sealed and cannot be generic. This rules out cross-language inheritance in WinRT and also ensures that all languages can instantiate the type. (For example, JavaScript has no notion of generic types.)

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) You can declare events by using custom delegate types or based on the `EventHandler<T>` convenience type. However, event argument types cannot inherit from non-WinRT types such as the `System.EventArgs` class. For this reason, the generic parameter constraints `T` have been removed in .NET 4.5.

An example of a WinRT class definition is shown here. It contains one violation against the rules just mentioned. Can you spot which member is not valid?

[Click here to view code image](#part0076_split_006.html_p1660pro01)

using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;
using System.Reflection;

namespace MyFirstWindowsRuntimeComponent
{
    public sealed class Class1
    {
        public string GetGreeting(string name)
        {
            return string.Format("Hello, {0}!", name);
        }

        public Random Random
        {
            get { return new Random(); }
        }

        public static IEnumerable<string> GetTypeNames()
        {
            var systemRuntime = typeof(int).GetType().GetTypeInfo().Assembly;

            return (from t in systemRuntime.ExportedTypes
                    where t.Name.StartsWith("System")
                    select t.Name);
        }

        public event EventHandler<int> Tick;

        public void OnTick(int x)
        {
            var tick = Tick;
            if (tick != null)
                tick(this, x);
        }
    }
}

The problem is in the `Random` property, which exposes a type that is not a valid WinRT type. [Figure 32.17](#part0042.html_ch32fig17) shows the compilation error that results for this violation.

![Image](images/00827.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.17 Invalid WinRT type definition.

Notice the supported members and their implementations, though. For example, the innards of the `GetGreeting` and `GetTypeNames` methods use functionality that’s defined in the BCL, even though those types may not be WinRT based. What goes on inside the component doesn’t matter, so long as the public API surface is valid for use through the WinRT.

* * *

Note: Exposing Asynchronous Methods

Asynchronous methods, declared using the `async` modifier in C#, have to return either `void`, `Task`, or `Task<T>`. You saw this in much detail in [Chapter 31](#part0041_split_000.html_ch31). However, what about exposing such methods in a WinRT component? Because both `Task` and `Task<T>` are not WinRT types and do not have any built-in CLR projection support, this is not possible in a direct manner.

However, there’s a solution for this using the `AsAsyncAction` and `AsAsyncOperation` extension methods that are available in the `System` namespace. Those methods convert a `Task` or `Task<T>` object in the corresponding `IAsyncInfo`-based types for use in WinRT. To expose an asynchronous method, you can mark the method as private and put a public method next to it, using `IAsyncAction` or `IAsyncOperation<T>` as the return type, and using those extension methods to bridge with the private implementation.

* * *

#### Building Windows Runtime Components

After removing the `Random` property, we can compile our component, resulting in a WINMD file, as shown in [Figure 32.18](#part0042.html_ch32fig18).

![Image](images/00828.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.18 Our WinRT component’s WINMD file.

Just like all the Windows APIs for Windows Store applications are described in a Windows Metadata (WINMD) file, our own component is turned into such a file. Under the hood, the compilation process consists of two steps. First, the C# compiler kicks in to compile our code. But instead of writing the result to a .dll file, it emits a .winmdobj file by running with the `/t:winmdobj` flag. Next, the WinMdExp.exe tool from the Windows SDK is called to turn the .winmdobj file into a .winmd file. During this phase, checking for WinRT compliance is carried out, as you saw earlier.

The resulting .winmd file uses the Windows Metadata format, which is largely based on the .NET assembly file format. [Figure 32.19](#part0042.html_ch32fig19) shows our component in ILDASM.

![Image](images/00829.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.19 Inspecting our WinRT component in ILDASM.

You might find a few things surprising when looking at WinRT components through ILDASM. First, notice how there’s much more than just our own class definition. In particular, two interface types were added to describe the public API surface of our type. One interface describes the static members while another describes the per-instance members. Also observe how the `GetTypeNames` method on the static interface `IClass1Static` returns an `IIterable<string>` WinRT type, even though we were able to write it using an `IEnumerable<string>` in C#. As a result, the exposed APIs only contain WinRT types, which is one of the interop requirements.

What’s visible to other languages through the WinRT is the `Class1` type, highlighted in [Figure 32.19](#part0042.html_ch32fig19). This class implements the autogenerated `IClass1Class` interface for instance members but also contains a custom attribute of type `Windows.Foundation.Metadata.StaticAttribute` to describe the static members. Furthermore, the class is declared as activatable using a custom attribute, allowing usage from WinRT languages (much like the activation sequence for the camera APIs, discussed before).

Upon inspection of the `Class1` members, we can see all of those are empty. This is shown in [Figure 32.20](#part0042.html_ch32fig20) and is similar to what we saw during our exploration of the Windows APIs themselves. As far as the WinRT is concerned, the .winmd file merely acts as a metadata container describing the public APIs.

![Image](images/00830.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.20 Our WinRT class doesn’t contain IL code.

So, where does the (managed) code live for our component? Rather than being compiled into a separate file that requires registration on the system, the IL code gets emitted into the same .winmd file, but in a different class. This is what the `<CLR>Class1` class is for, as highlighted in [Figure 32.21](#part0042.html_ch32fig21).

![Image](images/00831.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.21 The hidden implementation of our class.

Notice that this (private) class isn’t marked with the `windowsruntime` flag, in contrast to the publicly exposed class shown in [Figure 32.19](#part0042.html_ch32fig19). Just by looking at the method names, it’s clear there should be some code here. For example, our LINQ query for `GetTypeNames` resulted in two anonymous methods for the where and select clauses. Just to convince you that those methods do indeed contain IL code, see [Figure 32.22](#part0042.html_ch32fig22).

![Image](images/00832.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.22 IL code in the class implementation.

Basically, the .winmd file for our managed code WinRT component has a split personality. On one side, it exposes itself as a WinRT component using a public type that’s declared with the `windowsruntime` flag. On the other side, it contains IL code that can be executed by the CLR upon activation of the class type.

#### Using Windows Runtime Components

Using our WinRT component is quite straightforward, simply by adding a cross-project reference to our solution. For example, when we want to build our Windows Store application’s user interface using JavaScript and HTML5, but using managed code for the business logic and data access layers, we can use a WinRT component to bridge the two worlds. This is shown in [Figure 32.23](#part0042.html_ch32fig23).

![Image](images/00833.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.23 Referencing our WinRT component project.

Once we add a cross-project reference, the IntelliSense in the JavaScript project lights up and knows about our public types and their members, as shown in [Figure 32.24](#part0042.html_ch32fig24). This great developer experience is made possible thanks to the rich metadata description of our WinRT component in the .winmd file.

![Image](images/00834.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.24 IntelliSense in JavaScript.

One thing we can do is to create an instance of our class, simply by using the `new` keyword in JavaScript. When we explore the instance members, we can see that the projections took care of presenting the API in a style familiar to JavaScript developers. For example, the `GetGreeting` method is exposed with camel-casing syntax to become `getGreeting` instead. Also, the use of events turns into an `addEventListener` and `removeEventListener` pair of functions, which are the typical way of dealing with events in JavaScript. [Figure 32.25](#part0042.html_ch32fig25) shows those members as they show up in IntelliSense.

![Image](images/00835.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.25 Events as seen from JavaScript.

To show the interoperability between the JavaScript-based Windows Store application and our managed code WinRT component in action, we can run the application under the debugger. The interaction with the event clearly shows how a `Number` value in JavaScript is sent to our WinRT component and comes back out in the event handler. This is shown in [Figure 32.26](#part0042.html_ch32fig26).

![Image](images/00836.jpeg)

FIGURE 32.26 Handling a cross-language event in JavaScript.

* * *

Note: Debugging WinRT Components

To debug a WinRT component, you can simply use Visual Studio. When the component is used from a JavaScript project, the project’s configuration settings can be tweaked to enable stepping through managed code. In [Figure 32.26](#part0042.html_ch32fig26), this setting is disabled, showing a debugging session with breakpoints in the JavaScript code of the application.

* * *

### Overview of the Windows Runtime APIs

A thorough exploration of the WinRT APIs is beyond the scope of this book. Nonetheless, we give a quick overview of the most important namespaces and some essential types:

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) `Windows.ApplicationModel` contains various types to deal with the application model for Windows Store applications. This includes the `CoreApplication` type that represents the running application and can be used to control its life cycle, for example to handle suspend and resume operations. Other aspects of this namespace deal with data transfer across applications, search functionality, and so on.

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) `Windows.Data` provides APIs to use data in different formats, including HTML, JSON, and XML. Those APIs provide functionality to parse data, encode and decode strings, and navigate data structures such as the XML DOM.

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) `Windows.Devices` provides access to a wide range of hardware such as the GPS (through the `Geolocator` type), a number of sensors (accelerometer, compass, gyro, light sensor, orientation sensor), printers, input devices, and so on. It also contains APIs to interact with Short Message Service (SMS) capabilities.

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) `Windows.Foundation` contains core interfaces and types used to represent collections, asynchronous operations, and so on. Some of those types are directly mapped onto CLR equivalents. For example, the `IIterable<T>` type corresponds to `IEnumerable<T>`, and various other collection interfaces have direct mappings onto BCL types.

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) `Windows.Graphics` exposes APIs for both onscreen rendering and printer interactions. Functionality includes bitmap encoding and decoding, APIs to detect screen orientation changes and a wide range of printing configuration settings (stapling, duplex, collation, and so forth).

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) `Windows.Media` is used to access various multimedia capabilities (including webcams), transfer media to other devices (based on Play To technology), manage playlists, and much more.

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) `Windows.Networking` contains a whole range of modern APIs to deal with popular networking protocols based on TCP and UDP. It also includes first-class support for HTTP-based web sockets. The namespace also includes background transfer for downloads and uploads with pause and resume capabilities, various mobile broadband network APIs, near-field communication, push notifications from online and cloud services, and data plan APIs to analyze and reduce bandwidth usage.

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) `Windows.Security` supports authentication using a variety of services, including Microsoft Account, OAuth, and OpenID. It also provides credential management APIs to securely maintain password vaults and prompt user credentials through safe user interfaces. Finally, rich cryptography APIs are provided, supporting symmetric and asymmetric encryption as well as hashing.

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) `Windows.Storage` can be thought of as the WinRT’s counterpart for `System.IO` in the BCL. It has notions of streams and data readers and writers and provides isolated file system access operations through `StorageFile` and `StorageFolder` objects. In addition, it provides for per-application data storage, compression functionality, file picker dialogs, and search operations.

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) `Windows.System` is a collection of slightly more low-level APIs to deal with threading using the WinRT’s `ThreadPool` class. Besides threading, it also provides access to the lock screen, user profile information, and launchers to start applications.

![Image](images/00008.jpeg) `Windows.UI` contains the Windows XAML APIs, including a bunch of modern UI controls, data-binding capabilities, UI automation, and much more that you expect from modern UI frameworks. If you have used XAML before in WPF, Silverlight, or Windows Phone, you’ll find those APIs very familiar.

For an in-depth exploration of those APIs, refer to the MSDN documentation. However, because all of these are based on object-oriented design principles, it should be really easy to use the WinRT APIs based on your C# and .NET knowledge.

### Summary

When building Windows Store applications using managed code languages like C# and Visual Basic, you’ll feel right at home thanks to the interoperability provided by the WinRT. For the first time in the long history of .NET, the rich capabilities of the operating system are readily available to managed code. Moreover, existing knowledge of object-oriented concepts, asynchronous programming, and so on carries over directly to the new world of Windows Store application development.

This chapter introduced you to the underpinnings of the WinRT, its metadata file format, and the creation of WinRT components. You also saw the various APIs that are available. For a more thorough exploration of Windows Store application development, refer to the MSDN documentation and various other books on the subject.
